title: Very neat and the autocap is brilliant
text:
First a preamble ..... I'm used to using larger format cameras and sometimes I think that I may expect too much from m4/3 although I was an early adopter. I have 5 other m4/3 lenses.

Well the lens is impressive at first sight.
It's well made , a joy to operate and positively tiny making my E-M10 into a very neat package.
Of course there are compromises on image quality given the size but , stopped down and focused manually , it does well enough with a surprisingly nice soft bokeh.

And manual focus is the thing.
At all focal lengths but especially at 42mm there appears to be a focus shift which means that the plane in focus is very slightly further than the location covered by the AF box. This makes the image softer than it should be.
The rule is Single AF + a manual tweak.

Even at wide open I can see this shift ( perhaps as little as 1/8 inch on a "macro" shot ) on a mid distance subject so it falls outside my understanding of " focus shift"
I'm now on my second lens and just hope that a firmware fix can be found to accommodate this characteristic.
Perhaps I've been unlucky and found two bad lenses.

LATER EDIT

Following Olympus's firmware fix for the EM10 this lens has sharpened up..
It seems that part of my problem may have been shutter shake and in the bright contrasty light of Florida the lens performs well stopped down to F11 where theory suggest that it should get softer.
My opinion of the lens has risen while my opinion of my camera has reduced.
As a small package for travel it's pretty good although not the ultimate travel lens.

title: Good piece of hardware, but usability could improve
text:
I bought this for increased productivity with the HP TouchPad. It has certainly helped. So let me break it down for you:

PRO

2. Compact design. Barely 2 cm wider than the TouchPad. Slim.
3. Easy to use and pair with the TouchPad. Two taps and you're ready!

CONS
1. Special characters are not available. When writing in Spanish I always have to use the on-screen keyboard.
2. Poor adaptation of the on-screen keyboard. Whenever you hit CAPS LOCK, it is treated as a continuous SHIFT hold. Any backspace (DELETE) you hit will delete the whole word. Also, CAPS LOCK is supposed to work for LETTERS ONLY, not numeric or special characters. It is not the case with this keyboard, as CAPS LOCK translates as an on-screen keyboard continous SHIFT hold.
3. Inconsistent performance in different applications. Shortcuts such as CONTROL + V seem to work in some text boxes, but not in others.
4. Poor adaptation of an average PC keyboard. Changing windows, scrolling, and other tasks you might be used to do in PC/laptop keyboards are not present here. One is expected to still use the touch screen for many common actions.
5. Not enough documentation is included in the package.

I would only recommend this keyboard if you intent on keeping HP webOS. It certainly fits it very well. If you are going Android and don't mind for third party hardware, I would recommend considering other options.

title: Functionally great, but didn't last
text:
I've had these headphones for almost 2 years now, and I'm now having to replace them. The usb power cord has stopped powering my headphones unless the cord is pulled at a ridiculous angle, and the power seems to be drained very quickly, making them essentially corded headphones with all the drawbacks of a wireless receiver.

Pros:
- Wireless! Make a run to the kitchen without missing a thing or having to pause your music.
- Very comfortable. I have a very large head and these were snug but fit my ears well and could be worn for hours at a time.
- Very satisfied with the audio and microphone quality. I'm no audiophile but it was satisfactory for me.
- Being able to adjust the actual computer volume from the headset was a huge plus. Customizable buttons also allowed me to walk around the house and still chime in on voice chat.

Cons:
- Huge pain to turn on and off. The power button is recessed into the headset, has very little movement, and you have to hold it down for a seemingly random amount of time in order to get it to make a connection. Turning them off was even worse. This is compounded by the fact that the headset will turn itself off automatically if it doesn't receive any audio for a time. I felt like I've spent far too much time over these two years fiddling with the power button. Why not just use a switch?!
- Power cord is frustrating to connect. The headphones use a usb-micro-b connection to connect to power. There are many connectors that would have been a much better choice than this. There is 0 chance of plugging in the cord to the headphones without taking them off. I find this annoying since you are also expected to charge the headphones is when the computer is turned on. Eventually I just hooked up the headphones to their own usb charger plugged into the wall, but what a pain.
- Sometimes the connection will just cut out and the headphones will attempt to reconnect for the next 5 seconds. This would happen if there was too much interference (like standing in front of the microwave, very understandable), but it would also happen if the power to the headphones was disconnected or reconnected. When my power cord connection began to fail, this would happen all the time, usually in the middle of a game where I can't stop to inspect the state of the cord.
- Sometimes the headphones would get into a state where the volume knob and buttons just didn't work. Not sure why. Turning the headphones off and on again would fix this, but annoying to deal with.
- Sometimes when the headphones were in stereo mode and the application thought I was in 7.1 mode, I would only get audio in my right ear. Switching to 7.1 would fix this, but I don't understand why that would be happening in the first place
- Minor gripe: The headphones are a bit heavy (understandably because of batteries) which meant that if you looked down they would easily slide off your head. This made doing tasks around the house difficult, kind of defeating the purpose.

I'm giving these headphones 3 stars instead of 2 because I got a year and a half of good service out of them. However, I wouldn't recommend these to a friend since the price tag is steep for a product that isn't as polished and stable as it should be. The only other headphones I've spent over $100 on were Audio Technica ATH-A500s which I bought about a decade ago, and I'm wearing them as I write this now. Headphones, especially pricey ones should be expected to last more than 1.5 years. In all, the benefit of wireless listening wasn't worth the aggravation it caused me. I'm going back to corded headphones for now.

title: Not the same for Shure
text:
I've been blessed (or cursed) with ears that detect subtle differences in audio quality, so I have always considered the higher-end Shure Earphones to be the cream of the crop, vs. Sennheiser and other "solid" providers. My beef with Shure earphones has been over durability, as I have replaced three pair due to frayed connectors. Hopefully the newer "modular" style from Shure will be more durable and at least will be less expensive to repair (all of the older SE's were one piece construction).

I own an older pair of E4's, a pair of 535's, and recently purchased the SE 425-V. I use the E4's for working out/running and the 535's for travel and personal listening. I also have a set of Grado PS1000 Professional Headphones for sound editing and mixing. (Shure also sells headphones now - but they are garbage. It's simply a rebranded headphone stamped with the Shure name and sold at a price point to complete with the even trashier Bose headphone line. It's sad to see Shure tarnishing its rich pro-audio history by trying to be a "me too" in the headphone market).

I've performed a side by side comparison of the old E4's, the SE 535's, and the new SE-425-V. Using the same equipment and file formats (AU-PCM, FLAC, & MP3). Performance of all 3 was fairly relative across the various formats. (AU-PCM provides the truest reproduction). The SE-425-V is inferior to the old E4's IMO. Highs are a bit grainy at low volumes and turn grungy at louder volumes. In the mids (btw 2-6kHz), the SE425 sound is hollow. They perform a bit better in the low ranges with a warm and sturdy sound, but still sounds a bit thicker at lower volumes than the E4's.

My order of preference are the 535's (although I still favor the old E5's), the E4's, and lastly the SE-425V. The story seems to be that Shure is addressing the durability issue, but I am beginning to wonder if the company is lowering its standards in the development and production of micro drivers in the earphones. The newer versions may test out technically sound, but the test is in the perception of the human ear.

As a long-time user of Shure pro-audio equipment, I have to say I am disappointed in the direction of the earphone line, and in the future will open up my ears to other options out there. The SE425-V is solid, but not at the Shure price point.

title: Router distant good, LINKSYS SUPPORT BAD
text:
Just purchased Linksys through the company site. Of course, setting it up starts the fun. Hooked up easily, replaced my old Linksys WRT54Gv5 with DD-WRT. I had hesitancy getting this since I have Insteon operating lights as well as my garage. I also have 12 Foscam cameras locked with static addresses (awesome program, dd-wrt is...). Well, here's where the problems come. Switching 12 cameras became a nightmare, spent over 5 hours now and 3 were fairly straightforward and port forwarded through to my smartphone, LiveCams on my iphone. Of course, 2 of them continue to disappear when I disconnect them from the router and "invisible" to the new router. Also, haven't made any of the static since I am not as familiar with the firmware as I am with dd-wrt.

Well, here's where the one star comes. I just got done wasting 45 minutes of my night calling the lovely customer service. I swear the initial person, who has no router knowledge, must be trained to just charge, charge, charge. Well, I can't be helped with cascading the modems (learned more waiting for her to get someone to help... never happened, "unavailable") nor can I get help with the Foscam cameras (again because it is not their product) unless I pay them or another company. Please... can a company be any more greedy? Well, this router is going right back where it came. I prefer to pay a company that will support its product, especially if I pay top dollar for it.

Again, router too hard to get to work for me (wanted to get my speed up to the 50 Mbps promised by COX) but the setup too cumbersome as well as the customer service was beyond BAD. If this is Belkin's idea of support, your great product (rephrase POWERfUL product) will go down in flames. One is being sent back to you because your support is nonexistent.

Update: Of course after working on the cameras further, rebooting it 3 more times, the router finally saw the camera. I moved my rating up from one star (HORRIBLE CUSTOMER SUPPORT) up to 3 stars since the router is really powerful and the firmware is usable until dd-wrt has a stable version available.

So in summary: I would give the router 5 stars. It is a great, top dollar router.

I would again give customer service 1 star. Felt like they were just keeping me on the line, then trying to make an excuse to not help me since a tech was not available. "No, can't help with cascading since the other router isn't under warranty", "No, can't help with any of your Foscam cameras since they are not our products", UNLESS you'd like to pay extra money.

Hence, 3 stars is my averaged rating.

title: Just wasn't what I expected, went with Nexus 7
text:
I don't have much experience with tablets since the Ipad2 (which I do use a LOT) and did a bunch of research via reviews/comments when searching for one for my moms birthday. I went with the Kindle Fire HD 7" since I already love Amazon and thought the Prime integration would be worth it and that it would be the easiest to use for my Mom. Here's a quick rundown of how I/we feel post-purchase:

1. For the fist time in my history of shopping on Amazon, the Prime + Overnight didn't work out and it arrived a day late. Very surprising especially since I'm in LA and it wasn't cutting the even deadline remotely close) Ontrac is more to blame I'm sure, but still, it missed the birthday.

2. I paid for the ads not to be shown - didn't want my mom thinking this was some gimmick. There were no ads, but you also can't change the home/lock screen background. I wanted a picture of the family and you simply can not do it, that was a huge shock to me and probably influenced the rest of my/moms experience.

3. The over-all navigation and experience just isn't anywhere near as simple and straight-forward as the old Ipad2, the only buttons on the device are hard to find/feel and it was confusing my mom. The device would lock up for a split second or fall back to the home screen for no reason sometimes, and it only added to the confusion. It was also difficult to get my moms gmail account synced up with calender/contacts... by this time I simply couldn't let my mom keep using this and knew I made a mistake.

The Nexus 7, after only 10 minutes, already feels a lot better in ALL of these regards, and includes a charger as well (not an extra 20 bucks) Everything is easy to customize, Gmail perfectly syncs of course, and it has GPS to boot in WiFi only model. I LOVE Amazon and there is no equal to them for shopping, and apparently the Kindle (non color) is also the very best, but they really can't compete in any way with the Kindle HD, it just doesn't touch the Nexus or Ipad experience. I hope that changes but I highly recommend the Nexus or Ipad.

title: Ideal for nearly Everyone
text:
Bringing back the stylus of old resitive touchscreen technology has come with ridicule, but critics could not be more wrong. Combining technology of old with todays technological advancements offers a new valuable feature set that sets this tablet apart from the mainstream. With so many tablets offering virtually the same real world performace and feature set, when one comes out with a unique feature set it makes the decision of which to purchase much easier. As long as you know what that feature set has to offer you.

PROS:
The processor and memory allows you to breeze through menus and execute any operation to include any app currently available on the market without a hiccup. The screen is bright and clear with no notable differences side by side with my daughter's iPad Mini. Battery life is on par of all the others easily getting through a heavy days work without charge. However, these are not the features that should draw you toward this tablet as many have these same bragging rights at a smaller price. The precise control of the Wacom's 'S' pen technology is its defining feature. You can truly use this to replace pen and paper when taking notes during a lecture or meeting. Try the same thing with your finger or fat tipped touch capacitive stylus and you will quickly be back to a pen and paper after your notes end up looking worst than a 5 year old writing with a crayon. Refining pictures on photoshop is quicker than on a computer with a mouse and again offers the precision unmatched by any other (non-penabled) tablets. The same thing obviously holds true for artists or doodlers when using applications like Sketchbook plus adding the utility of pressure sensitivity for accurate shading without having to contstantly adjust through the menu. In addition to the 'S' pen, the IR sensor is more useful than I had imagined. I easily added all my TVs, Bluray players, projector, receivers organized by room even my 15 year old Aiwa system. Granted the app could be a little better by adding easier access to more controls for each device but does well enough to bypass buying a $100+ Logitech remote.

CONS:
Samsung fanatics ardently back the use of plastic to encase their premium devices, but the look and feel simply does not match the quality exuded by Apple products or Asus's infinity tablets. Although I would love for Samsung to take note and offer a premium casing to match the rest of the device, adding a quality case easily remedies this minor complaint.

OVERALL:
Anyone who wants to use a tablet for everything from an powerful productivity tool at work or school to taking full advantage of art and photo apps should look no further than this or possibly a Note 10.1. Personally, I have found the 8.0 tablet as easily useful as 10 inchers with better form factor to use on the go, but those who plan on using it for more for graphical design might want the extra real estate at the cost of resolution. If you have no interest in jotting notes, utilizing photo or art apps then save money and get a Nexus 7 or one of the other countless counterparts with similar features, otherwise look no further as the price of Note 8.0 is easily justified

If you need bluetooth for your phone or other device, this is not the machine for you.

It is a speedy little machine. I installed Office Pro 2010 on it and have no problems with its operation. I have also loaded Any Video Converter and Photoshop. It does a decent job of processing video and images. It's not the greatest at it but I didn't purchase it to process video. This is really a business machine. I crunch numbers and run Access DB.

What has put me off has been the operation of the machine. I built my 1st PC in 1985. I use key commands as much as I use the mouse or trackpad. This has been my biggest problem with this laptop. For example, I rarely exit apps by clicking on the "X" in the upper right of the open window (as 95% of others do). I use the ALT + F4 to kill open apps. Much to my dismay I have found I must hold the FN + ALT + F4 keys. I also use the native Function keys as windows has set them for years. With this laptop I must hold down the FN key and then press the F key I want. Otherwise it turns on/off the mic, the WIFI, etc. I have not looked in the BIOS to see if this can be reset to a default setting. Maybe someone out knows and can let me know.

I do like the keyboard and find it easy to type on and use. However I am still trying to adjust to the trackpad. I initially liked the idea of a track pad that took advantage of the Apple type press mechanism to launch actions. However I am finding my wrist getting sore with all the pressing. Fortunately Lenovo retained the tap/double tap with your finger to launch. I also like the 2 finger press to right click but it doesn't always work for me. I have resorted to using the bottom edge of the trackpad with my thumb to activate the right click.

Overall this is a good laptop but needs usability rethinking by Lenovo... or maybe I'm just geeking to old ;^)

Anyway, that's my $0.02 worth. Good luck.

title: Average Case with Nostalgic Good Looks
text:
This case reminds me of the genuine leather case I (still!) have on my 1950s SLR—a hand-me-down from Dad while I was studying photography in college. It also operates the same way, with a fall-away (or snap-off) top/front so the camera can stay in the half-case. With the titanium Sony A6000 seated inside it almost looks the same, too, which I appreciate for nostalgic reasons. This is a nice-looking, average case around which you can access almost all camera features (obviously not the battery/card compartment), and the NFC works well through the right side.

The reason this case is so affordable: it's made of bicast leather, which is actually a leather by-product. The top coating is plastic, and it's likely to crack and peel away from the split leather beneath. I shoot professionally, and this camera will be my "pocket" standby for the foreseeable future, so I intend to rough this case up! I don't expect this case to be attractive or around very long with heavy use. It will be my temporary case while I find a genuine leather one I like.

Beware: the strap that comes with this case is cheap, and the backside has little grip. You can't see the thin, slippery nylon ends of the strap in any of the product images, but they need readjustment (come loose) way too easily. When it's on my shoulder, I can't push the camera "through"/off the strap, even with maximum force. But while it's resting or around my neck it loosens/adjusts with minimal use/movement, so I'll never trust it. (The Sony strap that comes standard with the camera is far sturdier and more trustworthy, and the backside has more grip.) Also, the strap was coiled stuck to itself in some areas, almost as if with adhesive, and had to be forced apart in those areas to unfurl. It has a clear crease mark where it was folded in half, and it's retaining that folded point. The cheap strap is a bummer, because the case alone is decent (4 of 5 stars), and it would have been nice to use them together. No way though.

Sold by Mega West and fulfilled by Amazon, this was shipped immediately. Though I didn't request it, thanks for the 24-hour turnaround, Amazon! Unlike another reviewer, the case and "velvet" bag I received both have embossed logos on them. I've uploaded an image.

This is a decent choice for someone who loves the nostalgic look of the old classic film cameras in their rugged leather cases, but probably won't have their camera out in the elements or use it very often (not quite prosumer level). I'd expect to pay no more than $19.99 if I saw this hanging on a rack in any store. Don't trust that strap!

title: Rural town with hills impeding, and it works GREAT!
text:
Many of our neighbors have huge antennas on their rooftops, so we assumed that we'd probably need a similar setup to get any channels where we live. Our house is surrounded by several large hills that impede the local antenna pathways to various degrees, so we really had doubts that any indoor antenna would be useful.

Like other reviewers, I was unimpressed with the lightweight, seemingly flimsy quality of this antenna, as it seems to be not much more than a well-laminated piece of paper with coax attached. It seems sturdy, but just not beefy enough to gather up significant reception, especially without "rabbit ears" or equivalent. But we plugged it in, did a quick channel scan and some minor adjustments, and TADA! Broadcast TV!! For some reason it picked up some channels better when it wasn't flat mounted to the wall, so we found the most success rigging it up to the top of a floor lamp.

8/27 UPDATE: The described setup provided 18 channels including The Big 3, but we really wanted PBS and FOX which weren't working. Got a 30 foot coax extension cable, tucked the antenna up in to the top of an appropriately faced window, and now we get them both w/ associated subchannels! This is truly incredible, as FOX is broadcast from almost 80 miles away. It has been historically difficult to get and maintain a clear signal for FOX from various locations much closer and less impeded than we are here.

We are now getting a total of 22 channels which all come in great in HD (if available). It's a testament to the power of this device that the maps on tvfool show signal strengths appropriate for or requiring attic and rooftop antennas for several channels that we receive perfectly. Some channels we "shouldn't" get at all, yet we do! This handy little unassuming unit really is that good! We are absolutely thrilled with the performance of this antenna. Next step is a major-name DVR, and we'll be good to go.

title: Roamio is Tivo's Best DVR to date
text:
I've been a critic of Tivo in the past three years, due to a range of issues from the performance problems (and incompleteness) of the Tivo Premiere's user interface, which only got slower on the Tivo Premiere Elite (renamed XL4), the extremely crashy apps like Netflix, as well as setup headaches and pricing methodology of the Tivo Mini. Through all of the problems, I've still been a fan. Somewhat beaten up and with no rose-colored glasses, but still a fan.

The Roamio Plus, and the entire Roamio line, says one thing loud and clear: Tivo is back.

Every major complaint I've had about the Tivo Premiere line of DVRs have all been squashed. The faster processor eats the user interface for breakfast. Performing tasks (like Search) that were a pain due to the slow interface are now enjoyable. The new Netflix app hasn't crashed once after dozens of hours of use. All of the most-used menus have finally been switched to HD.

Beyond fixing old problems, they've added new, welcomed features. Recording up to 6 programs at once speaks for itself; very cool. The new RF remote doesn't require line-of-sight to the Tivo box. Streaming to iOS devices is integrated into the Plus and Pro models. (Android support is slated for Q1 2014 at the time of this review.) Finally, they have built-in Wifi. :) And if your kids tend to lose the remote, there is a handy "Find My Remote" button on the face of the Tivo that makes the remote play a tune.

For anyone wondering why they would need a box with 6 tuners, it is because this box is designed to be part of a whole-home solution. You, your spouse and kids can all record your shows comfortably with little risk of recording conflicts. In addition, the extra tuners can be used with the Tivo Mini, allowing your family to watch recordings and live TV on any TV in any room. Those 6 tuners can feed every TV in the house. If you live in a house with a full family and 3 or more TVs, those extra tuners can become amazingly helpful.

All in all, the Roamio Plus is a joy to use, and I am enjoying Tivo once again.

Pros:
- Records SIX programs at once
- FAST.
- RF Remove doesn't require line-of-sight to the box
- Apps (like Netflix) are fast and stable
- MoCA support (ethernet over coax)
- Built-in WiFi (finally!)
- Integrated streaming to iOS devices (Android coming in Q1 2014, they say)
- Power efficient (roughly 21 watts.)

Cons:
- Still missing Amazon Prime Instant (Come on Tivo/Amazon, this is kind of big!)
- Some relatively minor initial bugs still need squashing (but they're actively being fixed)
- Still doesn't serve me eggs and toast in bed.

title: Good value for a decent kit
text:
Let's be honest, this isn't going to be all you ever needed for a lifetime of product photography. It is, however, a good piece of kit for the price and a painless way to find out if product photography interests you. I read the reviews available here and on the web and decided it was worth the risk. This kit exceeded my expectations for a $40 kit.

Lights:
The lights are fixed height and low-powered. I barely keep any space between the fabric of the tent and the lights. This is so I can keep it above the 1/focal length shutter speed recommendation while maintaining ISO 100. Using a timer or remote eliminates camera shake. The lights get very warm after less than 5 minutes. I simply turn off the surge protector they are plugged in to when I am positioning a shot. I will need to upgrade the lights in time, but it's a low cost entry-level kit.

Fabric:
The fabric arrived on rolls, which minimized wrinkling of the material. The white cloth was stained, although easily cleaned. The fabric does not go to the top of the tent. It falls about 1 - 1.5 inches below the top of the tent. I have not noticed any ill effects because of this as I am shooting straight on or slightly down on the subjects. The 4 colors are good for selecting a color that complements the product.

Tent and case:
The case is attached to the tent which helps for setup and tear down. The tent lends nice soft light to the products. The tent is open on the bottom but is built sturdy enough. The case material feels sturdy. The pockets are nice and deep and allow the lights to fit in nicely. I also store a surge protector in the case instead of the tripod. I use a Manfrotto tripod for my DSLR instead of the tripod that comes with the kit. As such, i can't comment on the tripod or its effectiveness.

If you're dead set on professional product photography, you will need better lights. There are other kits that appear better in quality of the tent as well as the lights. They also cost quite a bit more. If you're a part time product photographer or someone who is interested in exploring it, this is a great value. The case is very convenient and keeps things organized. I wish the backdrops could fit in the case, however. The kit isn't horrible, but it isn't great. I would purchase this kit again if I were in the same position.

title: Terrific Value
text:
=====Actual model purchased was S4250 but since specs are identical I am posting my review here as well=====

I happily paid 149.99 for this camera thinking that the specs were too good to be true but it's worth the gamble. WRONG! This is a great camera even at $150 assuming you are coming from a lower resolution point and shoot as I was(Sony DSC-W1 at 5MP and excellent in it's own right). 14MP is amazing for this average joe of a photographer.

Today I went to my local arboretum and took some greenhouse flower and outdoor landscape photos in diminishing afternoon light. All handheld and when I viewed them on my PC at home I was extremely pleased with my results. Very crisp photos with great detail and color saturation even in natural light. As expected I could not focus in these light conditions at maximum focal length but that is the limitations of this type of camera that incidentally does not allow you to zoom or focus manually. Most of the 24x zoom range on this camera should be reserved for outdoor conditions. The image stabilization works very well and you can get away with hand holding it if you're just looking for a useable image otherwise bring the tripod along. It does however have a neat function in SP mode called "Natural" that will expose one image without flash and one with with one press of the shutter. In most cases I was most happy with the no flash images. The flash is intelligent and does a nice job of matching the amount of flash output to the existing natural light. I really like the fact that you must manually pop up the flash so it will not fire unless you want it too.

The user interface is also user friendly if you take some time to familiarize yourself with the user manual which is available on the cd or as a pdf download from Fuji's site. I found this camera's menus much easier to navigate than my Sony DSC-W1's. There are plenty of options for the more demanding user as well as the Auto and Program functions that works surprisingly well for most situations.

So why didn't I give it 5 stars? Two reasons. The first one is that you cannot use this camera for any purpose without removing the lens cap. Since they began putting such large displays on these cameras I would really like the ability to review my photos without taking off the lens cap. The second is the LCD monitor. My Sony has spoiled me. When it was introduced it had one of the largest LCD displays available at the time and is fairly clear even in moderately bright light. I got into the habit of checking each photo after taking it. The S4250/4200's LCD is low resolution for it's size as well as being very difficult to see in anything but indoor lighting conditions. I am not comfortable with having to wait to go indoors or viewing on my PC to check my photo's condition, even though my results were surprisingly acceptable.

As I said earlier this purchase was a gamble. I was researching superzoom cameras for an upcoming trip to Alaska and the price for this feature set seemed like a great bargain and too good not to investigate. I pulled the trigger knowing that I might be disappointed but if so I could return it and continue my search, which is not something I normally do. That said, I am definitely not disappointed in this camera but I will be returning it for these reasons and purchasing the Fuji HS25EXR, which has a brighter LCD and allows me to turn the camera on without removing the lens cap. The CMOS sensor, 2MP extra, longer zoom and manual zoom/focus doesn't hurt either! Hell,it's only money!

NOTE: This review is meant for the more casual and budget conscious photographer and the high rating is meant to reflect that as I feel that is Fuji's target audience. Please do not respond with technical evidence to the contrary as that will only confuse me. Thank you.

title: Bushnell H2O Roof 8x42 Binos
text:
This review is for the Bushnell H2O Roof Binoculars sizes 8x42 and 10x42, both of which I recently purchased. These binoculars are inexpensive but have many of the characteristics of expensive binoculars. They are water and fog-proof, they have BaK-4 prisms, and they have a well-constructed and rugged body. I purchased roofs rather than porros after my Nikon porros lost their collimation. Nikon repaired them for $10 plus shipping (which was very fair), but I did not want to go through that again. Roofs are generally more durable. These binos appear well collimated (I did every test I could find on the internet, including shining the sun through them onto a screen), they can quickly be focused quite sharply, and there is very little color aberration. The 8x42s have remarkably little distortion near the outside of the field of vision; the 10x42s have more, but are still quite acceptable. The eye relief is good, so I can wear these with or without glasses. The rubber eyepiece collars are a little hard, but I purchased Field Optics eyeshields (I have no interest in the company) which both shield outside light from entering from the sides and soften the feel of the binoculars against the eyes. Both binos feel slightly heavy for their size, but are really okay. The straps require some lacing, but if carefully done, are okay too. The case is slightly tight, but acceptable. The front and rear lens covers can be attached, which is great.

The biggest problem with these binos is that they are roof binoculars with only multicoating. They are not fully multicoated nor phase coated. The lens quality is good, but not great. Thus the images are clear and sharp, but not as bright as you might get with a porro of the same class or an expensive roof bino. In good daytime light, this does not matter, but in really overcast light, the view is acceptable, but could be better. Not surprisingly, the 8x42s are brighter than the 10x42s. However, at night, using a tripod, I prefer the 10x42s since they permit better viewing of the moon and the stars. Surprisingly, the focus is so sharp that I can produce pinpoint images of Jupiter without flaring.

Thus we have inexpensive binoculars pretending to be expensive binoculars and doing a pretty good job of deception. The muted brightness is only a problem in poor lighting, but otherwise these binoculars are impressive for their price. I give the 10x42s four stars and the 8x42s four and a half stars.

title: Great! IronKey is now compatible with Windows 8
text:
I reviewed this item previously and gave a negative review. This has changed: IronKey has released an update of the IronKey software for D200 and S200 series, and the 250 series too, I believe. They made a good effort and I have to say that they did pretty darned well. IronKeys are a 5-star secure flash drive at a very reasonable price.

I have been a very loyal fan of IronKey flash drives for years, all of them purchased from Amazon. I run a small professional practice and I must have a way to travel with files, back up all my records and files, and keep it all secure. It is a wonderful bonus to have a password manager that is secure and automatically enters the name and password for web sites. Plus a secure web browser (Foxfire resides on the secure drive) and other very useful features. IronKeys are wonderful. Great security, good functioning with great secure backup, password handling, the works.

But the backup, one of the critical functions, didn't work in Windows 8 or 8.1. Other features were difficult to use if they could be used at all in Win 8. Imation had bought out IronKey; when I asked they responded they were not supporting Win 8 with D200 and S200 series IronKey secure flash drives. Nor did they expect to. That greatly diminished the value. None of the functions were as automatic as they should be and had become sort of cumbersome. That made the several IronKeys I owned relatively useless in terms of the reasons I purchased them. Particularly the secure backup feature. I need that one a lot.

However, a few weeks ago they released an update for the IronKey software of the specific IronKeys I own, in the D250 and S250 series. I downloaded the new software update and ran it, but with each IronKey flash drive the software froze and stayed frozen for hours, until it timed out. I discovered that the contents of the data folders were gone. I ran the recovery file that was also available and it just would not work.

However, I did what has always worked very well with IronKey products: I emailed their support services. I got a response in 24 hours with exact directions. I followed the directions and my drives were restored, with the data intact.

I have used the drives for a day now and ran all the software features. As the directions stated, some features have minor glitches that I am sure just can't be overcome with Windows 8-8.1. But nothing I can't easily cope with.

I should note that in the period between, I tried a number of other flash drives with security software. And some security software that is offered by itself. Kingston Data Traveller, Sandisk Extreme, ADATA dash drive, and several software suites. None of them came close to the convenience and utility of the IronKeys. Not even close. Nor did any of the software I tried.

So Hooray! Once again I have the IronKeys I love, especially the secure backup feature. Works great again. And the password manager that just can't be beat. And their support service remains A-1. Thanks Imation and IronKey. My faith in IronKey products is completely back.

title: Good speakers. Easy to insall. A bit heavy on the wallet, but can be worth it
text:
I have had these speakers for about 2 months now. Overall, I am satisfied with the purchase. As long as they last for a long time, I will not have to change my rating. They are super easy to install. As long as you know your way around your bike, you will not encounter any problems trying to get these mounted. I am new to motorcycles, and I still didn't have any trouble getting them on the bike and working. I chose to wire in a relay to get the speakers to turn on and off with the ignition. Now, I leave the speakers on, and I don't have to worry about switching them off or risk draining my battery. My experience in the electrical department is not that vast, so I did need a little help from the internet, and some time to build up the confidence (about a half an hour once I located it) to tap into a switched wire for the relay.

On to the question that most people want to know about: How is the sound? I would say that it is sufficient. Volume is not a problem. I ride a fairly quiet bike (Triumph America cruiser), so I am not fighting a loud set of pipes. With that said, I would venture to say that they can still handle a loud set of pipes fairly well. The overall quality of the sound is pretty good. I would characterize the sound as similar to the sound you get from a smartphone, but on steroids. You are basically going to be able to hear the same tones that you can while listening to music on your phone. You will be able to hear a slightly lower set of notes (bass), but mainly if the engine is not running. I listen to a lot of rap music, so you know that I like my bass. Even though it is missing while using these speakers, I as totally satisfied with them anyway. If you know anything about speakers, you will understand that there is only so much that a 3 inch speaker out in the open can do.

What really helps these speakers out, and smartphones as well, is to have an equalizer available to tweak the sound a bit. You will really be able to tune the sound to suit your needs/desires. I have an Android device and currently use a music app named PowerAmp to handle this department. Any app with an equalizer will do, but this is the best one I have used (MixZing is my second favorite). I have used a few others, and the sound improvements some how are better with this app. My favorite feature is the lock screen interface with touch controls. This allows to simply press the power button to bring up the music interface and swipe to the next song when needed. This is essentially allows me to keep my eyes where they belong, on the road. Another app that I installed with the speakers was a bluetooth auto-connect. It keeps me from having to navigate menus on the phone to get the phone and speakers connected every time that I get ready to take a ride. My bike is my primary transportation, so this could get old very fast.The bluetooth works flawlessly. I ordered a [[ASIN:B0055PH0XA RAM Mount Universal X-Grip Cell Phone Holder with 1-Inch Ball]] to mount my phone conveniently next to the speakers, so I do not and have not experienced any interference. By the way, this phone mount is awesome. It is easy to use and I do not worry about losing my phone to the pavement at all.

My final thoughts say that these are a good set of speakers. I was actually surprised by the weight. They are kind of heavy. Nothing ridiculous, though. The weight makes the feel like a solid product. The chrome doesn't seem to be too shabby either. They appear to be built to last, at least they outer housing does. The speaker cone itself will probably go long before the rest of the speaker. If they were a bit cheaper, I would say get these without thinking twice. But, because of the price, I would say that you should consider other options possibly. I cannot compare these to any of the other options out there (Lanzar, Pyle, Shark, etc) because I have not used any of them. Some of the other options edge out these in price, but I am sure that these edge out all of the others in convenience. There aren't any amps to worry about finding a place to mount or hardly any wiring that needs to be taken care of. Attach these to the battery, mount the speakers on the handlebars, and get ready to hit the road with your favorite tunes.

Ride Safe!

title: A Fair Review - The Good the Bad and the Ugly
text:
For brevity, I'll call the NSZ-GS7/8's a "GTV"

I want to be "fair", but fair also means there must be good points AND bad points.

If you bought one of these SOLELY for streaming movie and video content, then this box performs very well. I really like the double sided remote. PIP makes it very convenient to switch between the GTV and my Plasma TV ..... Something none of the other "G-BOX" units you find on Amazon and Ebay can do. I use my TIVO for all our "TV viewing", so the GTV works seamlessly with my existing setup. It is the only box I've found that uses a Pass Through HDMI hookup. My Wife doesn't understand all the "technology", so with the GTV and Pass through HDMI, she can still use the TV like normal and not have to constantly move the "input selection" . If the wife is happy, this alone makes it a worth while buy.

It installed without a hitch, and the setup screens did all the work. The Remote is what makes the unit so easy to use, and ..... It uses RF instead of Infrared, so you don't have to aim it to use it. The overall experience is a "look and feel" of quality. You know the feeling you get when you sit in a luxury car versus a 15 year old Pickup truck. This is the same experience. Everything works very smoothly and has no crashes or hiccups... it just works.

Using the GTV, I can stream content from my Amazon Prime account AND YouTube.
While I have a TIVO and a ROKU, neither of them can do BOTH Amazon Prime and YouTube on the same unit.
(One of the main reasons I bought the GTV)

BUT

If you bought one of these thinking it was like your OTHER Android tablets or phone. and (that) you can use all your favorite tablet or phone apps
..... Sorrrrrry, think again..... that part SUCKS

First, about two weeks ago, I bought a NSZ-GS7 - only to find out a week later there was a NSZ-GS8 that came right after I bought it. WHILE I had it, I tried unsuccessfully to side load some of my favorite Android Apps. Every single one produced the infamous "Parsing error", and refused to install. If I go to the Web based www.play.google website and try to install apps that are already installed on my ASUS Prime, virtually ALL of the apps come up as NOT COMPATIBLE. I also have an XFINITY account, but Xfinity's Player app that works on my ASUS is not supported, and will not sideload.
That is an extreme turn off.

The most telling example is:
Explain to me why a GOGGLE device does not support GMAIL?
Doesn't the "G" in Gmail stand for "Google".... What is wrong with this picture?
So I was forced into installing K-9 Mail, which is "non-native"

Yes the Google Play store has a lot of "Android" apps..... but 70% of the ones you can use on your tablet or phone are Incompatible with the Sony Internet Player (GTV). I could go on and on with apps on my ASUS tablet that won't install on the GTV. Basically if it doesn't say "Google TV" in the App's description, it probably won't work. IMHO - Sony has grossly mislead "us" into thinking it's a "real Android" and you can use the "Google Play" market the same way we use it for our phones and tablets.. NOT TRUE, Not even by a 'stretch" . so - THAT lowers my "Star rating"

Anyhow, I took the GSZ-GS7 back (Best Buy) and got my money back..... and Then bought the NSZ-GS8 with Jelly Bean From Amazon because Best Buy didn't have them (yet). I figured that "maybe" some of the drawbacks had been fixed when going from Android 2.3 to 4.2 jellybean. I want to sideload apps, so I thought "maybe" my NSZ-GS7 was defective...
Not So.
It Still can't sideload apps (and) the same 70% incompatibility problem is still there when using the Goggle Play Store.
IF there is a way to sideload apps ( that the Google Play Store doesn't think are compatible), I haven't figured out how to do it.

I also have Xfinity. I can view Xfinity using their app on my Tablet, But Xfinity will not support ANY device that uses an HDMI including the GTV. I won't fault GTV on THIS one, but hey.... this really torks me that I can't stream what I'm PAYing for.

BTW - I never could get the NSZ-GS7 to set up to control my TIVO unit from the GTV Remote.
But, When I got the NSZ-GS8, it set up in just a few minutes. So I think (maybe) the newer unit and firmware "fixed" that issue. I don't remember, but I don't think the TIVO 3 was IN the "supported database".

In all honesty I can't give the NSZ-GS8 a 5 star rating. True, most of the problems revolve around "DRM", and Licensing.
But
"it is what it is"... and I doubt Sony will change their attitude any time soon. They didn't seem to learn their lesson the first time around (Remember VHS versus BETAmax). Sony Lost that one, and very well could lose THIS one too if they persist in having the same "attitude".

I'll keep my NSZ-GS8, but it will be a "love / hate relationship" until I can have what I think I should have.

As far as I'm concerned while the NSZ-GS8 is one of the better units in this "market",
It's still a work in progress

Jim

text: I have been reviewing super zoom camera's for the past 2 months. I had it narrowed down to the Canon SX50, Nikon P510 and the Sony DSC-HX200V. I've always wanted a camera that could zoom in to the moon and show great detail and the Sony does just that. Although the Canon SX50 has a greater zoom (50x) it is lacking with 12mp's. My favorite feature of the Sony is the "defocused background" that will take 2 shots, creating sharp focused detail on the object shooting and blurring out the background creating a beautiful portrait that was previously only possible with a professional DSLR. The Sony is very simple to operate with several "auto modes" that are great for the quick point and shoot for your everyday use. The Video produced is a Stunning 1080/60p which is Crisp and beautiful for playback. I Love the 3D Stills options and  Panorama. It takes phenominal Low light images with incredible clarity and detail without a flash. I would buy this camera again without hesitation. If there were any problems I could easily return it but Love the camera. The down side to this camera is the inability to delete photos from the Memory card with the computer. You have to do all of your photo/video management with the camera functions only. which isn't nice at all. In addition you have to charge your battery while it is in the phone, the is no external battery charger included. The instruction manual is poor to fair at best. Even with the online manual it does a poor job of specific details on how to use the many functions. they are pretty vague..for instance, if you want to use the "defocused background" all of the manuals will tell you what the function does but does not elaborate on how to actually get the function to work correctly. I select that option then aim the camera, half press the shutter button for the very fast auto focus and recognition, then full press of the button. 50% of the time it will take the picture beautifully, the other times it will say "unable to perform specified function at this time" and I have no idea why. I dont know if i am to close or to far away from the object and it does not explain it anywhere how to use this function properly. Overall though the camera is great, you wont find all these options in any other camer. it feels great. Love it

Round 2: I returned the 1st tablet to Amazon, and they replaced it with another one, but the GPS was not working on this one either. Apparently, the problem is with firmware, and Google this week (August 22, 2013) released a fix in the form of a new system update, JSS15Q. The next problem I faced in fixing my tablet was that unlike Apple, Google can take months to roll the updates out to all the tablets. Just triggering settings > check for update reports that the tablet is up to date, when it really isn't. Fortunately, on the Internet I found a method to FORCE the tablet to update the firmware to the latest version. Since Amazon doesn't permit URLs in reviews, I can't tell you where to find it, but if you do a Google search with terms android, force and update, you will find it at the lifehacker website. I won't put the steps to update here, but it is quite simple and worked on the first try for me. My GPS worked and I am happy with the Nexus. So far, I haven't found any other problems with the new Nexus, but I still give it a three star review because Google/Asus should certainly have done enough testing to find out that the GPS didn't work before releasing the tablet. End users should not have to fix their own tablet by going to Google forums and finding out how to do it themselves. So be warned, if you want to buy this tablet, it is a nice one, but be prepared to fix it.

Incidentally, calling Google support didn't help. They could confirm that my GPS wasn't working, and suggested I send it in for warranty repair, but they would not admit there was any problem with the Nexus in general, despite there being hundreds of postings on their forum about the GPS problem. Finally, last week, someone from Google came onto the forum and said they were releasing the update that should fix the GPS, but until then, all was silent. title: Defective Motherboard - worked for 6 hours - Gigabyte Warranty Support will place you in a tailspin until you give up
text:
First off, my review IS NOT about how good the Gigabyte motherboards are...I suspect they are decent quality. I purchased the ga-q77m-d2h board for the balance in price and features.

I have friends that are very happy with their Gigabyte motherboards and they haven't experienced a "problem" board yet. I just happened to receive one of the "duds". However, I do wonder if the Q77 chipset series boards are problematic for Gigabyte because reviews seem to reflect 50% bad. I needed the Q77 chipset for the virtualization features, otherwise I would have gone with a Z77 board.

My frustration was with Gigabyte Warranty support. I'll be as brief as possible, while leaving in important facts that lead me to believe Gigabyte IS NOT INTERESTED IN replacing defective boards and instead they seem to be sticking it to the resellers by suggesting we contact them first. So I have a lot of sympathy for the resellers.

1) Had the board installed, OS installed, everything running just peachy for about 6 hours...that's when the troubles started.

2) When I first booted the system and made a few changes in BIOS, the system suddenly reset...well I didn't want to believe I had a problem so I chalked it up to "user" error and continued.

3) After Windows 8 was installed, every once in a while the display would go black for a second or two. Chalked it up to a Win8 glitch.

4) Was prepping to install Win 2012 Hyper-V server in a different disk and went into BIOS to change the boot disk. BIOS then started acting flaky and displayed a long list of boot profiles (way beyond the normal 2) and then listed the usual "PM - <disk>" entries"...but one entry was strange because it simply listed "harddisk". Well out of curiousity, I selected "harddisk"..that's when the board fell apart, reset and then quit functioning beyond spinning the CPU and System Fans (and constantly resetting, or being hung requiring a power yank).

5) So, now I'm left with a system that no matter what I try will not present display, keyboard, BIOS, Post beeps, etc. No power to the USB ports either. Tested the following, many times over and in many combinations (and probably more that I'm not thinking of):

a) disconnected everything excepting fans and power buttons (USB connections, audio connections, external connections, etc.)
b) pulling memory, trying memory in different slots, trying memory with just one dimm
c) pulled power switch, leds, etc for case and manually selected power jumpers
d) tested the power supply thoroughly

All of these tests led to the same behavior of constant reset cycling, or having to power the system off via the switch, or in some cases by pulling power (or switching off PSU).

6) Went to Gigabyte support page and submitted a web ticket providing all the details of my testing (NOTE: Ticket included my phone number...this is important to realize for later parts of the process).

a) I assumed I would receive an email CCed to my address to reflect my incident (since they asked for an email address)...no such luck.

b) tried to register my account so I could check the status of ticket. Registration failed saying I [already had a registered account under email address]

c) tried to use "forgot password"...error: "account doesn't exist"

7) Called Gigabyte tech support next morning.

a) They could not find my submitted web ticket via phone # or via email address.. And support said my registration likely failed because I entered a period somewhere on the form (let's just forget about the fact that the web page error was "account already exists"). I was then told that the WEB support "team" was not the same team as the PHONE support team...Really??okay, starting to get bad vibes here :-)

b) when I started to re-describe the issues and the testing I applied, I didn't even get a couple of sentences out before I was interrupted and asked who I bought the board from. Once they heard Amazon, they said [your best option is to have Amazon take it back...you have 30 days]. Essentially, let's make this the reseller's problem and easy on you.

8) Through the returned process with Amazon and the reseller I was told I would have to pay shipping back, would have a 20% restocking fee, and if the item was shipped free I would be billed for that shipment as well. So in essence, I might be out $50 for a board that cost me $130. So, back to Gigabyte support I go.

9) Gigabyte support again cannot find any previous contacts with them, despite providing the phone # and email address.Provided phone# and email AGAIN. Suggested tests before they would work with me further on the board RMA:

a) pull the motherboard from the chassis and test (maybe grounding issue). Hmm, PSU was fine, system ran for 6 hours...grounding issue, Really? Okay, I'll bite...

b) pull the CPU and verify no bent pins. I balked at this suggestions since it would be awfully difficult to bend the contact points and/or spring points short of sabotage. Also, why did the system run for 6 hours if pins were "bent".

Despite my concerns they insisted I go through these tests and still wouldn't commit to swapping the board if verification still pointed to the board.

10) Board still failed while out of the case. No "bent" CPU pins, surprise huh?

11) Called Support back:

a) was told they couldn't find my case based on phone# and email address. Now I'm TICKED and told them it was obvious they were giving me the run-around and I didn't not appreciate it.

b) after waiting a few minutes while they "dug" further, they finally found my incident...[phone number had been mistyped in the last digit]...Really?? Mistyped 4 times by me (web ticket) and multiple support people? Come ON!! Now I'm even more irked.

c) Told the tech what about the additional testing and they still acted like they didn't want to replace the board...until I demanded they replace it.

d) Next suggestion was to "register" with their WEB site for an RMA...Yeah, right...register with the web support site, which is a different team and doesn't share info with support...

e) I then asked if the RMA group would send me a new board BEFORE I sent mine back because I didn't want to have to [fight] for my receiving a replacement board after shipping mine back...Was told I would have to talk with "Customer Support" about that process. I called BULL and said [you know what the process is, just give me a straight answer]. All support did was to constantly apologize for my frustration at their incompetence. I gave up, said "never mind" and am now working with Amazon and the reseller to return the motherboard.

Again, might be a great product, but good luck EVER receiving a warranty replacement.

title: New favorite radio
text:
I've had my PL-660 for 4 days, putting it through its paces. Tecsun has really outdone themselves with this receiver. The sensitivity is better than anything I've owned. I have had the Grundig G3 and G5, and the Sangean 909. The other receivers are like toys compared to this Tecsun. I especially like the sync circuit on this radio. It locks both quickly and rock steadily. The selectivity is excellent. It really separates closely crowded stations. Not just on shortwave, but on medium wave and FM too. DXing on the FM band is possible with this radio. I get my favorite DX catch, 90.7 from Berrien Springs, Michigan here in south suburban Chicago easily. Just with the whip antenna. It's obvious to me that Tecsun has set the standard with this receiver. Give this baby a try. You won't be disappointed.
Update July 16, 2013: I checked the merchants and one called Global Comerce Japan is listed as selling this radio for $99,598.00. I'm assuming this is the price in yen, not dollars. Do you people at Amazon pay attention?
Update August 6th, 2013: Checked again and Amazon has removed said merchant. Update August 19th - Global Commerce Japan is back. Now selling for $1031.98 plus $25 shipping. Unbelievable.
Some reviews mention that you can't play the radio and recharge the batteries at the same time. WRONG. The batteries DO charge while the radio plays. The indicator doesn't show this but it is happening. Let your radio play for 24 hours while charging. You'll find the batteries fully charged.
Update: December 16th, 2013. I bought another, this time the silver version.Yes, I'm radio obsessed. My new PL-660 plays at least as well if not better than my old one. The only drawback to this model is lack of up-down buttons but it is by NO MEANS a deal breaker. Just wish it had them.
Update: May 12, 2016. I bought a Sony sw7600gr a couple of weeks ago. I must say Sony is STILL the best. This Tecsun is a close 2nd.

title: Trust the stormchaser, THIS is the one you want!
text:

I have been a media storm chaser for over 15 years now. I've owned a TON of weather radios. From 2005 to 2009, I had switched to using 3 Midland WR300s here at home. They functioned fine, but I was never happy with the reception of the units. I had to purchase external antennas for all of them, which did not improve their reception. When one of them failed, I took it apart to diagnose the problem, and was shocked at what I found. The quality was terrible, even by Chinese standards. It did not take me long to decide it was not worth my time to mess with it. After research, I decided to try the Reecom R-1630. I ordered ONE to try. I was FLOORED when I was able to see the difference in reception side by side with my Midland WR300s. The Reecom is in a whole other class in reception sensitivity. Not only do I now PERFECTLY receive my local NOAA stations, but I also receive NOAA stations from other areas more clearly than my Midland radios receive my LOCAL stations.

Midland WR300:
Inferior reception compared to this Reecom
When the radio turns on so you can hear the weather alert, the Midland keeps going for another FIVE MINUTES after the storm warning information is finished. SO, at 2am, you hear the radio blaring what temperature it is in different cities, etc unless you get out of bed and push a button to silence it. With this Reecom, when the alert information broadcast is finished, the radio goes back to silent by itself!

title: The Best Kindle Yet
text:
This is the fourth Kindle I've owned, and it's definitely the best. I read a lot of books, so I usually upgrade whenever Amazon introduces something significantly new. And this is definitely much improved over the last generation.

First of all, the screen is amazing. You can't see the pixels, even if you are looking for them. It's as much of an improvement over the Paperwhite as the Paperwhite was over the Kindle 4. For the first time, I honestly can't tell the difference between printed text and text on my new Kindle. And once you use this screen, you won't ever be able to go back. Going back to the Paperwhite, the text looks ugly and grainy. It's funny because that's exactly how I felt about my Kindle 4 after using the Paperwhite.

The backlight seems improved over the Paperwhite (at least the first-generation). The backlight color does shift a bit from top to bottom (orangish at the top and bluish at the bottom), but I only noticed because I read other peoples' reviews. And if I'm not looking for it, I don't notice it at all. It really isn't a big deal.

It's also tiny. Significantly smaller and noticeably thinner than the Paperwhite, while at the same time stiffer due to the magnesium frame. The screen with the smooth glass front is a treat to use - my finger glides across the screen.

As for the Pagepress, I like it, although the feedback is pretty subtle. I sometimes miss the feeling, even when I have it turned to the highest setting. If you don't like Pagepress, you can always turn it off, and the swipe or tap left and right still works.

The relocated power button took a bit of getting used to, although now that I've acclimatized, I'll say that it's in the right place (I can hit it without taking my hand off of the Kindle).

I will say that there is something weird about clicks at the top or bottom of the screen (like when I want to switch between pages and locations). They don't seem to register correctly all of the time. I'm sure this will be addressed with a firmware update.

There are a few reasons why it doesn't quite merit 5 stars. I'm hoping that the second generation model will address these issues.

First up is battery life. The battery life really isn't great. With my Paperwhite, I almost never had to charge it. This one I have to charge somewhat frequently (about every two weeks so far). Over Thanksgiving I read about three books, and I ended up going through about a charge and a half in that time. I'm not sure whether the new screen uses more power or the battery is smaller, but I expected a bit more battery life in a premium product like this.

And my second minor nit is that you can't see the Pagepress buttons while reading in the dark. I've kind of learned to guess where they are (most of the time), but Amazon should make them light up in the dark. If they were to add that and improve the battery life just a bit, this would be perfect.

Overall, a great device. If you have an original Paperwhite, you probably want to upgrade. If you have something earlier than a Paperwhite, you will probably be so blown away by the Paperwhite that you might as well just get that instead, but if you want to be spoiled for anything else, buy the Voyage.

title: My jeep may be the 'odd ball'.
text:
It works in my 2014 Jeep Wrangler, but I had to modify the connection. I didn't read about a modification anywhere else, so maybe late 2014, the connector changed or my jeep's wiring harness is a freak? Who knows, anyways....

Here is what happened. I took out the stock deck and released the white clip to remove the antenna connection. I went to install this "plug and play" adapter and it would clip into the jeeps harness, but it wouldn't make the connection to allow radio reception.

So I got looking at the harness and the adapter. I noticed that the adapter would fit into the harness, but not with the white clip was in the way and not allowing a good connection. So I removed the red safety tab on the harness (keeps the clip from opening up) and pulled the white clip off. I then pushed and twisted the harness and adapter together. Then inserted the adapter into the aftermarket radio. Radio...I have it!

So if you have a Wrangler and the connection isn't allowing for radio reception, just do the above and you'll be good to go. I have had zero issues and the radio works as it should (and clear).

title: Great features but NOISY motor!  Rumble and noise is-38db.
text:
I've been living with this turntable for several months now. I would say that it's equivalent to a low-to-mid level turntable from the very late 1970's. It's full of features and the ability to play 78's is nice. It has a solid feel to it and - for the most part- sounds OK. But there are a few semi-important issues that prevent this from being a REALLY nice turntable.

1.) The anti-skate is just not effective. It works to a very mild degree, but not where it should be. I had to rig up a small fishing line with a 2 gram weight to counteract the pull.
2.) The tonearm is just too high. It gives plenty of adjustment range to raise it even further, but the VTA can't be brought within specs for a good alignment. I solved this by adding additional pads under the record to effectively raise the platter height. Once I did that, there was quite a bit of improvement to the sound quality...which tended to be overly bright and brittle sounding in the inner grooves.
3.) The motor has plenty of torque, but it's far from the quietest table I've every used. In fact, my 30 year old turntable is far quieter. It really transmits vibrations through the pick-up and out the speakers. There is a noticeable wub-wub-wub-wub sound that permeates quiet passages. I've done everything that I can think of to quiet it, but I've only made a modest dent in the sound. It is the motor cogging and it's being amplified though the chasis and right down the tonearm. I can lift the vinyl right off of the platter as it spins and STILL hear it. NO GOOD! I've drilled out the motor mounts, installed rubber bushings, put dense foam around the plate that secures the motor and installed rubber washers at the tonearm base. I've managed to cut that noise about -15db, but it is still there. The noise is located between 200and 300Hz at -38db stock. This ruins the usefulness of turntable for me and it's a shame, too. I'm going to keep tweaking it, but I don't think I can get much more noise dampening out of it.
4.) The preamp and USB board is pretty bad. It's noisy and dull - plus, they added some kind of mute function when the audio falls below a certain level. It's bad if you use another cartridge with a lower output. I bypassed my board and can hear a noticeable difference in dynamics and brightness. There are videos to show how to do this - but you need to add a ground wire and have an external preamp or receiver with phono inputs.

I would recommend this table for basic use or for the non-discriminating - but NOT for vinyl transfers. I could swear the $100 turntables from 1978 would beat the pants off of this when it comes to rumble and noise. Maybe mine is at the low-end of their manufacturing specs, but they could have designed this a bit better.

The only caveat is that my system is 32-bit, which means that I can only truly utilize approximately 3.5GB of the now-4.5GB present, although that's not by fault of this product, and is somewhat rectified by installing the PAE Linux kernel.

In any event, this product has not only stood the test of time (I would say 1.5 years of use is plenty of time in computer years), but has also stood the test of diversity. Not only does this product meet my expectations, but it surpasses them, and at the cheapest price I could find at the time, too!

title: Awsome piece of tech
text:
I've never owned any smart phone or tablet of any kind. I bought this to break free of my laptop, which IMO is only comfortable to use in a table/desktop situation.

My aim was mainly to be able to surf anywhere in my home. I bought the 8.0 Note after reading all the reviews about what a handy size it is(not too big, and not too small), and went for the Note specifically because the S-pen sounded useful.

All I can say is, I love this freakin' thing! Where has it been all my life?

This is what the internet experience was meant to be... something akin to having the comfort and flexibility of reading a magazine.

The Note downloads web pages extremely fast... in fact all functions are lightning quick, which just makes it a joy to use.

I use it as a reader, the screen size and light weight are real pluses here... I use it as a day planner, the S-pen is surprisingly accurate and relatively natural feeling to use once you get alittle bit of a hang of it... there is still a lot of S-pen functionality left for me to learn, but it's so cool to be able to take notes and schedule a calendar without digging through notebooks, and paperwork.

I just figured out how to use the Peel app to run my TV... it's just basic functionality(volume/channels), but what makes it pretty awesome for me is that it's also a fully functional TV guide. I'm only viewing over-the-air television, so unless I buy some form of TV guide I'm left to surf through the channels to figure out what's on. Now the Note just tells me what's on, I tap the program I want and I'm there... pretty sweet not having to search the room for the remote either.

Cons...

I guess it is a bit expensive as far as Android tabs go, but it packs a lot of functionality that I guess no other tab this size does.

Mine is a bit creaky, but as long as it keeps functioning like a rock star It doesn't bother me.

I can't really compare the screen to some of the super-duper ones out there as I have no experience with them, but playing games, watching video, and using as a reader.. I can't say that I'm disappointed. Doesn't blow me away, but I don't feel short changed either, IMO it looks great.

As far as battery life is concerned, I get 2 days normal usage out of a charge. In my experience the screen brightness is what really sucks the juice out of it. If you can live in the bottom quarter-ish of the brightness scale you'll do well. Also turn off things like Bluetooth, auto-sync, GPS, wi-fi when you can, and enable power-saver mode. Battery charges in around 2 hours for me.

I dig this thing so much, I bought a refurbished Note 10:). I'm really liking the Flipbook app, and I'm thinking the 10 inch screen will be more satisfying with online magazines and videos... so the 10 can stay at home and the 8 can go on the road with me.

title: Great device, poor support
text:
My wife and I each have Motoactv device. One 8GB, one 16GB. They're very clever and functional for our bike riding, simple to use (once you spend a bit of time learning shortcuts), and provide a wealth of good info that really does help us improve our cycling. The music is what sets this device apart for me in that I don't need to carry an ipod/mp3 player in addition to computer when riding.

HOWEVER, it's amazing how poor Moto's support is for the device. Most recently, a problem on the Motoactv portal precludes the display of elevation data. This problem has remained for over a month and there's not even an indication or acknowledgement from Motorola that there's an issue. The very active Motoactv Forum is replete with pleas from customers like me to address this problem. Moto's response?, not a peep. Oh, and why make it so difficult to transfer workout data to Strava, Endomondo, MapMyRide, etc? One must download a CSV file, convert it .tcx, and then upload to one of these superior software programs. Moto's own portal won't even total up your weekly, monthly, or yearly stats!

Granted, this device must rank low in Moto's triage consideration, but until they get with it I will advise other potential customers that they should look elsewhere, either Garmin Edge (+ ipod), iPod/Smartphone with Endomondo/Map My Ride, Polar, or other competing device. Moto's lack of follow through and support is extraordinarily disappointing.

update: The Motoactv portal just seems to get worse. And Matt, the Uber Xpert manning the Motoactv forum site, appears to be missing in action. Regardless of browser, network, or computer used, the portal will no longer display any information from recent rides. Just get the message "Unable to process the request" when selecting the workout.

I was impressed that it came with a silicone keyboard cover that was included. Very slick how you can remove the keyboard from the dock! Very easy to remove and re-dock the keyboard. The magnets holding it in place were strong enough to keep it secure when i flipped it upside down, and it took a few good shakes while being held upside down for the keyboard to fall out of the dock. The keyboard can still be used while charging in the house or from my new trent imp52d. The range was unbelievable, not that you would walk away from the ipad and continue to type or use the keyboard when walking away from the ipad screen, so I tested this by playing music while pressing the play/ pause buttton. The range surpassed my expectations.
Once I charged it up it was extremely easy to pair with the ipad. All the buttons worked fine as expected. I was pleasantly surprised that the keyboard had additional buttons on it to control the ipad. For instance the volume, mute and screen brightness could be controlled directly from the keyboard and it even had a home button! Even keys for locking, play pause, forward track, previous track, a key to access the photo album, a search button, and a virtual keyboard button. Over all it is a great accessory for ipad owners. I tested this with Ipad 1, Ipad 2 and iphone 4s. I dont own the latest ipad so i couldnt test it. All things considered I am extremely happy with it. Its functional capabilities surpassed my expectations. Great product New Trent.

title: Zummo 665 an expensive POS!!!
text:
The 665 is a good GPS, "whenever it decides to work". I've been through 4 of them.... They all had the same problem, the map animation on the screen disapears in mid use. The voice instructions work, the icon is there, but no road whatsoever. Your icon is floating in white space. The first 665 I bought was factory refurbished. It started acting in this erratic way, I called tech support and they walked me through reboots, updates etc. finally It was recommended that I replace the unit... I did and the exact same scenario occurred. I returned that unit. I bought a brand new unit directly from Garmin.... Same thing.... I was now hopping mad, called Garmin again... Again reboots, updates, etc. etc. etc. i sent it back and requested yet another unit...They personally configured and updated the replacement unit ( I guess they assumed I was a raving moron and was the cause of this anomaly ). Regardless, this "new" unit does the exact same thing. I found out that by rebooting the unit it seems to reset the software for several weeks before another reboot is necessary. I never returned the unit.... I ride all over the country and other parts of the world... And a water resistant GPS is really a great thing to have with you.... When it works.
Here's a must do, get a sim chip for the 665, load all of your important routs there. If you have to reboot your unit and your not fast enough lifting your thumb off of the screen, all of your routs will be deleted !!! If you have them on the sim chip, all you have to do is access the "my data" folder, and import the routs. It saved my ass at least once.
By the way, my wife has a Nuvi in her car... It never gave a moments grief. There is definitely something wrong in the architecture of the 665... Now if Garmin just figures out what that is, and findes a fix, I would give it 5 stars.... At it stands it gets no more than 2. And that's only because of the other features it has i.e.: blue tooth, satellite radio access, red light cameras, traffic reports etc. all of those work fine.... Just no maps....

title: Happy Camper..
text:
Got here fast. It's actually a very nice radio, has a feature called ETM which makes finding stations a breeze, speaker is acceptable.
I wouldn't suggest using only the internal speaker for music,as it's rather tinny sounding but for talk radio & such it's just fine and signals on shortwave are usually rather noisy anyway.

It has an FM stereo option, includes earbuds, I don't recall if it says it in the description but they even include a long wire antenna for shortwave reception it has a clip for the antenna and a clip to attach to something like an aluminum window frame.
If you only use the telescoping antenna you will probably not be happy with the SW reception, at least I wasn't in my area (25 miles outside Los Angeles), it does improve with the included SW antenna though.

The included AM antenna does help tune in local AM stations, it even has two dials on the ends for "Fine tuning" AM reception.

You can use rechargeable AA batteries, it will even charge them through an on-board charging circuit just plug in to a USB port on you PC or other USB charging device, the cable to charge is not included but it accepts a miniature USB plug, I had one laying around so I was able to use that.

The build quality is quite solid, it doesn't feel like it's going to break if you use it, the tuning dial is detented and has a nice "Feel" to it, made in China (Of course) but you wouldn't realize that from the quality.

Overall a good purchase, I'm sure it will last for a long time.
