title: Almost perfect, great purchase.
text:
I love this little amp. It is sooooo much better than the Vox AmPlug I also own. Top notch build quality similar to FiiO's other headphone amps. The Vox feel very cheap in comparison. Another key difference is that the FiiO has a permanent rechargeable battery versus the Vox's use of AAA's. Pros and cons for both methods, but I prefer the rechargeable solution personally.

The plug pivots out with a button in much the same way many new car keys now do. This is nice not only for storage, but also to provide some play if you accidentally bump the amp on something to minimize damage to it or the output jack on your instrument.

With the gain turned all the way down, the tone is VERY clean. So much so that I forget that it is even turned on. Turning up the gain adds a noticeable hiss along with the distortion, but nothing you wouldn't expect out of a traditional amplifier.

My only real complaint is that the dials for Volume, Gain, and Tone are on the bottom edge of the Amp (same as the Vox) and are proud from the housing. title: A really impressive product and value
text:
I'm Lou, writing this review for this product we purchased through Mary's Prime account. I'm writing the review because frankly, I don't understand the negative reviews.

I've retailed and repped boutique home audio. I've installed custom tri amped car stereo with DSP and all the trimmings. As a custom home builder, I've installed acoustically isolated and optimized home theatre. I've generally been an audio tweak.

For our 2002 Odyssey, which just never breaks down and continues as our second vehicle, I wanted to keep it simple and I didn't want to give up any cargo space or passenger comfort. I wanted to invoke appropriate technology, application and cost.

You need to know what else I put in the car to understand the review: it's an audio system, nothing works in isolation. I was a step ahead because I already had a pair of Boston Acoustics component speakers (surface mounted tweeters for direction), from a car the kids totaled. I upgraded the radio to an Alpine 145BT Bluetooth unit with Sirius for $150, and that's all I'm running at the moment. No external amp.

* This unit lessens the need for an external amp, if you have a quality radio (head unit). I have reduced the bass level from the head unit, easing up on the mid range speakers, letting the subwoofer properly take over the bottom end.

* This subwoofer fit under the front of the driver seat. It didn't even take away any foot space from the mid seat passenger. I fuse tapped the power from the driver side fuse box, used chassis for ground and ran the harness wires under the kick panel to under the driver seat. Very quick and easy. I just laid the box under the seat and ... done.

* It looks really slick - great styling - it would look great if made visible in a custom installation.

* It sounds very nice. You have to tweak the rolloff and volume for your material, but get that right and it blends in very nicely. I can definitely make it bump my butt, but that's not how I listen. I want deep bass, but I don't want it to overshadow.

* The controller is a big deal. Normal installation: Listen, hop out, crawl under the seat, into the trunk, wherever the bass amp is, turn a knob or screw a sixteenth, get back in the car, listen and repeat about a hundred times. Then play different material, decide it's all wrong and start all over again.

The controller let's you adjust the rolloff, rollin actually, and volume as you're driving down the road. You can do it by feel, you don't need to take your eyes off the road.

* I drive and listen and bask in the glow that the woofer, amplifier and controller all cost $150. It's a great value.

Don't let it's lesser size prevent you from trying it. It sounds really good. I suspect negative reviewers were expecting a boom box or perfection for $150 or perhaps the units were defective or not properly installed. I may have written a glowing review because the product exceeded my expectations, but ... it exceeded my expectations. I have no idea how you could improve on this deep bass, in this space, at any cost.

title: Great Binoculars... Bright, crisp and clear.
text:
Just got these and they are sharp and bright and much lighter than you'd expect considering you're holding two small telescopes up to your face. My first use of them was at dusk and it was immediately obvious how much brighter my view through these binoculars was compared to the straight view by eye. I wear glases and found that there was plenty of eye-relief. I didn't have to roll down the eyepiece cups to get good views.

I have two small complaints, however. The caps on the objectives (front end) of the binoculars are great - they fit snuggly. But the eye-piece caps barely hang on by themselves. My second complaint is that the carry case feels like leatherette covered stiff cardboard with a spindly little strap. But at least it has a case!

The strap for the binoculars themselves has a nice wide band and hangs comfortably about the neck.

As I expected, with these binoculars I had no trouble spotting the Andromeda Galaxy even with a half full moon *and* in heavily light polluted suburban environment. With the lower 9x power, it also means I didn't get naseous from trying to hold high power binoculars steady.

The objectives are set deeper in so they stay pretty dry. It was raining the day I used them on a boat. The birds were far away and even in flight I could see them well. title: One bad decision ruined a good design
text:
I just finished putting together a new system based around a core of NZXT products (case, cooler, fan control, etc) because the components had impressive features, the reviews were good and, coming from the same company, I expected the pieces to work well together. To my surprise and disappointment, every single product that I used from NZXT had moderate to significant flaws in design or execution. Either the product wasn't well thought out - features that looked good on paper didn't work as you'd expect - or the product was poorly made - software worked badly, pieces were flimsy or components were of low quality. While on paper their products may hit all the check marks when it comes to features, I can't say I could recommend any of the pieces that I had experience with and I have my doubts about NZXT's portrayal as a top-tier company focused on innovation and quality.

In this case, the design behind the fan controller is pretty good - the layout is clear and intuitive, the functions are flexible and the form factor is perfect for most cases. The touch screen isn't the best (don't expect mobile phone responsiveness to the touch here) but it's fine for the intended use; how often to you plan on adjusting your fan speeds up and down? Some of the touch spots are far away from where you'd expect; having to press a half-inch to the right of the speed profile icons doesn't make sense and for the longest time I thought that feature was broken (especially since the other touch spots seem pretty accurate)

There's a lot of flexibility in the design - you can see fan speed as RPM or as a percentage, there are two ways to adjust fan speed (up/down arrows or by the slider bar) and you can use different profiles (silence, performance and custom). Unfortunately, as seems to be a common theme with NZXT, documentation is somewhere between poor and nonexistent. There's a cursory walkthrough but they don't do a good job of explaining the various functions and you're left on your own to figure things out - fortunately it's not that complicated.

But the Achilles heel, the thing that makes this a useless piece of junk, is the LCD display. Viewed dead-on from the front the segments are all hazy and half-lit. Look at it from 45 degrees to the side and it looks as if the unit isn't turned on. (The photo for this product must have been Photoshopped because from that angle, below and to the left, the screen is terrible) The only good viewing angle I found was dead on and either 20 degrees above or below face of the display. From that angle it's sharp, clear and colorful but from any other the display is difficult to read and completely unacceptable.

title: Future of computing and I love it
text:
Very skeptical at first since I have always owned macbooks or regular windows laptops. But now I am convinced in what Google is telling us - this is the future of computing. Lots of apps, storage in the cloud, no more downloading updates as you always get the latest app real time. App selection is enormous for just about anything you need including games. My kids use this for school and this has now become the main laptop for all in the house.
As for this HP 14 model: Very nice build quality, really nice, big HD screen and the battery life I have been getting 7 to 8 hours consistently. In fact I have been going two to 3 days without a charge under light usage. The processor is very quick and I love the fact that you can just shut the cover and open instantly to what you were doing. Video chats and a host of other technologies will keep you busy. Keyboard is a light touch but still good - not quite like a lenovo or macbook. The outside cover is grippy which is really nice for carrying. Lots of USB and slots for display, and memory. The best part of this is with chrome you never have to worry about virus software etc..
As for the t-mobile 4g - I think its the icing on the cake. If you get good reception it is fast. If not then its like any other cell phone data speeds when downloading. It worked nicely on a trip as the kids used it in the back of the car with no complaints. It is free and if you exceed the total data limit it just throttles you down for the month. No bills. If you want you can purchase additional bandwidth by the day or monthly which is nice again if you are travelling.
Overall, I am very happy with this purchase and definitely worth the bargain price especially as everything moves to the cloud.

text:

Pros: Easy to use, great support, and it supports game systems very well.

Cons: Once you lose your disks or have to reformat, it becomes a waste of space in your desk because you have to pay $70 just to be able to redownload the software and use it again. They didn't care about the serial number on the hardware device - apparently that's not a method to prove that I actually own the product.

The verdict: While it's a great product, and I recommended it to people previous to losing my disks and not being able to access the software, I can no longer recommend it. The fact that I can't provide the serial number of my actual device for a download is pretty silly.

title: Good value and works as advertised.  Review with some configuration details not in the included literature.
text: I was able to gett the main configuration completed using WPS from my U-Verse router and the WPS button on the front of this device.  I transferred the unit upstairs and couldn't tell there was another access point in the house.  The domain login they advertise to use for further configuration did not work for me, so I looked up the MAC address (found printed on the unit itself) using my main router's DHCP list to get the IP address of the extender.  If your router doesn't have this function, you can always run "arp -a" from a command prompt (Windows run "cmd") and you will most likely find the DHCP assigned local IP of this access point.  From there I was able to type in the IP of the device, login (admin/admin is the default user name and PW, which I highly recommend changing first thing), and change the default user name/password/SSID to distinguish between devices.  When using WPS, the WPA2 password stays exactly the same as your main router, so you just choose the proper name, type in the password, and you're done.  Very easy device to setup and it allowed me to get a decent signal upstairs to a corner of my home that got 1 bar with several dropped connections up to 3-4 (out of 5) bars with a solid connection (i.e. no drops).  Great product for the money and the support website is easy to navigate as well.  Updated the firmware for good measure, which is found at [...]  I did have to unplug the device to complete the firmware update, but otherwise it was a very straightforward and easy process.  I would give it about 10min after starting the update before unplugging it, just to make sure you don't brick the device.

title: DDX-371 on a 2004 Lexus RX 330
text:
Installed Kenwood DDX-371 on a 2004 Lexus RX 330 with basic audio & no navigation. The audio quality is better than the stock radio. I use to have a truck with Pioneer AVH-X2500BT. So my review is more of a comparison to the Pioneer

The good
1) Touch screen is responsive than the Pioneer even compared with the Pioneer AVH-X5600BHS (I installed this model in my 2007 4Runner).
2) I liked the Kenwwod's iPod Menu better than the Pioneer's iPod Menu.
3) you do not need another $20 piece of junk bypass to make it fully functional like the Pioneer.
4) Bluetooth connects the moment you turn on Bluetooth in your phone. What I mean by that is, let's say if you turned on the radio/car when Bluetooth in your phone is turned off and you decide to turn on Bluetooth later it still connects to the radio automatically. This is a pain in Pioneer AVH-X2500BT and the AVH-X5600BHS, I had to manually connect my phone with Pioneer unless I turn on Bluetooth before turning on the radio or starting my car. Pioneer does searches any paired Bluetooth devices during start up and prompt do you want to search again?
5) Less Hiss noise compared to Pioneer. Please do not get me wrong it is not that bad at all even in the Pioneer but it is less in Kenwood in comparison
6) The phone calls over the Bluetooth was good. People did not had issues hearing me and I did not had problem hearing them so as the Pioneer. I did not tried streaming audio over Bluetooth.

The bad
1)On the USB playback, the manual says this unit can recognize a total of 5000 files and 250 folders (a maximum of 999 files per folder). I never tried it to the limit. To me this is useless anyways because I have my 15 yer old MP3 collection will be easily over the folder limit specified here.

2) No seek bar for audio or video. This was good on the pioneer radio you can skip section of audio files. There is a fast forward option in kenwood which I found is not easy to use.

3) It takes longer to start up and play audio from iPod compared to the pioneer.

4) No equalizer only tone control, I knew that but I'm not happy with the 3 band tone controls. At this price Kenwood should offer at least a 8 band equalizer

5) The front to rear fade was not clear when compared to Pioneer. for e.g. if I move the controls all the way to the rear I still hear audio from my front speakers. I'm not sure if the metra harness plays any role here. Audio completely cuts out in the Pioneer from front to rear and vice versa

Overall Kenwood DDX 371 pretty much is in tie with comparable Pioneer radios. If the above said cons are not much of an issue for you please go ahead with Kenwood. For me the seek bar and the EQ are deal breakers.

For those who are looking for Lexus RX 330 specific information here are some tips

Mine had the basic audio no navigation
I used the Metra Access AX-ADBOX1 and AX-ADTY01. You do not need the Metra Axxess TYTO-01 unless you have JBL audio. I'm not sure about Mark Levinson audio systems
you will need Metra 99-8159S Double DIN Stereo Dash Kit for Lexus RX 330
I did not used the steering wheel controls but it is a straight forward connection with ASWC-1
The instructions came with the metra harness are confusing at best. the idea is to connect the aftermarket radio to the AX-DTY01 and that connects to AX-ADBOX1. I guess the factory amps are digital amps and the AX-ADBOX1 is a analog to digital converter. There is a audio level control on the AX-ADBOX1 you need to adjust to make sure there is no distortion.

Update 2014-10-22

I had earlier stated you need additional cables to play audio from iPod turns out it is not the case (please see comments for setting details), hence making this a 4 star review. I have removed my previous comments and workarounds on the audio cables I had posted here

title: Could have had one more star.
text:
You know, this HX series can trace itself back to the high end Minolta P&S cams like the A1(5mp) and A2(8mp) from 2004/5. With that in mind, there are three things about the HX200V that would make this 6 stars, were they included. Threads for filters, dedicated remote port and the ability to sync with an external flash, all of which were on the A1 and A2. Those things would help make this more of a photographer's cam. Plus, it was having bought the filters, remote and external flash for the A1 that helped me decide to get the Sony A200. Still, I bought this for the features it does have like the ability to switch control of the zoom & focus from the lens to the body and the full manual mode. Some say the boost to 18mp doesn't help and makes the pictures fuzzy, but the HX200 has many resolutions to choose from. If you've been shooting at 10mp or less before now, I think you'll see that what we assumed was "sharpness" was a lack of detail. Kind of like making the jump from VGA to even just 2mp.Newer pics on older displays don't quite match up. As far as picture quality, I noticed the HX200 likes contrast. I'm impressed with what it can do with HDR in B&W. I like that there are links to the more obscure functions in the in-camera guide. Other than that, I like the feel, features and price-for-features. The scene modes and effects are nice and fun to have, but the aforementioned additions would, on the whole, be more useful. And, Sony might sell more aftermarket stuff.
Now, if we could only get these manufacturers to support their products beyond the first year....

title: Technological Masterpiece

At first I compared the Canon T5i to the Nikon D3200 and settled on the Nikon, but when I went to hit the order button the price of the Nikon kit had gone up by several hundred dollars so I went the next level up and started over. After much research I settled for the Canon 70D over the Nikon D7100. As a straight up still camera, the Nikon holds the edge, but when all things are considered I thought the Canon the better fit for me.

I really like the built in wireless. You can use it with the Canon apps to take simple shots or the third party DSLR Controller app (Android) and control many if not most of the 70D functions from your droid phone or tablet. The autofocus with the STM kit lens is so quiet, you think is must not be working. It also works perfectly while shooting videos where the focus changes during the shot. Absolutely no noise from the lens is picked up in the audio. The onboard flash is weak, but when coupled with the Canon Speedlite 430EX II flash they can work as a master/slave team and “talk” to one another to provide superb results.

The Canon 70D is a technological masterpiece. It produces excellent quality stills and videos under a variety of conditions. I highly recommend the product.

This SkyProdigy6 is the largest optical tube in the series and will show great views when the sky is clear.

This is my second SkyProdigy, I purchased the SkyProdigy70 from Amazon previously,and was delighted with it; and had been wanting its biggest sibling ever since.When Amazon offered an excellent deal on a 6, I grabbed it.AND I'm keeping both!

I give 4 stars because of the necessary (but not mentioned in ads) calibration,and the handheld controller can be difficult to read for those like myself with less than perfect vision due to small print and limited brightness.

title: Incredible service
text:
My computer uses 3 large monitors, and 2 smaller USB monitors. I had just bought a specialized VGA monitor made by DeskTop Aviator that acts as an aircraft GPS for some flight simulator games like FSX. BUT ALL of my standard monitor outputs were in use!

At the moment I also have 17 USB devices connected to my computer. Not what you'd call a standard setup.

My problem started when I plugged this adaptor/cable into the last USB 3.0 connection on the back of my computer. No Go. Un-happy camper. It worked just fine plugged into a USB 2.0 port with a standard monitor. But NOT the special monitor that I had ordered.

*
THE SHORT STORY
Plugable Technologies worked with me to resolve 2 unique problems, and in the end substituting a slightly different adapter/cable, the [[ASIN:B00A2E1MQA Plugable UGA-3000 USB 3.0 / 2.0 to VGA / DVI / HDMI Adapter for Windows and Mac]]. Check out the Picture that I added on the main product page. CLICK ON -> "See 1 customer image".

I can recommend this one for most people who don't want to buy a newer multi-monitor video card. Got a newer laptop? This would be one of the best ways to add a second, or third, monitor. Got an old cheap laptop? Probably nothing will help.

A great thing about these USB to VGS adaptors is that they'll work with either USB 2.0 or 3.0 ports on Windows or Macs.

For some, I'd suggest that you get the [[ASIN:B00A2E1MQA Plugable UGA-3000 USB 3.0 / 2.0 to VGA / DVI / HDMI Adapter for Windows and Mac]]. Not only is it newer technology, but it includes adapters for VGA, DVI, and HDMI. For only $10 more you're getting a set that'll work with almost any monitor that you're likely to buy in the near future.

*
A LONGER STORY.
Plugable Technologies found out that, what I had thought was the latest USB controller driver was actually 2 years old! And I had downloaded the driver from the USB chip manufacturers website 2 weeks ago!

But Plugable sent me the link to an Intel website where the REAL newest driver was.

So now the original adapter/cable worked with USB 2.0, 3.0, and standard monitors. But not with the unique DeskTop Aviator monitor that I had just bought.

That's when they suggested substituting the [[ASIN:B00A2E1MQA Plugable UGA-3000 USB 3.0 / 2.0 to VGA / DVI / HDMI Adapter for Windows and Mac OS X 10.8.3 Multiple Monitors up to 2048x1152 / 1920x1080 Each (DisplayLink DL-3100 Chipset)]].

The Plugable UGA-3000 adaptor/cable was able to get around the little monitors deviations from standard. EVERYTHING now works the way that I want it to.

*
IMPORTANT NOTE!!!!!!
The chips that control this adaptor are made by DisplayLink. DisplayLink is also used in my 2 small USB monitors. IF YOU'RE ALREADING USING "DisplayLink" CHIPSETS YOU HAVE TO MAKE SURE THAT YOU STAY WITH "DisplayLink". Other technologies WILL NOT BE COMPATABLE!

On the other hand, I've had great results with DisplayLink and wouldn't consider anything else.

End note - Just to see what would happen, I plugged the UGA-3000 adaptor into an old ViewSonic monitor AND a USB 2.0 port. It worked fine.

Big deal.

I THEN watched a wide screen movie thru the UGA-3000 cable. Plugged into a USB 2 port! The movie displayed just fine, no problems.

The moral of the story is that if your computer is good enough, *the UGA-3000 adaptor* is more than good enough. EVEN if it's plugged into USB 2.0 port!

title: Back cover: 4 starts Screen protector: 1
text:
AmazonBasics Clear Back Cover for the iPad mini comes as a set featuring a clear, polycarbonate "shell" to protect the back of the iPad mini and a screen protector "decal".

The back cover snaps on easily, but holds tight and doesn't come off easily and not in daily use and toting it around in my bag and camera case.

The back cover seems to offer scratch protection to the back of the iPad mini, but does not have any shock absorbing features. If you are looking for a case that will tolerate the rigors of use in a family with small children, you might want to look at options that do have more rugged protection. The back cover is fairly easily scratched, during use, and while this can seem reassuring as those scratches could have been on your shiny new iPad mini, I don't think it's an indicator of product success or failure, but just a fact. I actually took it off and used a sharp graver to "engrave" the inside of my AmazonBasics back cover to make it a little more personalized (I don't recommend this as I'm sure it negates any warranties on the back cover).

For the price, the back cover is a good purchase for a little extra, lightweight protection.

The screen protector that came bundled with it is not great. For the price? I guess it's better than zero screen protection but it is one of those sticky ones where you really have to put some elbow grease in to get out bubbles and I found that I couldn't get all of the bubbles out and tried "reapplying" it and wound up having bubbles and dust trapped between the screen protector and my iPad mini screen surface. With bubbles, and then with dust, my shiny new iPad mini looked like it had seen quite a bit of action, so I removed the screen protector and just kept the back cover on it.

For our other phones, iPad, tablets, kindle fire we have tried other screen protectors but we keep coming back to the Moshi iVisor for bubble-free installation and long term use. I think I will add one to my iPad mini, combined with the AmazonBasics Back Cover, for a lightweight solution that does not detract from the design of the iPad mini. [[ASIN:B00A0LVPM6 Moshi iVisor Screen Protector AG (Anti-Glare) for iPad Mini - Black]]

title: Love them!
text:
My sister has accused me of treating these like a piece of jewelry. I'll constantly wear them draped over my neck as they weigh next to nothing and will connect at a moments notice to my device. The packaging says they will save up to 8 (may have been 10) pairings at a time. The connection switches by going to the headphones on the device's menu to connect.

Sound quality is nice. They are better than my Skullcandy Smokin Buds (which I've been told by a Seinheiser owner are absolute cr*p). The bass comes through moderately, if you are a bass head you probably wont be satisfied as these really aren't built for it.

Fit is something to get used to. They are larger than normal earbuds but only slightly in diameter. Most of the added bulk is in the "depth" of the earbud. They are also heavier, but if you are only wearing them (and not another pair of regular earbuds) you likely wont notice. There are multiple "bits" included for fitting. I've gone with the medium for more of a seal in the ear. With other typical earbuds I go for the medium or small. These tips are slightly more solid than the other earbud tips, which could be why some would have a hard time establishing the perfect fit.

The wing like attachments are excellent. I had been in the market for ear hook headphones when I found these. I have to say this design is preferable. The little point fits right into the curve of your ear making a secure fit that is hard to dislodge. I've even had the earphones pulled slightly out with the tips still in to create more of a "speaker" effect for when I don't want to block everything around me out but still want to listen to a little music.

The only thing difficult to adapt to is having a battery in your earphones. It's another gadget that requires charging. The included cable is only about four inches long so there is no using them while charging. Battery life is fine though, rated for eight hours. I've never tested that assertion, but they will last a few days of intermediate use without charging. Unfortunately, I usually don't catch the battery low warning so the "death" comes as a surprise.

Call quality is decent without any complaints coming through the people I spoken with. It is still bluetooth though a good incarnation of it. When battery life is low (just before shut down) the sound will start to cut out.

All in all, they are decent headphones with good sound quality and battery life.

title: Awesome Sound from Mini Speakers
text:
I decided I needed a pair of mini speakers when I realized I could play some soothing lullabyes for my little boy at bedtime. I heard that iHome was a good name to try, so I decided to give them a shot, and since I received these iHM78s, I've been completely satisfied with them.

They hold a charge enough for six hours play time according to the claims made by iHome, and so far I've found nothing to challenge those claims. I am sure I played them enough over one five-day period to eclipse that amount, though I never really play lullabyes at full-blast.

Amazon tells me they weigh 5.4 ounces, but holding them, my hand tells me they weigh almost nothing. They are super-portable; collapsible, with a cleverly-conceived magnetic base to make them compact and easily fit in the travel pouch. But these things just mean they're good at being "mini" speakers... it is the sound that really won me over.

Playing music for my son at bedtime, I've found myself dozing just as quickly as him. The sound, above all, is crisp and clear and clean. Even something this small delivers bass that you would swear is coming from speakers ten times the size. Again, this is at a volume conducive to delivering sleep to a boy who runs around the house in circles for hours at a time.

The next test was to use the speakers over my vacation, where I wanted to listen to the audiobook version of George R.R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire. And it being vacation, I wanted to be in a hot tub with icy cold beer to listen to it. The volume up to be heard over the sounds of the water, I could hear the narration with severe clarity and I enjoyed it completely. I then took a long nap.

I've also loaned these speakers to my Mom to listen to her first audiobook, and she loves them. She gave them back to me, but I think she was hoping for another audiobook. At least I have a good idea what to do for Mother's Day.

In short, I find no reason not to give these speakers five stars, given the incredibly reasonable price and the outstanding performance of the speakers. I would never expect to blast Metallica over these speakers and expect Bose performance; they do what they are supposed to do for portable speakers and they do it magnificently. I highly recommend them. If I find a reason to lower my rating or if I realize a disappointment, I will revisit this review. Until that time... I love them!

title: Powerful wi-fi router, requires some expertise during setup
text:
I have been using this router for about a month month. I waited until this version came out to get the more full implementation of the AC specification. Overall I am very satisfied with this router. I also purchased an AC access point that I use to connect to this and provide my IPTV signal to my television.

The reason for the missing fifth start is due to the complexity of setup, especially with the access point. Other than the complexity, it is a great router and I would highly recommend it. In testing, we have run IPTV (steaming TV) and two XBox 360s playing first person shooters at the same time. This equates to a great deal of intense streaming at the same time. We experienced no issues! An for that this is the perfect solution for our household. We have two remote TVs where we need to provide network access and two gaming systems. Because our house is not wired for network, we use wireless. This is a fantastic system and provides exactly what we need. Worth the money.

Now on to the setup. Out of the box, it is my believe that no matter the brand, if router and access points support the same protocols, their setup should be easy enough that no networking experience is required. Call me crazy, but that's what I think. Keep in mind I have deep experience. I recognize though, for the money, things should be a little smoother on setup. Anyway, I did end up having to do a bit of customization, changing some of the network settings, etc. The changes themselves are not that complex, but getting to them was. Next my access point was on a completely different network, so I had to change that too. I just seems that the networking companies should agree to a base setup that will not conflict with TV cable boxes and other networked items and just make things easier for you and me.

All that said, I am very happy with this purchase and would recommend this router, especially if you have remote in-home networking needs such as remote TVs, etc. Just be prepared for the chance that you may have to do some customization while setting it up.

A note to those who have experienced firmware issues. This is the type of thing that the suppliers should really a) take care of and b) make a heck of a lot easier to remedy. I feel lucky that mine does not have these issues. In all honesty though, the capabilities are quite impressive.

title: Apple Users Beware (i.e. Airport Extreme and MacBook users)
text:
Apple users beware.....this drive does not play nice with Apple and PC devices on one network. It is also not "Mac Ready" out of the box. It is formatted with NTFS which Mac's can read, but can't write to. You can reformat the drive to HFS+, but then your PC can't read it or write to it. You can partition the drive into separate NTFS or HFS+ partitions, but then computers on your network can't read each other's files unless you buy third party software (i.e. MacDrive for the PC). Last option is to format it to use FAT32, but then you're limited to 4 GB size files, which makes it difficult to backup movies, etc...

I bought the 4TB Fantom Gforce3 and there are several other issues with it:

1. It does not play nice with an Apple Airport Extreme. The drive stops spinning after a few minutes and the Airport Extreme does not spin it back up making it inaccessible over the home network. It will show up (sometimes) as a network drive, but then the folders in the drive don't have anything in them when you try to access them remotely over a network.

2. Because of the above problem, it seems like TimeMachine on a MacBook wants to do a full backup every time and not a partial backup once the full backup is complete. This takes a very long time over WiFi. The drive appears as a new drive when it spins back up. In addition, backups on TimeMachine fail unless you have the drive spinning, which you can accomplish by unplugging both the drive and Airport Extreme and restarting both. This is hardly a good solution for accessing the drive and will allow access for about 5-10 minutes while the drive is still spinning.

3. It caused the Blue Screen of Death (BSOD) on my Windows 7 Desktop PC when I hooked it up directly to the computer and tried to access the drive over the network as an external drive attached to the PC through a MacBook running Mavericks. This didn't happen when I tried to access the drive with a MacBook running OS X, but the folders were empty (again). Not until I accessed the drive directly through the PC did the files in the folders become visible remotely on the MacBook running OS X. BSOD occurred ever time I tried accessing the shared external drive with the Mavericks MacBook.

Summary:
I basically bought this drive to serve as a network "Cloud" storage device which all my devices on the network could access and backup their data to. Based on the issues above, this drive can't fulfill this capability. Hooked up directly to a PC or Mac, it seems to do ok. So, one computer = one Fantom drive. To use this drive, I would have to hook it up directly to each supported device to access files or backup data. I think the main issue with the drive is that it spins down to save energy and wear/tear on its internal components. This causes the drive to essentially become unreadable until it spins back up.....which it doesn't do on a network.

UPDATE: I returned the Fantom drive for a refund and purchased a WD My Passport 2TB USB drive. Plugged in the My Passport drive into my MAC, reformatted and partitioned it, plugged it in to my Airport Extreme, purchased 3rd party software so my PC can read MAC formatted drive......bottom line.....EVERYTHING WORKS LIKE A CHARM! I now have a network cloud storage device that works. Just confirms that the Fantom drive was a P.O.C.

title: Solid sounding clock
text:
After reading many reviews and listening to the sound of competing - and more expensive - models at different retailers, the price for this made it worth a try. I am very pleasantly surprised in a number of ways. First, in terms of sound, it is pretty impressive for such a small device. It definitely is not a unit to crank, but that's not the point. On the other hand, it fills our bedroom with reasonable quality sound when played at low to mid volumes. The lows are a little thin, but vocals come though very crisply and the mid-range is totally acceptable. Simply put, it sounds bigger than it is, but it is not a sound system.

Second, the form factor is very appealing. It is a smaller unit than the pictures make it appear - which is a plus for the nightstand in my opinion. The clock is dimmable and it is a very mellow orange tone. Consequently, it is totally visible, but does not light the room at night. It is slimmer and very understated in its appearance. My wife commented positively on its appearance, which is a rarity for most electronics.

I have read comments that are negative about the controls, but I see no problems. I actually like the dial control on top. I have some concern about the app for iPhone, but I will defer comment and judgment until I have used it for a while. As with most devices these days, the instructions are weak, so i will play with it on weekends until confident it will work reliably.

The dock options are good, but I have an iPhone case with a dock protector. So, I purchased the blue cel dock extender for $7 (high quality product as well!) rather than take the phone out of its case each night and synch is perfectly fine even with the extender.

The remote is a nice addition, but really it is best for adjusting volume and skipping song to song. Jumping between albums, playlists, etc, needs to be done from the the phone/ipod.

At the $45 +/- price point, it is an outstanding value. Sound quality and appearance are very slick for the money. Initial impressions are very good. Solid option for an iPhone alarm clock!

Update: If you do not synch regularly, this clock is not a great time keeper. It adds 2-3 minutes per week if not synched with my phone. Not a big deal, but a little silly in this day and age.

title: Makes My Life Easier
text:
I purchased the Satechi 12 Port USB Hub with Power Adapter & 2 Control Switches along with the [[ASIN:B001TH7GUU AmazonBasics USB 2.0 A-Male to A-Female Extension Cable (9.8 Feet/3.0 Meters)]] as a way to have more access and control of my USB devices. I mounted the Satechi Hub in the fairly useless inch-and-a-half tall center draw of my desk. Using Velcro strips I was able to place it on the left side of the draw with the power and extension cable running out the rear of the draw to power and the computer which is on the floor to the right of my workspace. I have several thumb drives that are used for various things right at my fingertips now, I also have a [[ASIN:B002USHTWM Smart Pad Multi-Touch Gesture Touchpad/Trackpad USB Mouse with Keypad for PC Windows 7/Vista/XP]] that I use in conjunction to a HP wireless multimedia keyboard (wireless receiver installed in hub), Microsoft USB Trackball and [[ASIN:B0018O9JIG IOGEAR USB 2.1 Bluetooth Micro Adapter (GBU421)]] that I use with the [[ASIN:B003DQ1DCM Sony Ericsson Hi-Fi Bluetooth Stereo Headset with FM Radio]]. My workspace is now very user friendly. No more messing with the tower when updating files to the various thumb drives and I have realized much better battery life of the keyboard now that the receiver is so close. The switches don't seem to play a part in the day to day usage but If I wasn't using any of ports, I could potentially turned off one side.

Overall, I am very happy with this hub and have not had any issues what so ever. I would absolutely buy this product again if the need presented itself.

title: Beware using with Mac
text:
Bought this from another vendor.
Was looking for a Blu Ray Drive to rip Blu Rays (hey don't judge me) on my Mac. This unit was reported officially to be compatible with Mac and I saw a YouTube video of someone who bought this and used it with their Mac. Chose this unit because it was cheapest in its class (External BD-ROM drives) that I could find and was on mail-in rebate.
You can see where this is headed... Plugged in drive to my mid-2009 Macbook Pro running Mountain Lion. Drive powered up when plugged in (used the dual USB cable included) but drive was not recognized by Mac OS. Did not appear in Drive Utility. Looked on ASUS website and followed their troubleshooting steps which did not help and did not solve the problem. There is no Mac OS software to be found on the ASUS website for this unit. Tried same on my early 2009 Mac Mini. Same thing- drive did not appear after plugging in.
Tried in a Win7 Bootcamp partition on my MBP. Again did not show up in Explorer when plugged in. Tried on my work WinXP laptop- same.
So maybe it was a defective unit. Will be returning. Not happy with lack of online support resources on ASUS website for this unit. Bought an LG CP40 external blu ray drive. Worked perfectly with my Macs but cost a bit more (worth it) and they don't even list Mac compatibility on their packaging.

title: Best Bang for your Buck
text:
I'll be honest, I never saw myself owning a tablet, but honestly I felt this one was a bit too good to pass up.

Pros:
- Cheap! If your not buying off of Amazon, you can find this tablet at $230.00. It's one of the cheapest on the market.
- 7 inch display
- Gripable back
- High resolution screen
- Very fast
- Runs Jellybean 4.2 (comes with 4.1)
- Updates now allow for keyboard swiping
- Compact, able to hold in one hand
- Good button Locations (on/off and volume are located at the side)
- No crashes, can handle multiple apps running at once
- Little to no heating, even when extremely active
- Great Battery life
- None slip air pockets on back
- Google now, Sbeam, and other awesome features
- HTML Browser
- Has 32GB of Flash Memory
- Has 720p video (comes with a quality cap that you can break with an app to get the full potential.)
- Has 1 GB of RAM
- Has GPS
- Has Blutooth
- Weight is .7 lbs and is well distributed
- Scratch Proof Corning® Fit Glass

Cons:
- Auto correct is sometimes dumb.
- No USB port
- No SIM Slot
- Poor speakers
- No back facing camera
- front facing camera has poor quality (1.2 MP). The Video is 720P, haven't tested it yet.
- No Flash Support
- No Radio (can stream online radio)
- No GPRS (Cannot connect to 4G, 3G networks, though there is a Nexus that can)
- No EDGE

Now something I love about this tablet is the screen resolution. 1280x800, it has better image quality than the iPad Mini. The Nexus 7 has 216 ppi compared to the iPad Mini's 163 ppi, overall the Nexus 7 has a higher density pixel display. My uncle, who works for Microsoft is envious of it's quality display when compared to his iPad Mini (he hates Microsoft products). The display has a contrast ratio of 908:1, which is very excellent. It's really too bad that there aren't amazing speakers to go with this amazing display, and that's the devices's greatest failure in my opinion.

The speakers are soft spoken, and when raised too high emit some weak strained audio. They work, they get the job done, but when it comes to watching some Netflix in bed, I get out the headphones. Otherwise they're okay for the on the spot you tubing and what not, they just could be better is all. Here are the stats on decibels:

Loudspeaker Voice 68dB / Noise 65dB / Ring 75dB
Audio quality Noise -69.8dB / Crosstalk -72.1dB

The keyboard is pretty intelligent and smooth. There have been updates since it's release and one of them included the swipe keyboard. It works really well. My only complaint is that occasionally it auto corrects something oddly, but that's not something an update could easily solve.

Now for me the camera wasn't a very big deal, it's primary purpose I assume would be for skyping. If I'm planning on a skype session, I would probably bring the laptop out. So I don't think I'm ever going to really need the camera. The camera genuinely sucks though, it's pixally and could have been a lot better. Still, I suppose when Google made it, they weren't really intending the user to take high quality photos with their tablet. I'll give them leniency here, since it's a fairly useless feature on a tablet anyways.

The Nexus 7 runs on 1GB of ram, and has a Tegra 3 Quad-core processor. Basically it runs very fast. It has yet to freeze up on me, not counting when a crappy app crashes. It can run multiple apps with breeze and smoothly transition through them. Apps load very quickly, as do webpages. Boot up is a matter of a second or so. I love how the unit doesn't overheat, ever.There are two very large copper heat sinks that surround the tablet that give it this ability. I've used this tablet throughout the entire day with multiple apps open, streaming videos, playing games, and it only gives off a mild warmth.

The system software itself is amazing. Jellybean works splendidly and is indeed very buttery. Transitions through apps are very graceful and pleasing to the eye. I personally like the color layout the system has (black and a particular blue text). The navigation is very easy to figure out and the tablet is very easy to use. There are a lot of system adjustments you can do, and my personal favorite feature is the message for the lock screen. I have an if found message, being the forgetful person I am I thought this was a nice touch since I don't want to sharpey my name on the device. One of the greatest featues of Android, in my opinion, is the ability to customize your device. There's a nice array of widgets out there, that and some neat live wallpaper. Unlike the iPad Mini, one Nexus' display could look vastly different than the next one, while the iPads only differ in background and App choices. The system is very simple and easy to use, very user friendly.

When it comes to browsing the web I've heard a few Flash complaints, since it runs HTML. There are several ways to get around this, but I thought I would just mention that no, the Nexus does not come supporting Flash. The Nexus 7 runs an HTML5 browser, and I haven't had any difficulty with it.

With 32 GB of space, you have some room to upload your favorite songs and movies, store some pictures. For $230.00, this is a great amount of memory. Honesty, its a steal, have a look at other tablets and their storage vs. Price - price range.

The battery is long lasting. One charge lasts throughout the day on heavy use. Using it lightly, it can last well over 100 hours. This thing is very efficient battery wise. The only thing that drains the battery is the GPS for obvious reasons. Streaming movies, I'd estimate it would last around 11 hours. I've read somewhere that this has to due with it's quad core, and it's extra core. This extra core only runs while it's in sleep mode. This alone helps vastly improve battery life, that and the quad core makes the Android overall very efficient.

Finally the design of the tablet. For some, the rubber-pastically like back may be unattractive, to me it's a plus. It prevents slippage, and while the iPad Mini's backing looks more attractive, on cold morning I'd be afraid of shattering it on the floor. There are small indentions all over the back of the Nexus for the purpose of creating more friction. It's supposed to allow a firm grip, even if your palms are sweaty. The face of the Nexus looks very sleek, it doesn't gather much smudge and is very simple to clean. I think the silvery lining around the edge of the device adds a nice touch as well. The face of the screen is made with Corning® Fit Glass, which is scratch resistant. I have yet to get a case for the device, but from what I can tell, there aren't even light surface scratches.

Also just a quick bit about Corning® Fit Glass, I'm guessing it's a Corning® product. Asus is using Corning® Fit Glass in all of its newly announced products. Earlier Asus stated that they would be using Corning®Gorilla®Glass2 in all of their 2012 products, so I'm not what's really going on. I'm assuming it's a Corning® product because the title is capitalized, "Fit Glass", on all of the product descriptions, other people assume it's just scratch resistant glass that Corning® fitted for Asus. Whatever your take on it, the glass has so far proven resilient for me, so they are probably using the same technique for making the product as they have for Gorilla®Glass, or better.

Here's Asus' statement on it: "ASUS TruVivid technology with Corning® Fit Glass for improved color clarity and scratch resistance."

Overall I love this tablet. It's certainly the best bang for your buck. It looks like quality, it feels like quality, best of all, it is quality. I enjoy the size, and feel the 7 inch screen is just right. I can hold this tablet comfortably in one hand, and could even fit it inside my pocket. It's the best deal out there when concerning price and quality. Comparing it to my Uncle's iPad Mini, I'd say it can do everything his can do, only cheaper. As for the Kindle Fire, it's nothing compared to a tablet running full Android with access to the Google app store. I've looked through the Amazon App store, there's such limitation on which apps can be used, it puts a limitation on the device itself. Kindle Fire is much too Amazon based for me, and I like the more open ecosystem that Google's Nexus 7 has to offer.

title: Formatted for Macs, likely to work with a PC
text:
When Amazon offered me the opportunity to review this product, I jumped at the chance. I was intending to purchase a new computer soon anyway, and the opportunity to try out a thunderbolt device and experience the faster transfer speeds I have read about was too good to pass up.

I was also excited to see that when purchasing from Amazon, the cord is included in the box. When purchasing from Western Digital, the cord is sold separately. This may sound like a small benefit, but given that thunderbolt cords can run $50-60, it's actually quite a nice perk.

Unfortunately, the Amazon product page does not, at the time of writing, say anything about whether this device is meant for PCs or Macs. I went to the Western Digital webpage to see what they had to say, and they say that the device is formatted for Macs. I am a PC user, and do not wish to switch to Mac because I use a number of industry software programs that are only available for PC.

However, I've seen a number of reviews lately of new PC motherboards and laptops that do have the thunderbolt connection, so I wondered if, despite Western Digital's initial formatting for Mac, the product might work just fine on a PC.
In order to figure that out, I called up Western Digital's support line (1 (800) 275-4932) to ask. They say that because the hardware for PCs is so new, they have not yet been able to fully test whether or not their devices work for a PC. In theory, they say, their device should work just fine with anything that has a thunderbolt port, because the manufacturers of thunderbolt friendly devices would have created the port to use with devices just like this one. But they certainly can't guarantee it because the hardware simply hasn't been out long enough for them to have tested their devices with these new configurations.

In order to use the drive with a PC, you'll need to start by formatting it because it comes formatted for Mac. Western Digital has instructions for formatting your drive on their website, and that should be pretty simple.

One disadvantage to using this product with a PC right now is that the drive utility software which allows you to switch from RAID-0 (fast) to RAID-1 (duplicating data for a dual backup) or JBOD (just a bunch of discs) is only available for Macs. However, the main appeal to me was using the RAID-0 setting, which Western Digital says is the default. (And for any computer newbies who are paranoid like I am, you should know that formatting your new drive will not change the default, as that is a hardware setting.)

Support staff did say that they are working on creating drive utility software for their drives that will work for the PC. Unfortunately, since PCs with the thunderbolt connection have been slow to come out, they are unsure of when exactly the drive utility software for PCs will be available. It partly depends on how fast the market embraces this technology.

As far as the benefits of this new technology, the faster transfer speeds speak for themselves. Support staff let me know that you can see some of the testing information for these devices in writeups from the recent CES tradeshow. It would be particularly helpful to have this kind of speed when doing things like video editing, 3-D design, or any other activity that requires fast storage or moving a lot of data constantly. It can be used as a scratch disk to load video or audio clips faster, to crunch numbers or to create a final file from a build file even faster. While a faster storage device will not make up for a lack of RAM on your computer, if you have a high-end device and use it for activities like these, you should see a major bump in productivity from the addition of a device like this.

Some other notes:

You can daisychain up to six devices.

You get 30 days of free phone support to help get you set up, and I was only on hold for about two minutes prior to speaking with a human being. There is also pretty good online support available.

Support staff are excited to talk with PC users and help walk us through any issues we may encounter. If you find that level I support does not know how to answer your questions, ask to speak with a level II support staff person since they will be eager to take notes and share the experience with the people working to develop the products.

I personally do not yet have a PC that will work with this device. Now that I've been able to speak with Western Digital and ascertain that it will probably be worth my while (and the extra cash) to invest in a PC with a thunderbolt port, I am eagerly researching the best models of motherboard and building my computer. I will absolutely report back as soon as I get my computer and am able to test this device with a PC.

title: A top performer
text:
This preamp has just about the highest gain and lowest noise figure of any consumer product on the market. In my experience, its real-world performance lives up to its specs.

If you need maximum gain, minimum noise, and reasonable price, this preamp deserves first consideration.

As an RF engineer who understands something of noise and its impact on communication systems, I also want to address a falsehood that seems to be floating around the Web lately. Some "experts" say that a preamp will only overcome losses in an antenna distribution system and will not actually "improve" performance. Apparently they mean that a preamp will not make weak channels receivable by boosting their signal level, their contention being that boosting weak signals also boosts incoming noise and provides no net improvement.

This contention is not true in many cases. It would be true only if the most significant source of noise in the system were ambient (i.e., coming into the antenna from the atmosphere along with the signal). Such is usually not the case at VHF and UHF--the most significant source of noise in these systems is often the receiver itself, particularly the first stage or two where noise has the most effect on performance.

A cheap DTV receiver or converter box is likely to be the limiting factor in reception; weak stations will simply not have enough signal level to overcome front-end noise in these components and generate the signal-to-noise ratio needed for the digital bitstream to be decoded successfully. In these cases, a high-quality preamp with a very low noise figure will definitely help, boosting signal level without adding much noise of its own and vastly improving the signal-to-noise ratio at the input of the receiver itself.

My own system is a case in point--I tested reception right at my attic-mounted antenna so there could be no "distribution losses." Without the preamp, I received two or three channels. With the preamp, I received 20 (counting all of the subchannels for each station).

So in short, a preamp CAN give you more stations to watch if it has a low noise figure--and this Antennacraft unit has one of the lowest that I have found.

title: I don't know what is with all the bad reviews....maybe there has been some software updates?? Mine works great!
text:
**See my other reviews for all the things I've tried on this consumer adventure I went on trying to find the right stylus setup (don't want to repeat reviews for all the products here)**
First I'll say I was VERY hesitant to buy this because of all the bad reviews, but I was at my wits end with trying to come up with a combination to take notes on my iPad. So After 2 Jot Pro's, a Musmee Notier, a Jot Touch 4, a Jot Script, and a couple screen protectors, I have finally found a combination that works and I am excited!

Purchase History - I have had an iPad mini retina with spigen glass screen protector since I bought the iPad. Love the glass but I could tell right from the beginning that it was a hindrance to stylus', even the normal rubber ones. I guess it is a longer distance for the touch signal to travel so no surprise there. So then I wanted to take notes on iPad so I got the Jot Pro and Musemee Notier. Neither worked well with the glass so I got Zagg Invisibleshield HD screen protector. Slapped that on, and still not very good. The musemee did better on Zagg but I hate the design of their tip. I tried to make the Jot Pro work with heat sink grease and scotch tape (you can look up all these fixes online) but none of them did the trick.

I was very frustrated at this point. So I bit the bullet and bought a Jot Script, and Spigen Steinhal Ultra Optics screen protector. I tried the Script with the Zagg and it didn't seem to work when it was off (I was misled by a video review of the script where someone was writing with it in the "off" mode so I thought it should still write when ON or OFF, however this is false. Even on the glass screen the Script would not write in the OFF mode). So I pull the Zagg off and put the Steinhall on, fire up the Script and it writes great. I am not the biggest fan of the Ultra Optics screen protector, but it does the job of protecting the screen and I can finally write notes with it.

I am not having any of the problems the bad reviews talk about...maybe it's because I have a mini retina or maybe they have updated their product recently, but the jot writes great and is really ease to use as a stylus anywhere on the screen (as long as the bluetooth is on and pen is powered up). The Jot Pro also works great too now with the Ultra Optics screen protector, so I think that will be my stylus set is the Jot Script and Jot Pro. The Jot Pro is nice because no power is involved, however the Script without a disk tip is really nice too. I will use and test out both but both perform well and write about the same. The pro actually probably writes a little better because there is a slight delay on the writing with the Script, but not enough to cause a problem.

One thing I regret doing is taking off the Zagg too soon. I think the script would have worked fine with the Zagg and actually this new Jot Pro is working with the glass on my phone so I think there might be some manufacturing variability in the Pro. Point being that I think this Jot Pro would have worked with the Zagg.

Well I feel like I've written 10 reviews for all these different things lately, but I found something that finally lets me write with a fine point on the iPad. GOODBYE PAPER! (in theory but we all know paper will never really go away)

title: Good value speaker for $59.99
text:
Before buying this speaker I narrowed down my choices to two wireless bluetooth speakers: The Logitech Z515 and the Jawbone Jambox.
Here are the main differences between the two:
- At the time of this post, I decided to go with the Logitech Z515 on sale at Best Buy for $59.99. The Jawbone was somewhere around $170 on Amazon.
- I've listened to both and I can confirm that the Z515 is at least twice as loud as the Jambox. However, I do think both are designed for different listening environments. The Logitech is better for an outdoor small sized BBQ or picnic, whereas the Jambox is so small it would not be loud enough for an outdoor event due to its acoustics. I recently took my Z515 to a picnic which had many tables and about a hundred of people with other loud music going on at the same time. With my Z515 on full blast paired with my Galaxy S2 phone, I played music for hours and it was audible for our own picnic table. The Jambox would not have been loud enough for that environment. - The Jambox has better sound quality, especially after updating the firmware through Jawbone's website. It made a HUGE difference. Although the Jambox isn't as loud as the Z515 it uses the acoustics of a small bedroom or apartment much better.
- Both the Z515 and the Jambox do not have a lot of bass being such small speakers so they are equal in that regards... however the Jambox has much lower bass frequencies and the little speaker will shake around if you are playing music that has a lot of bass in it!
- The volume on both can be controlled by whatever device you using to connect via bluetooth.
- IMPORTANT: The Z515 does not automatically connect to your bluetooth device when you start it up... for example you have to go into bluetooth settings in your phone and connect every time. However, the Jambox remembers your devices that you originally paired to it and automatically connects to it if it recognizes your source.
- The Jambox can also be used as a speaker phone for your bluetooth on your phone if you want to talk on the phone, however the Z515 does not have that capability.
- The Z515 is a little heavier and both are very portable, however the Jambox is so small you can fit it in your pocket. Both come with a protective cover to keep each speaker from getting scratched.

In conclusion, based on the features and the price points of $59.99 for the Z515 or $180 for the Jambox, the Logitech Z515 is clearly the better buy in my opinion. If the Jambox was louder, I probably would have shelled out the money for it instead since the sound quality is clearly better. However, the $120 price difference between the two is too large to ignore.

Edit May 2013: My brother bought me a Jambox for my birthday since Jawbone dropped the price to $120 back in November. Now that I have both the Jambox as well as the Z515, I use both for different situations. I take my Jambox on trips where I need a small portable speaker that doesn't need to be loud, and I take my Z515 on trips where I need to blast music and I also listen to it when taking a shower because it is loud enough to hear through the bathroom door.

title: Not quite what I expected.
text:
I don't want to say this is a bad telescope, because it gets the job done, but I can honestly say this was nothing like what I expected.

My biggest complaint is that (unless I'm doing something TERRIBLY wrong) the pictures of Jupiter on the Amazon site are very misleading. If you expect to be able to see images like that, you are going to be as disappointed as I was. Jupiter looks like a tiny white star, as does just about every other planet I try to look at. It's still cool to look at, and you can make out the two moons (as two tinier dots), but it doesn't look anything like those pictures. The only really cool planet to look at is Saturn, because you can see the rings, but it's still a tiny thing.

Other than that, the SkyAlign feature hasn't worked very well for me either. I would line up three bright stars (or two and the moon), it would say it was aligned, but then it would never point at the right thing. This could be user error, though, as I don't see many complaints about this.

If you want to look at the moon, this thing is great! You can really make out the craters and everything. It's also good for just general star gazing. This is my first telescope, so it's entirely possible that my complaints are just inexperience. It's just for $500 I expected a much better view of the planets than what I got.

One last thing I'll throw out there is that the camera attachment (sold separately) doesn't seem to work to well either. I actually got better pictures with my iPhone through the lens piece than I did with a Nikon D5000 using the attachment.

If I'm doing something wrong with this telescope, then PLEASE someone let me know and I'll happily change my review.

title: Extreme compression and missing bass.
text:
EDIT (2013-04-30):
I just found out that if I am charging this bluetooth receiver at the same time that I am streaming music, the device gets too warm and cuts off the audio. This happens through a 12v car charger. I tried using different plugs in my car; one in my dash and one on my console. I also swapped charging cables and used both my Belkin 12v-to-USB adapter and Scoche adapter. In either case, within two minutes of my car turning on, the audio fades out while I'm streaming music. If I unplug the USB charger, the audio immediately snaps back to full volume. After two to three minutes of use (charging + streaming), the device gets incredibly hot to the touch. I have initiated an return in order to send this product back for a refund.

--------
ORIGINAL REVIEW:

First the positive notes:

The device is smaller than I expected. It reconnects to my iPhone 5 nearly instantly when it turns on, so I don't think I'll have to worry about fixing pairing issues.

Now the negatives:

1) The package comes with the device, a micro-usb cable for recharging the built-in battery, and a 3.5mm jack female-to-female adapter. The adapter was completely broken on the inside; I could not plug in my Bluetooth or headphone into either side of it. It made a "crunch" sound, and inserted off-center.

2) The sound is best described as "tinny". Unlike other Bluetooth streaming devices from Motorola or JBL, this one completely cuts the bass out. Only the frequencies reserved for treble is passed through. Cranking the EQ on your computer or car will only end up making the "booming" midtone sounds, but it will still lack bass.

3) There's extreme compression on any audio, to the point that it sounds like an FM transmitter rather than a Bluetooth connection. I used to own a Bluetooth ver. 1 device (Bluetooth is up to its 4th revision now), and it sounds on-par with that 1st generation from nearly a decade ago.

I connected the Bluetooth to my car and my computer as the input, and streamed from a Samsung tablet and an iPhone. Any combination of testing yeilds the same result. The device is either defective, or it doesn't work as advertised.

It may seem harsh, but I will give this item a one-star rating. Although it works, I must say it doesn't work "as advertised" since cutting out 80% of an audio frequency significantly changes the tone of a musical piece that a customer will attempt to stream over this wireless connection. This is not a device that should be used for audio streaming unless you are fine with having the same audio quality as an FM transmitter (with substantially less bass).

title: Use your Camera to Format the Card
text: I purchase this for my Canon Rebel XT which I primarily use for my outdoor activities photos; like camping, hiking, kayaking, scenic, and etc.  Rarely do I use this camera for sport shots so the card's speed is not as much of a concern for me.  Initially I verified I could write and read file from the new card using my PC and taking a few shots with the camera, everything appeared fine.  But during its first field use after about 5 shots the camera displayed an error.  It occurred to me the volume format or block size on the card may not be compatible with the camera.  So I used the camera to immediately format the card in the field.  The Rebel XT recognized the card size and correctly formatted it.  After that I had no further problems and took about 50 photos that day.  I did do a few burst photos and the speed appeared to be very good.  Download speed through my PC's card reader was super fast.  Those people that have poor download speed should verify their card reader and PC supports at least USB 2.0, USB 3 would be better, and the hard drive speed in their PC is 7200 RPMs. USB 1 or a slow hard drive can greatly increase download time.  Also keep in mind a real time virus scanner can increase download time too.  Since the volume format and block size on the card can affect write performance those concerned about photo transfer time to the card may want to verify they used the camera to formatted the card.  The camera's programming should pick the correct volume format and block size for the best performance. Before performing the format you may also want to verify your camera is using the latest firmware version, if not consider updating it.  As far as reliability only time will tell.

title: Not bad, but not great either
text:
I got these primarily because I hate having a wire dangling from my head and getting in the way while I listen to music on my iPhone; especially when I'm on the move.
As far as sound quality, music through the Sonys is pretty decent. I'm comparing these to my Shure in-ears that are known for having some of the best sound reproduction qualities around. Compared to those the Sony set has slightly more bass and low mid-range which most genres can benefit from. So at least in this respect the Sony's meet the standards I was hoping they would.
The downside is that the plastic ear pieces are practically useless when it comes to blocking outside noise. I have to fiddle with them almost endlessly to get the right positioning and suction just so they will sit in my ears properly. And they move around so I need to keep messing with them. My Shures have the memory foam type ear pieces and are designed to go slightly further into the ear canal than the Sonys are so they have a much more stable fit and block outside noise much better. I've used those as just ear plugs at a few concerts. The Sonys barely block normal street noise, let alone the noise from being on a subway train during my commute. I have to have the volume at almost twice the level as I do with my Shures just to recognize what song is playing.
The other negative issue with these is that with my iPhone I do experience instances of the sound cutting out. However, it only seems to happen when I'm in heavily populated areas like the Times Square area of NYC. When I'm underground in the subway or in a more sparsely populated place, I don't have this problem. So it seems like it's probably due to some sort of external interference.
Anyway, the problem with the noise cancelling is a design flaw that I feel Sony should have accounted for. I don't think I'd have bought them if I'd known about it and I wouldn't recommend them to anyone who is planning on listening to music in a loud environment.

title: Great for what it does, inexcusable for what it doesn't
text:
The Coby Kyros MID7042-4 is a great, inexpensive tablet that is responsive and easy to use, but before you can use it you have to add some apps; many will find it refreshing to get an Android device without all the clutter, but some of that clutter is useful. When you try to add apps you'll discover that without a custom ROM you can't use Google Play and you can't add any Google-specific apps, like those for Gmail or Google Reader, so you'll have to make do with what you can find on GetJar and Amazon, which is admittedly a lot to make do with, but if you have something you love on your Android phone you may have to do some digging to find it for your Kyros, if it's even available. Some apps won't work with the Kyros or won't work well - I've spent weeks trying to get Astrid to work properly; it works, after a fashion, but I can't use the voice input or sync it with Google Tasks, so it's just short of pointless.

Aside from that the Kyros is a very good tablet and a pleasure to use for watching movies or reading and for the price it's hard to beat. [NOTE: I wrote this after buying the tablet for about $110, not $150+]

A note about shipping:
My tablet arrived on the very next business day after I placed the order, even though I asked for standard shipping; there was a slight imperfection on the screen so I sent it back and got a nice note of apology and a replacement tablet within three business days!

title: Not as great as everyone claims it to be
text:
Focusing

My lens have the common focusing issues that everyone else reported (that goes with all Sigma lenses I guess). I micro adjusted the focus on my 5d3 and it becomes sharp at MFD and 3 ft, but then on 6ft or infinity, it requires focus adjustment in the opposite direction. What's worse is, after 6ft, the amount of adjustment it requires varies depending on what focus point is used. All of that aside, even within the proper focus range (within 3 ft let's say), it shifts focus sometimes (2-3 shots of 10).

Vignetting

I will just say this openly, this lens is the worse lens I have ever seen when it comes to vignetting. On a full frame camera like 5d3, the corners are so dark, every picture will require post processing. Processing them requires quite bit of noise introduced around the corners and it looks pretty bad. If you shoot wide open in low light, dark backgrounds will be a big problem when post processing is applied to fix vignetting.

Underexposing

The lens randomly underexposes certain shots by 1/3 to 1 1/3 stops, which is massive. Coupled with vignetting, this makes the pictures look even worse. The theory is the metering of high end cameras probably don't work well with the aftermarket Sigma lenses. It might be fine on you rebel, but not on 1DX.

Noise

It has a squeaky noise that comes from the focus motor. It comes and goes, but certainly annoying and totally unacceptable when recording videos.

Sharpness

Yes, the lens is sharp. It's sharper than the sharpest Canon lens I have owned, but at what cost (see above)? Generally speaking, Sigma lenses were always sharper than the Canon ones (50, 85, etc), but they all suffer from similar issues. Seems like Sigma knows how to make a lens sharp and they know the sharpness is what appeals to this "prosumer" crowd - i.e. not professional in that they won't be able to fully assess a picture with all its pluses and minuses. Most people look at the sharpness of a Sigma lens, its cost (less than L glass), say "wow", and buy it. But the devil is in the details.

My "copy" is probably bad in terms of focusing (accuracy and noise), but the other issues I reported (vignetting and underexposing) are the characteristics of this lens and are common. It also boggles my mind that how this AF is just completely random when it comes to Sigma lenses. Why can't they get this right?
