title: I can't believe after all of the research that I did, I don't like it.
text:
I sew a lot, so I keep movies and tv shows streaming on my computer for entertainment. I'm also read a lot. I also buy a lot of music. All of these things have Amazon in common. I am a good customer. So since my computer was suffering under the weight of all of those downloaded files and since I was getting the blue screen of death about once a week, I decided to take action.
I researched and looked for a solution.
My thinking: if I could get a tablet that could take the Amazon content off my computer, I might be able to extend the life of my laptop. I looked at the Microsoft Surface and the Amazon Kindle seriously. I read all of the reviews, I put out messages to friends who have one or the other, I asked questions. In the end, mostly because of price and ties to Amazon, I opted to get the Kindle Fire HD 8.9". Since most of my online activity includes Amazon, I thought it would be the better purchase.
My first complaint is about the shipping service. I am a Prime customer. I deserve better shipping than what I got. Now, I do have many of my Amazon purchases sent to a PO Box. I know, how un-American of me, but I don't live in a sweet little neighborhood with mailboxes out front. I live in the wild west with directions to houses that go something like this: Go five miles out and take the only road that you see left. Go another 2.56 miles and when you see the bush on the left, turn right. Now, the UPS driver that serves our area knows all of us. He knows where we live, he knows where we work, he knows our children and where they work. He knows if he can get down our road if it rains, he knows who our friends are and where he can leave it if our road is impassable. Fed Ex sends a different driver almost every time. Packages get lost or left with the wrong person. No worries. They signed for it!! Now, if you were me, would you have your expensive Kindle purchase sent to your house or would you go ahead and have it sent to your PO Box. Most people can find the post office. Even FedEx. My Kindle sat at the FedEX facility in a large city in my state for 36 hours!!! There is no excuse for that. The post office does have expedited shipping, why can't Amazon use that? Or let me have the choice between UPS and FedEX on everything that I purchase. That would be great and worth the $79 that I spend every year to enjoy Prime shipping.
Right out of the box, I could have used a manual. I'm not stupid and I'm not of the "no tech" generation. I'm of the "it's passing me by" generation. The little iphone sized card called "Getting Started" isn't very informative. I found the on/off button and the volume. I found the USB charger outlet thing. That mini USB connection feels so fragile. I miss the big ones. They at least felt like you could plug it in and not be damaging it. The cord and the connector are stiff and I'm really worried that I'll mess those pins up when I plug it in. I don't care for fragile things. I like things with a more substantial feel.
So, I finally get my Kindle. Being so rural, I admit that my internet options are limited. But, I chatted online with someone from Amazon about the Kindle and the possibility that the internet wouldn't work. It does work, but it doesn't work like Amazon said it would. I said that I have DSL. I didn't hide anything. Internet reception is just ok. If you live in a really rural area and you have to rely on DSL, it is going to be slow. The Kindle will stream a little less well than streaming on your computer. It won't get better. You've been warned.
Next, I have had a few electronic devices. I was a technology geek for awhile, but just got tired of trying to keep up. So, I know some things and haven't a clue about others. Here is something I do know. Screens need to be calibrated. If Kindle has a way to calibrate screens, I haven't found it. Another good topic for a manual. The reason I say this is because when I try to move a book off of my device or from the carousel, I'm supposed to be able to put my finger on the image and hold. After holding, a menu pops up and says, "remove from device, or carousel" depending upon which screen you are in. This is the most frustrating procedure!! Six, eight times I placed my finger and hold and the image just shivers and there is no menu. And typing a help message to the Kindle crew was a disaster. The space bar wouldn't engage and if I wanted to move the cursor, I couldn't move it with a key, I had to place my finger on the message in the approximate position and hold. It took me 30 minutes to type a simple help message of 5 lines. The screen needs to be calibrated.
Next, my audible books didn't transfer. I had my audible account long before Amazon bought them, so my passwords were not synced. Last night, when I tried to use the help, I got a "contact us" (the awful email). This morning when I looked I got an explanation. I changed my audible account in order to use my Amazon credentials. Still nothing. There is no way, that I can find, that will let my Kindle know that I've made the changes. Help search was no help and this would be a good time for a manual. I still have had no word from the help team at Amazon. I also had trouble with my email account, but that did work itself our this morning.
Finally, as I'm checking out all of the features, I went into books. I downloaded several books and went exploring. I went into my ESV Bible hoping that I could take my Kindle to church (larger fonts). I could not figure out how to move around in the book. Once you are in it, any book, all of the options, like the back arrow and the home button disappear. Okay, maybe you access those buttons like the settings, you pull down with your finger from the top, right? No. I completely stumbled on tapping the book to get the options back. Manual. Or at least another little iphone sized card with helpful hints. Good Grief.
By this time, I'm pretty frustrated. I'm happy that I saved my boxes and that I opened everything carefully.
After sleeping on it, I got up this morning to take another look. I did get my email account on, but I still don't have access to my Audible account. I can access Prime Instant video and it will stream. Until the buffer is full, it pauses about every 30 seconds. I pause at the beginning and then once it buffers, I watch. But that dual antenna thing doesn't work in rural areas. That was the main question that I asked, and I always got the same answer: If you can stream on your computer, you can stream on a Kindle. True, but you neglected to mention that it doesn't stream AS WELL.

What do I like?
The picture and the video are good.
The sound is good.
I like the fact that I can move content from Kindle to Cloud and back again. That feature on the PC versions of Kindle and Unbox would have been very helpful and I wouldn't have found myself in that original predicament. Anyway, I'm glad to have that ability. That is probably THE reason that I won't return this to Amazon.
The core stuff that the Kindle is meant to do...works.
I uninstalled Unbox off of my computer this morning and regained 220 GB of space. My computer already runs a little better.

Bottom line: After taking some time with the Kindle Fire, I'll keep it. I think that it will do what I wanted it to do. It will take over my Amazon content. I can do my browsing on it. I don't go that many places. I can't watch hulu because I don't have a hulu plus membership and I can't watch anything on CBS, but I can still do that on my computer. I'm going to reserve judgement about whether I'd buy the Kindle again. Maybe in time, I'll love it or at least like it better.`

Two years and a couple of months later...I am revising this review down to one star. The battery died and there is no easy way to change it. There is a hard way, and I did that. My touchscreen is now useless. My Kindle is ruined. You can easily change the battery on everything from an electric toothbrush to a television remote to a cell phone to a car key fob. But, Amazon made a product that is really, really hard to install a battery into. That is inexcusable. I regret buying the Kindle Fire. I am also phasing out my business with Amazon. It will be hard, but I think it's necessary. Any company who deliberately makes a product that will fail after two years (the tech support says the Kindle battery is good for 500 starts or about 2 years) and doesn't give a repair option is just wrong. I'm not asking for a warranty; I'm not asking for free; I'm asking for the option to repair, not buy new. Tech support said, "sorry, you are out of warranty, there is nothing we can do." Bye, Amazon.

title: A couple of quirks, but well worth no monthly fee!!!
text:
5/5 rating for more piece of mind! 4/5 in the end for a few gotchas that you must be aware of on an iPhone (not tested on Android). 

Back Story
========
I got this for my mom who is in final stages of life. She lives alone, but does have two different neighbors right next door who have always been there to help when she needs even the smallest of things. She is a diabetic and has lately had a hard time keeping her blood sugar levels normal (a few ER trips from that), her walking has become more impaired, and I live across the country, so I also worry about her from afar. 

Piece of Mind
==========
This device has helped give us both a bit more piece of mind with us being so far apart.  It helps me to know that if she is in trouble, she can reach me to help her get ahold of 911 and then anyone else. 

The Device
==========
The device is a small pendant the diameter of a quarter and a little over an inch thick.  One side of the pendant is depressable. It can be attached to a thick, rubber watch band (included), or worn like a necklace; a necklace loop attachment is also included, but the chain/rope can be anything you choose.  For ease of use, explained below, I recommend a necklace setup. 

Setup
=====
V.ALRT requires an Android or iOS device that supports Bluetooth 4.0. Modern phones and a few versions back are A-OK. Detailed setup instructions are included in the box, and are relatively simple for a caregiver to follow. 

Usage
=====
To use the device in an emergency situation, just press and hold the pendant for about five seconds, Once you release your finger, the device will blink slowly between red and green, letting you know it has been triggered.  Under default setup, the phone will start an alarm sound as well. Also, if Fall Detection is enabled in the app, a fall will give the wearer 60 seconds on the phone to cancel activation. 

How It Works
==========
If there is an emergency will call and/or text up to 3 contacts in your phone. 

## Calls
The app call each call-enabled contact in order. It doesn't actually use the phone app. Rather, it makes a voice call using the V.ALRT app itself. As of this writing, **the recipient contact will be receiving a call from (888) 909-4944**, so be sure to add this into your contacts (I labelled the contact V.ALRT).  The reason for this in-app call (at least in iPhone-land):

* Apps that trigger calls to the phone app require the owner to confirm that they want to make a phone call.  In this case, that may not be possible. 
* Even if it could make a phone call to the native phone app, speakerphone would not be enabled, so the person in distress and the callee wouldn't be able to hear each other if they can't put their phone to the ear. 

If the person does not answer and/or it goes to voicemail, once the call ends, the app will begin calling/texting the next contact in the list. 

## Texts
The texts, by default will include a link to Google Maps with the distressed or incapacitated persons location, as well as a callback number that, when called, will be auto-answered by their phone, and even placed on speakerphone (same experience as the aforementioned phone call).  Also explained above, texts are sent using the V.ALRT service, so expect a text from (419) 800-0998. I put that number in the same contact as the V.LRT contact. 

## Cancelling the Distress Signal
If the device wearer has regained mobility and control and they'd like to stop the string of calls, they can open the app and press the cancel button to cancel the alert--pretty straightforward.   

Things to Note
===========
## App Needs to Always Be Running
Because the pendant needs to be able to send commands to your phone, the app always needs to be running, at least in the background. iOS, however, tends to shutdown unused apps now and then, or if your phone battery dies or your phone is shut off or restarted. Luckily, you will receive a push notification if this happens, and the pendant will also make a tiny beep every 10 seconds and flash a red light if this happens. To remedy, just reopen the app. It's not too much of a hassle once you understand that periodic issue. 

## Bluetooth Must Stay Running
Bluetooth must remain running in order for your pendant to stay connected. The app and pendant will let you know if they become disconnected, and sometimes, even with Bluetooth on, I've seen this happen, but it reconnects automatically in just a second. The app will also notify you that it is reconnected.   

## Fall Detection
While my mom and I haven't tested a *true fall*, I have dropped the pendant four feet from the grond, and it does immediately go into alert mode, so I do feel this should work satisfactorily. However, **this feature is not enabled by default**.  You must do this in the app. Also, I have a feeling fall detection will be more accurate if the device is worn as a necklace instead of on the wrist. 

My Final Thoughts
==============
I refuse to fork out $50/month to something like Life Alert when I have found a device that pretty much does something similar, especially since I never miss a call from Mom. Even though there are a few things to be aware of regarding keeping the phone and the device connected, it's still worth a single $59.99,  i think Mom can handle the few understandable quirks.  Although I have found little advertising V.ALRT on the web, I think they have an amazing product available, and should work to spread the word about this more. It may not be the go-to to every situation, it does enough to make us feel like Mom has one more lifeline if she needs it. Well done, VSN Mobile; I will definitely be recommending this to others!

title: Good display, could use documentation, slow interface.
text:
I like this display (and the 4x20) because the I2C only requires a couple processor lines for it to work. I've thrown a lot of updates to it and I haven't had any communication protocol issues (which I have had with other similar displays).

The backlight is bright (draws about 15mA at 5v) when on and the backlight (on/off) can be controlled with the I2C bus. I removed the jumper and used PWM to control the brightness. The pin with the "LED" next to it should be used if you're going to do this. I put a 330Ohm resistor in series which draws 5ma (instead of 15mA) and is still bright at 5v. Don't use 10ms PWM cycle as you might see some harmonics (flickering) with the display refresh at around 50% duty.

The display (w/o backlight) draws a little over 5mA at 5v.

What I don't like:
Documentation. Finding information about the LCD1602 controller and the PCF8574 I2C chip wasn't bad, but there is no schematic of the I2C board. Having this would have saved me some time in reverse-engineering. Like another poster, I re-wrote the drivers. What SainSmart include isn't exactly correct for Arduino.

4-bit interface: Even though the I2C chip supports 100Khz, each character write requires four I2C writes to latch in data (if you actually abide by the lead/hold times of the LCD1602 controller). I think the driver provided uses a separate I2C access for each write (1add+1data x 4) which will take >700usec per character. Re-writing the drivers, you can do this with only one I2C access (addr+4data), but that still means each character will take >400usec to send. Still, unless you want to wait for the I2C bus, I recommend using an interrupt driven/buffered I2C driver.

title: Research your product better
text:
The camera itself works fine, it is an issue with one of the bundled items that is a problem. When a vendor offers a much coveted item such as the ROAM Contour, and then adds value by including extras with the camera as a "bundled offer", all the bundled items should work with the camera. Whomever purchased the extra hard cases for the ROAM and then offered them as a bonus incentive to purchase from this vendor should have at least checked to see that the ROAM camera indeed fit the case. If someone checks the specs of the ROAM camera, they will note the ROAM is about 1/4" longer than most of the Contour cameras. The Contour ROAM with the lens cap on will not fit inside the hard case. Upon calling Contour, they acknowledged that the case that is generally offered for use with the Contour cameras does not fit the ROAM camera and they don't offer one that does.

After contacting Amazon about the issue, they had no other offer of remedy other than "sorry" (no partial refund, no credit, no replacement), and that they would make sure that the bundled offer of the hard case would be addressed. I see it has not, so I am informing the potential buyer of the issue. I'm sure the vendor purchased this extra item in good faith as an incentive for the customer, but should ultimately be accountable for these types of issues, should offer remedy, and not lay the financial burden of "oops" upon the customer.

title: Decent earbuds for swimming
text:
I have used many, many different MP3 players for swimming. I swim one mile a day and could not get through the boring cadence without the help of music and I have found that these are the best ear buds I have ever used. I have found that the biggest weakness for any underwater MP3 players are the ear pieces. If you are kicking against a wall when making that reverse very few ear buds can take that pressure.

The H20 Sure 2 ear buds are good but pricey, but in the latest version the rubber ear pieces have become thinner and therefore collapse easier against the pressure of the water. My advice is to get some other rubber ear pieces with more durable rubber and substitute that rubber with the rubber that comes with these ear pieces. I have several of the older pairs that had the more durable rubber and have been using them in place of their newer thinner rubber pieces. But it's still a decent for use on your waterproof MP3 especially since many of those ship with even crummier ear pieces that are not very good at keeping water out.. Also the thinner ear buds are probably fine for most people doing light activity in the water but if you do a lot of lap swimming than follow my advice re the rubber portion. A couple of key items to remember when using these:

1. The cord is long so wrap the cord around the connector at the top where you plug it into the player. Use a bread bag tie thingy and wrap it securely. Don't use a rubber band as the pool water rots if fairly quick. You can also wrap the wire around the goggle bands as well. Despite this nit, I still recommend this product wholeheartedly. Now you can also get the short cord version.

2. Start with the larger ear bud rubber ends first then work your way down to the smaller sizes if that doesn't fit. If you use the larger sizes, you get a tighter barrier against the water. But again follow my previous advice on the rubber ear piece

3. You should consider wetting the ear buds lightly in the water before you place them in your ear, it seems to keep them more secure in your ear for some reason.

4. When you insert them in your ear pull back the top of your ear with your opposite hand, that will stretch it and allow the ear canal to gently wrap more snugly around the ear bud.

It is rare when the water enters the ear canal if you take these three steps and you will enjoy the music much better. Once water gets in your ear you are hosed for the rest of the swim and that goes for any ear piece. Happy swimming!

title: 9165T-LM could be better
text:
Let me begin by saying that I have always been a fan of the Magellan navigation devices. My first device was a Magellan, and then I went to Garmin, then back to Magellan. I paid a premium price for the Roadmate Pro 9165T-LM. It has a few good points but overall it has been a disappointment. One very positive point is the ease and accuracy of finding RV parks. They have a very good listing for RV parks, even those that aren't Good Sam parks. I have used the device to find over 30 RV parks and, so far, it has routed me accurately to the parks. Talking to other RV folks this is much above the average. I've only had to rely on it to route me properly for a large rig on one occasion. It did route me on a truck route as opposed to a tourist town with very small streets. This was through Estes Park, CO. The large screen is nice and easy to read. However, negatives are far worse than positives. Map updates are infrequent and not nearly as accurate or routinely available as my Garmin device. The day before I left for a trip I upgraded the maps on my Magellan and Garmin. Going through the recent new Interstate exchanges in Texarkana, TX the Garmin had all the new exchanges; the Magellan didn't. The unit locks up very frequently and requires resetting; sometimes while driving it requires a reset. On one occasion the unit was routing me through Port Isabel,TX and I took a one block long intersection, not on the device map, but clearly it had been there a long time, and the unit became completely confused. I turned in the direction that I thought was the correct way to travel to my next destination and the unit began telling me to turn around. I finally decided I was wrong so I turned around and the unit immediately told me to turn around again. I turned around again, now headed in what I felt like was the correct route, and it told me to turn around once again. I continued to travel in the direction that I felt was correct and it told me to turn around until I was about three miles from my destination, which was about a total of 10 miles from the intersection to the destination. If I hadn't looked at a map prior to the trip I would have had to have stopped for help. This was really frustrating. I've used the device to route me to over 100 point to point addresses and the accuracy has been fairly accurate but a few times it was completely wrong and misguided me.
Being a long time navigation system user I have learned to always keep a map handy, and this is true for any brand that I have used. However, this is an expensive unit with many problems such as, infrequent map updates, maps not as good as competitors, frequent lock up issues, and screen brightness issues during daylight hours, to name a few. Sorry Magellan, I just can't support you on this unit. I gave it three stars because it has some positive attributes but I really can't recommend it.

Update - I just experienced a bad trip with this device. I'm taking this down to two stars after the latest trip and I'm being kind giving it that many stars. On the latest trip it tried to avoid a well established ferryboat route and route us over an hour out of the way and I was not in RV mode. The navigation system continues to respond slowly, as it always has, and requires too many reboots.
This is the worst navigation device that I have used. In summary, it's too expensive, slow to respond, infrequent map updates, hard to view screen in bright sunlight, and routes you in bizarre ways to your destination. It has a nice large display, and does a good job routing to RV parks. That's the only two good things I can say about it. I dislike it and will never buy another Magellan product.

The problem I have is that I could never justify paying $200 to tune out the world while at the gym or on campus, especially while listening to my iPod. If you consider yourself an audiophile, you're probably downloading music as FLAC or as lossless as possible, or even on vinyl, which means you won't be storing that music on any media player.  But, to each their own.  If you like em, they I say buy into the fad.  If I wan't truly amazing sound quality, I'll listen to my music at home; I can't focus on it well enough regardless of who's logo is on my headphones when I'm out and about. title: Yamaha YHT-397 Review
text:
I bought the Yamaha YHT-397 last week and set it up when it arrived a few days later. Along with the system, I ordered RCA AH16100SN 100 Ft. 16-Gauge Speaker Wire (it comes with very thin speaker wire) and the Atlantic speaker stands for the rear satellites. Overall, I'm satisfied with the product. This is my first venture into the home theater realm and feel like I made a good choice. To clarify, I planned on getting this basic setup and upgrade the speakers as time goes by.

Receiver: The receiver has many different sound functions. These settings range from various movie to music (2.1/5.1) categories along with the obligatory surround sound category. Here's an example of the sub-settings in the movie category: Standard, Spectacle, Sci-Fi, Adventure, Drama, Mono Movie, Sports, Action Game, and Role Playing Game.

Also, I believe this receiver is equivalent to the Yamaha RX-V373 5.1-Channel AV Receiver which Amazon is currently out of stock; I think it retails for around 250 or so. It has 4 HDMI inputs which is plenty for my purposes; Additionally, it has various composite and component inputs as well as audio only inputs.

Speakers: The speakers are adequate.. nothing really to praise as they do an okay job. Definitely plan on investing in better speakers down the road, if so inclined. The speakers fit very well on the Atlantic speaker stands. Be aware: the speakers all have the clip down mechanism for speaker wire (opposed to banana plugs). In regards to the sub woofer, it is my favorite part of the system as it can handle what I throw at it with ease. Even at half power, the sub woofer creates monstrous bass that I can feel from across the room. However, one downside to the sub woofer is that it needs to be manually turned on so don't keep it in an enclosed, hard to reach area.

Summary: If you are looking for a home theater setup on a budget, I'd recommend the Yamaha YHT-397 5.1-Channel Home Theater System with the additional recommendation of upgrading the speakers later on.

*The included speakers are rated at 6 OHMs so change the receiver settings using. The manual will direct you in how to do this.

title: illustrations of how to improve this excellent product
text:
As matt noted on February 28, 2010, Henry Cargen made an excellent suggestion on March 25, 2008 about how to modify the Bayco K-100 150-Foot Cord Reel. Some readers may be helped by illustrations of the idea, so I have uploaded six pictures.

The first picture shows a brad-point drill bit with a diameter slightly larger than the diameter of my 16/3 extension cord.

The second picture shows the hole that I drilled with the bit. I positioned the hole so that the extension cord can wrap three-fourths of the way around the spool after passing through the hook-like clip. As the next picture helps to show, this three-fourths wrap around the spool has a purpose. To thread the cord through this hole, it is necessary to snip off the cord's original outlet. The original outlet's replacement is shown in the fourth picture.

The third picture shows how the cord wraps three-fourths of the way around the spool before threading through the hole that I drilled. This wrap keeps the edge of the drilled hole from cutting into the insulation of the cord--especially if the reel is fully unwound and the cord is yanked.

The fourth picture shows the cord end after I threaded it through the hole and attached a Leviton grounding cord outlet (012-515C-0OR), which I bought at a local hardware store. The outlet protrudes from the hub of the reel far enough to provide a handhold when plugging in or unplugging a power tool, but not so far that it whips around when the reel is unwound quickly. I plug the free end into a wall outlet and walk briskly to the spot where I'll be working; there's no problem even when the reel spins quickly.

Also note in the fourth picture that the connection between a power tool's plug and the extension cord's outlet is situated up at the hub (above ground). This elevated position adds safety by keeping the moisture-vulnerable connection above wet grass or snow.

The fifth picture shows the reel ready to be wound up. Note that a clockwise turn on the crank will pull the cord into the lower side of the spool (below its axis). This closer-to-the-ground point of entry makes it easier to stabilize the reel when rewinding the cord.

The sixth picture shows a handy optional touch. A small rectangle of prickly (hook-side) Velcro on the side of the plug keeps the cord from unwinding when one carries the spooled-up unit.

title: Too many annoyances add up to a poorly designed tripod + broke in two places after 1 year
text:
UPDATE - New review:

After using this tripod for about 18 months, I cannot recommend it. Yes, the legs are sturdy, but that's where the greatness ends. Here are the problems I've had with it; most are minor, but they all add up to make one of the most frustrating tripods I've ever used:

Major issues:
-Tripod broke after 1 year; one of the legs is jammed shut. Shortly after, one of the knobs on the head got stuck and will not move
-Ball head quick-release with the orange button is horrid; my camera fell off of it completely a few times; the one time I did not catch it, it luckily landed in snow -- otherwise it would have destroyed my camera
-Grey push buttons for tripod leg extension are terrible in design and frustrating to have to push/pull out

Minor issues:
-Quick-release plate is TERRIBLE; if you get this tripod, buy a different one ASAP.. It comes loose all the time and is obnoxious to try to tighten again, especially when out shooting
-Button to push to move tripod column up and out for rotation is a flawed and annoying design decision
-Carrying case is horrific and a real pain to carry - it swings around all over and is so uncomfortable it will leave marks on your shoulder (in some cases bruise); I thought this was just me, until I went on a backpacking trip with friends and some other people carried it. Immediately they complained about how awful the bag was and it was thrown around between people. We all joked about throwing the tripod off the cliff but we didn't want to litter.
-The swivel system is clunky and locks into awkward positions (unfortunately this is the case with all similar tripods I've used)

Overall, I got a different tripod+ball head combination for $50 that is similar with most of the above issues gone. I am glad this thing broke and forced me to get something less frustrating.

**********
Old Review:

Overall I'm happy with this tripod but it's not without its problems. It's sturdy and strong and generally high-quality (except for a couple of plastic pieces). Tilting and moving around are very smooth and the wheels and screws tighten/loosen smoothly. It comes with two quick-release plates, which is great if you have multiple cameras or a telephoto that you need to mount. The bag is very nice as well.

However, there are a couple of things that bother me about the tripod:

1. In order to extend the legs farther out, you have to press on these grey buttons on the side. In order to press them, you have to first push the legs in a bit then press the button while pulling the leg out. This is a terrible design decision. I don't have 4 arms and in order to do this without frustration I have to set -everything- down and focus on adjusting the legs.

2. I don't know if this is common among tripods with this tilt feature but the method of switching from standard tripod to tilting the central bar is horrible. After loosening the screws and pulling some odd switch out, you have to pull the central column all the way up, while holding a little bronze button, then shoving it up harder til it pops loose (but not past the 'stop here' mark). 50% of the time the column goes flying out of the tripod and I have to wiggle it back in. This is extremely time consuming and annoying. I don't know why they couldn't have made this easier.

So, having said that, my opinion is that this is a fantastic tripod for anything BUT macro. It's fully capable of getting down low for some neat macro shots (or unique perspectives) but to get there requires some frustration.

title: Amazing! Blazing Fast!
text: I have a Mac Pro 3,1 2008.  I realized too late that the Samsung 840 Evo 1TB I just bought was getting slow speeds than I was expecting.  Turns out the Mac Pro I have only has SATA II and not SATA III.  My only alternative was the Apricorn Velocity Solo x2.  After reading other people's review on it, I decided to give it a try.  It's EXACTLY what I needed.  Right now I'm getting speeds of 496.7 MB/s Write and 504.7 MB/s Read!  Before I bought the Samsung 840 Evo, I bought the OWC Mercury Accelsior_E2 PCI Express SSD 500GB.  The concept is great but it doesn't work with Bootcamp.  They say it's advertised on the webpage but it's worded clearly.  So after 3 days, I had to return it where they tried to charge me 15% restock fee and when a product is nearly $700, 15% is a big deal.  I complained enough where they waived it.  With the Apricorn, there is no trouble at all with Bootcamp.  Works perfectly as it should.  And my speeds are nearly exactly the same as OWC Mercury Accelsior_E2.  The card ALSO has a sata extension to add a second SSD for RAID 0.  When you do this, you get even higher speeds into 700MB/s to 800MB/s.  From what I've read the SSDS have to be the same.  And there is some discussions that they SSDS when in RAID 0 can deteriorate the drives over time but there is no real evidence of this.  The only downfall about these PCI-X cards is that on boot, they have to warm up a bit before it starts.  OWC card was doing the same even after they released a patch that was supposed to fix that.  Also if your restarting from OSX and booting in Bootcamp, it sometimes freezes up as someone else mentioned in a previous review.  He solved it by shutting down from OSX and starting up fresh in Bootcamp.  Knowing this after reading his review, I tried it and it worked fine.  No real big issue for me.  Overall, a great piece of hardware.  I would recommend it to anyone who is looking to upgrade their computer especially a Mac Pro 2008 or later.

title: Great value, but experience could be better
text:
[Impressions after 2 days of use]

I bought my Portege Z835-360 unit (Core i3, 4GB Ram, 128Gb SSD) on May 26, 2012 for $749.99 which is a very good price (2 weeks later and it's $699.99 already... oh well, technology). I decided not to go more upscale with the specs 'cause there are important compromises made by this and all other Ultrabook models as they all belong to the first round of Ultrabooks ever (Toshiba Portege, HP Folio, Asus Zenbook, Acer Aspire, Dell XPS13,etc.). So more money for better specs (Core i5, 6GB Ram) would not make up for the weaknesses of this model. As reviewers have all stated, Toshiba's is the one that offers the most for connectivity and ports. So that plus a very good experience I've had with my current (or should I say "old") Satellite A505 made my decision not-as-hard as it could have been.

Overall, it is a terrific value.
- Nicely priced. I think it is the cheapest Ultrabook around (and I don't mean it the bad way).
- Good Built Quality.
- Insanely thin and light. I think lightest of all 13-inchers.
- Good screen size. I don't perceive it as little or cramped (and I'm coming from a 16" screen)
- Full array of ports (1 USB 3.0, 2 USB 2.0, full-sized HDMI, Ethernet, VGA, mic and headphone jacks, SD)
- Decent sound. C'mon. It's a thin & light 13". Don't expect that much.
- Excellent battery life. I haven't drained it yet but it should be over 6 hrs of light use (no watching movies nor playing games).

Aspects that hamper user experience:
- Keyboard. This is my biggest complaint. Shallow keys and lack of feedback. I really have to type hard (meaning effort and noise) to have a confident and fast typing. It tires me after a long e-mail. Light years behind the experience when typing in a Sony Vaio.
- Fan. It kicks in without me having to do heavy tasks. It just runs every now and then, and has a high-pitch sound. Not that big deal for me, though.
- Touchpad. In theory, I like the regular touchpad with the 2 click buttons (at least in other laptops). But in practice, I find the buttons very hard (I mean, very hard) to click on. To left-click, at least I can double tap, but damn it with the the right click... Now, I think a clickpad would have provided a better user experience. Nitpicking, the 2 buttons are very shiny and attract a lot of fingerprints. Plus, they don't go with the design and style. So, why??
- Design. Nitpicking again. It is boring (especially compared to the A500, A660, P750 series) and it does look like an 80's laptop.
- Hard Drive Size. 128 GB is just not enough. I installed MS Office, Skype and Avast Anti-virus. Only 70 GB left.
- About screen. The lid is indeed very thin, flexible and flimsy. I haven't experienced any issues yet. But also, I haven't carried the laptop around or out of the house to really test it. I will soon.

I would highly recommend this Portege Z835 for anyone looking for power on-the-go. At this price point, it is the most attractive offer available.

I hope this review will become useful for anyone looking for an Ultrabook and seriously considering to buy the Portege. Should my impressions change in the following weeks and months after longer-term use, I will update!

title: It gets the job done...
text:
I purchased both the Eco Extreme and the Eco Terra, as I wasn't sure which would be the better fit. Plus I wanted to see how loud both of these things were. Seems like the only reviews I could find in video format were of people just throwing them in water.

The Eco Terra is significantly louder than the Eco Extreme. Is it $100 louder? Well no, but it does have some other perks that certainly make it worth the extra money. The Terra is the perfect size for toting around anywhere. Not heavy at all, and it has the nice shoulder strap and (4) attachment points (two on front, and two on back). It is a sturdy piece of equipment. The speakers sound better on the Terra also, most likely because it has a larger speaker housing that doesn't share space with your MP3 and personal items, like the Extreme does. I compared them side by side on batteries and the Terra dwarfed the Extreme in volume and sound quality. I LOVE that the Terra has buttons for controlling the iPhone. If you are going to use it with an MP3 player, just set up a playlist. I usually just use Pandora on my phone and I can skip, pause/play, as much as I want. I do wish this had a remote, though. The speakers are nice and loud and filled our entire community pool with music. I did not experience any static/distortion at any volume. I kept the iphone at one click below full volume and had the Terra all the way up. The center compartment is well sealed and held my phone nice and snug. The carrying handle is also a nice touch.

The Eco Extreme would be good for when you need something small to stuff in a bag, but I was looking for something for the pool, beach, and lake that I wouldn't have to worry about getting wet, and I wanted to be able to hear it from a distance. The Extreme had a hard time standing up straight. There really isn't a good flat area on the device to keep it upright with the speaker facing you. However, the Terra gets the job done very well. Keep in mind, these are waterproof speakers, so you can't compare the sound quality to those of regular boom boxes. This product was EXACTLY what I was looking for.

I use the Terra at home in my garage using the A/C power adapter when I'm not out and about with it. When at home, I use the Aux port on the back with a nice long cable, so I can keep my phone or ipod on the workbench and just control it like normal. That is a nice option to have.

title: Like Having a Brand New TV [temporarily]
text:
The original lamp in a six-year-old projection television had been going for some time, with the picture getting so dim that the television was almost unusable in daylight. It finally blew with a "pop." Although this replacement worked very well, it only lasted 6 months.

The new replacement lamp [from Amazon seller Dynamic Lighting], installed easily in a few seconds and the television is back to operating with a picture more bright and clear than it has been in years. The replacement seemed equivalent in every way to the original unit and superficially of equal quality. Unfortunately, it lacked the same longevity of the original bulb and needed replacement again just 6 months later. That said, I can't really say if the issue is the quality of the bulb or if the set has developed a bulb-blowing tendency; and, even replacing them at that rate is affordable and a whole lot cheaper than a new television. So, a second one is on the way.

Update: Second replacement lasted nearly two years. Hopefully, I'll be ready for a new tv before the 3rd replacement blows.

text:

Based on the reviews here, I finally decided on this one, and I'm happy to say it's PERFECT!

It charged quickly connected to my MacBook Pro -- about 2 hrs, maybe a little less. Turned it on, turned on the iPhone, went to the "Settings" on the phone, found Bluetooth, and there was the JAM XT. Selected it, and voila! they paired. Entire set-up took about 10 seconds.

I listen to a lot of classical music, so my first "test" was the Brahms "A German Requiem" -- lots of highs, lows, soft, loud, etc. Strings, voices, woodwinds, brass -- it's all in there. Everything sounded great -- nearly as good as my Bose system, but without the bass resonance.

OK, so I haven't had this very long (about a week), so its durability remains to be seen. But I'm impressed with the quality and style of this. If I notice any issues, I'll update this review.

Meanwhile, I can now fall asleep to great sounding music from a small-footprint speaker. And that's exactly what I wanted.

title: Does its job with a few noticeable flaws
text:
I bought these to avoid running cables through my apartment, which has an extremely inconveniently located coax port. They definitely work at a basic level. I have three main complaints about them:

1. I was unable to achieve a high quality signal between them.

Maybe the fact that I'm in a building with so many residents causes noise in the electrical system, but I had a difficult time finding two plugs to use that provided adequate performance on these devices. I eventually ended up running a short cable under a carpet in one room to get a plug closer to a middle wall and then running a cable under a bed in another room so that the two devices are as close as possible to each other.

Even so, the performance listed by the Powerline Utility app is 40-60% between them. This comes out to about 200mbps, so still faster than my internet connection, but much slower than my LAN supports internally.

2. The internet access cuts out occasionally.

The Powerline Utility claims everything is still working, but I'll randomly be unable to access the internet. This does not happen very often, but maybe a couple times a week. Researching this online suggested it might have to do with someone testing something in the electrical system, but since I'm in a large apartment building it's hard to really know what's going on. In order to fix it, I have to unplug one of the units from the wall and plug it back in again, which resolves the issue immediately.

3. The powersave mode doesn't always wake up.

I have the unit plugged directly into my computer's network port. Sometimes when I turn the computer on (most of the time), the Powerline unit does not wake up. I have to unplug the Powerline from the wall and plug it in again to activate the device. This is especially obnoxious because I plugged the Powerline in across the room in a hard to reach place to try and minimize the distance from the other Powerline unit.

I tried updating the firmware on the device, but the software claims this device is the wrong model or something. Running Firmware version AR-7400-MAC-5-2-5233-02-968-20120209-FINAL-B according to powerline utility. Googled this a bunch and tried different suggestions to no avail.

Summary:
All the above complaints notwithstanding, this device does still allow me to have internet without running ethernet cables down my apartment hallway. The actual performance is usually more than good enough, showing virtually no difference on speedtest.net compared to directly connecting. I mostly wish it would wake up when I turn the computer on and didn't randomly lose the internet connection from time to time.

title: Thin Paint on Rotting Walls
text:
I have about twenty years of technology experience, and about forty hours of it have gone into troubleshooting this particular festering pile of dog snot. Let me take you through a few highlights.

This product is an excellent example of why you always want to check four things before you buy computer hardware:
1. Did the card manufacturer make the silicon/firmware?
2. Are people experiencing problems, regardless of what operating system they're using?
3. Who provides driver updates? Do they work with my operating system?
4. Who provides firmware updates? Do they work with my operating system?

Let's go through these as they apply to this card in particular.

#1. Did the card manufacturer make the silicon/firmware?

Definitely not. That's not immediately a bad thing, but there are some reasons it's bad here. This product is a thin SIIG build around a Marvell 88SE9128 SATA3 interface and a small EEPROM (which holds a bootloader, some BIOS code, the main firmware, and possibly some configuration information). In fact, there is almost nothing else on the card except the physical interface ports, some LED headers, and some passives. That's it. So, clearly, SIIG has designed the packaging, and not much else.

#2. Are people experiencing problems, regardless of what operating system they're using?

Oh, hell yes. Severity is all over the map-- under Windows, people are mostly complaining about performance issues, specifically with SSDs. That can be tricky to troubleshoot, though, because SSDs have their own firmware issues. Under Linux, though, the problems are more severe. You'll find a lot more specific details and a very thorough discussion about those, because there are some very verbose debugging facilities in the kernel these days, and people have taken a good, hard look at this thing.

What they are seeing is drives that, when ordered to perform extensive SMART self-tests (and this problem is almost the poster-child for why the drives are supposed to conduct those tests WITHOUT controller oversight), test out fine-- but after a few megabytes of transfers through this piece of work, they start to hang. The basic problem seems to be that the physical link keeps going up and down. This is a serious problem that you normally associate with a bad power supply, but in this case it's because the card is reporting bogus CHS information, and the kernel can't figure out what the hell else to do, so it resets the link to try and reinitialize things. Nobody knows why the information is bogus, but I strongly suspect the transceiver silicon, because this chip has been embedded into a few motherboards (with different passive/termination designs), and people are reporting lots of problems there, too.

In my professional opinion, the poor performance people are seeing from this product under Windows is because those same errors are happening there as well, and being masked by the driver. There is some evidence to support this, but it's all closed-source so it's hard to know for sure without wiretapping the SATA link (which can be done). Obviously, that's less severe than flat-out failing, but it sure doesn't inspire much confidence.

#3. Who provides driver updates? Do they work with my operating system?
First, if you are using Linux, you should know that the Marvell chip in question has already royally pissed off the driver team that attempted to implement support for it. At one point, it basically didn't work at all; the "fix" in a particular patch was to blacklist Native Command Queueing (NCQ)-- with obvious performance impacts. Honestly, I'm not clear on whether that worked or not.

If you are using Windows, you can obtain drivers from SIIG by searching for "SC-SA0E12-S1" on their site. There are exactly two files: a completely bare driver with no installer whatsoever, and a "RAID Manager" that-- I am not making this up-- opens a _web page_ to manage the RAID controller, and requires-- I am still not making this up-- that you ENTER YOUR WINDOWS LOGON PASSWORD IN THE WEB PAGE to view it. I don't even want to think about the level of security malfeasance and design ineptitude that lead to requiring that, so, let's not.

In any case, the driver archive contains a bunch of different 32 and 64-bit drivers, with absolutely no installer whatever. Expect to have to go into the Device Manager and manually upgrade and install things, piece by piece.

#4. Who provides firmware updates? Do they work with my operating system?
Well, because Marvell did the silicon, Marvell provides the firmware.
To, uh, somebody.
Somewhere.
I presume.
They sure as hell don't provide them to YOU, End User-- search for "88SE9128" on Marvell's web site and all you'll get is a press release. You're supposed to go bug SIIG, since they built the card. If you've ever tried to get upgraded graphics drivers for the "mobile" version of a graphics card in your laptop, and gotten the runaround from nVidia or ATI, you have an idea what the situation is. So, that leaves you with SIIG.

Buried in that driver archive are two console applications. One of them is a RAID management app that is actually more or less what you would hope. The other is a FLASH utility to replace all the firmware. This is a _16-BIT DOS APPLICATION_, which _WILL NOT RUN_ on a 64-bit Windows system. Or, obviously, a Linux system. What most people these days are going to have to do is make a bootable USB stick with a _Windows 98 boot image_ on it (still not making this up). That isn't completely unheard of for firmware updates but it is a HUGE pain in the ass if you're not already set up to do it.

So then the big question is: is there a newer version of the firmware? Where do I get it?

Well, fear not. It turns out there is newer firmware-- on some weird hacker site in France. It is CLEARLY material that started life being forwarded from Marvell to an OEM, and it includes useful utilities for flashing the card (some of which appear to actually be _older_ than the SIIG driver). The firmware version is substantially "newer"-- but in my case, it didn't fix any problems, it just made the BIOS menu ("Press CTRL-M") go away. Oops. So, be careful if you decide to mess around with THAT stuff; I'm pretty sure it was intended for a version integrated into a motherboard. You might try upgrading _only_ the firmware and not the BIOS, and mixing and matching materials between the leaked version and the stuff buried in the SIIG driver-- but you'd better be a pretty serious hardware hacker.

I've had two of these damned things for months now, trying to get one or the other of them to run a pair of Western Digital Raptors on either of two different motherboards (an Asus and a Gigabyte, both recent). I have completely given up. I can't even get it to reliably run the freaking DVD drive. They weren't cheap, either, which is seriously ticking me off.

Furthermore, when configured as an actual RAID controller, you can't check the SMART status of the drives connected to it. As a result, I just use it as a passthrough SATA3 controller, and do software RAID, so that I can use smartmontools to check the drives. It ticks me off that this is necessary; even the Intel Matrix Storage Manager doesn't rule that out.

RAID controllers are expensive, so solutions abound-- thousand dollar cards, software RAID solutions, and motherboard solutions.

Whatever you do, don't use this piece of junk-- or anything else based on that Marvell chip. Or, in my opinion after using this thing, ANY Marvell chip. Consider Intel, LSI, whoever-- but watch out for RocketRAID cards built on the same problem chip (they have alternate designs; use those).

title: This is my third
text:
Good chargers for 4 cells are in the same price range as this 16 cell version. I have two La Crosse BC1000 which I use to perform refresh cycles but this charger is good enough for every day use and I only use the La Crosse / MaHa for infrequent maintenance.

This is an excellent way to charge a large number of batteries using a single power outlet. I have been using two of these chargers for a theater troupe that uses 23 wireless microphones (lavs) per show. The lavs run about 8 hours every evening and this charger always registers fully charged before I see it the next day. I have also used one for a train show where I have several 6xAA battery operated trains. Electrical outlets are scarce at these events and this compact charger with the single power supply is much easier on logistics than the alternative of requiring at least 3 x 4-cell chargers and a power bar that will accept the accompanying power bricks.

Charging speed is fast enough that a new set is ready before the next set needs charging. I am able to stay ahead of the dead battery game with this unit. And it does this without overheating the cells which would shorten their lives.

The individual indication per cell show how far run down the batteries were to begin with and how much is left to go. This has been useful as a quick test of remaining capacity when the batteries were not properly recharged the night before. I am able to select some sets that can service another performance skipping a recharge cycle. It has been useful as a battery tester in this regard.

Overall: very pleased which is why I have a third now.

title: I don't recommend buying the ASUS RT-AC68U wireless access point
text:
I never like giving a bad review, but I will make an exception in this case.

You may want to think twice before you buy the ASUS RT-68U wireless access point. I ended up getting rid of this wireless access point and going back to my old one.

Some of the problems that I had - wireless speed for devices would start off good, but then drop to a level that the only fix was to disable wireless on the PC or tablet and re-enable again. This would work for a while but would recur in probably about 24 hours.
The router would frequently disconnect from the internet. My PC would display a web page to say that the internet connection was reset. I would check the cable modem and logs on the device and there was no real good reason for the disconnect. After going back to my old wireless access point, I have not seen that problem since.
Coverage was never as good as implied and the only way to get best speeds was to literally be with a few feet of the router. At that point it's kind of worthless using wireless and so I went to wired and still saw all the problems mentioned in my review.
I would not recommend trying to use the USB3 to do any type of drive share - it crashed for me and caused the router to reboot. After that the router was not able to see that drive. There is nothing wrong with thr drive, my PC can see it ok. After that incident I started to google about this router and found that there are a lot of complaints. I got this router because I heard good comments about the RT-AC66U and thought that this was a decent step up. I was running the latest firmware.

To me it just became a waste of time trying to deal with this router and so I got rid of that router. I thought of trying dd-wrt but then I figured it would still be a waste. I just wish that I had not wasted so much time on this and had returned it sooner.

title: Perfect for streaming with XSplit, here's how to get audio working
text:
I bought this product so I could stream games on TwitchTV using the XSplit program. If you are considering doing the same, there are a few things I had to do to get the AUDIO to work:

Open XSplit
File > Add Camera > Dazzle DVC100
Resize to fit screen
Right click the "Dazzle DVC100" scene source below the video preview
Under the Cam tab, click Configure > Crossbar
Output: Audio Decoder Out
Input: Audio Line In

Install a program called Virtual Audio Cable.

Run audiorepeater_ks.exe
Wave in: Dazzle DVC100 Audio Device
Wave Out: Virtual Cable 1
Hit Start

Run audiorepeater.exe
Wave in: Line 1 (VAC)
Wave Out: Speakers
Set buffer to lowest
Hit Start.

You should now hear the game audio through your PC speakers, and you can also use your mic as well for commentary during your cast.

title: How To Make This Work-Don't Follow The Instructions
text:
This product works pretty well, but the instructions are totally wrong. If you try to follow them, you will be very frustrated like I was... that is until you can find the proper address to make this all work.

The goal is to configure the extender with your router information. Once it has that, you're ready to rock n'roll.

Here's what you do:

1. Power up TP-Link Extender by plugging it in.
2. Hit the reset button on the bottom to clear to factory. The blue lights should light up.
3. Plug in the ethernet cable into the TP-Link Extender.
4. Plug in the other end of the ethernet cable to your computer.
5. Find the new wireless network. If your desktop does not have wi-fi, skip this step.
6. VERY IMPORTANT. Instead of going to [...], go to[...]. You will see the log-in screen. For some reason, the other web address doesn't work.
7. admin and admin as the user and password.
8. Configure your TP-Link Extender. Be sure to enter in the router password if you have one.
9. Hit finish. Then unplug everything. Plug TP-Link Extender someplace you want internet. Wait 3-5 minutes. The lights should come on.
10. Now you have extended internet!!!!

Happy web surfing. Pay it forward.

Updated: Looks like Amazon blocked the link. It's 192 dot 168 dot 0 dot 254. Another option is to Google search this exact phrase:

How do I log into the Web-based management page of Wireless Access Point? (another case)

title: Great burst mode for sports and a long-lasting battery
text:
I've had this camera for nearly a month. I bought it to replace a Panasonic FZ-28 because I was having difficulty following the action in sporting events using the fastest full-frame (10 megapixel) burst mode with refocusing between shots, which was about 2 frames per second. The screen freezes momentarily after each shot, and 2 fps was too slow to allow me to pan successfully. The FZ-150 has a 5 fps full-frame mode (12 megapixels) with refocusing between shots, and that has proven to be fast enough for most, though not all, situations. If I were in a situation where refocusing is not important, the FZ-150 offers 12 fps with the full 12-megapixel frame, and I may try that in the future.

Eating memory with the burst mode is not a problem -- I got a 32-gig card.

I like the frame selection feature in 1080p video in which you can take a 2.5-megapixel photo without interrupting the video.

Battery life is impressive. I bought some extra non-Panasonic-branded batteries, based on my experience with the FZ-28, for which 3 batteries equalled a full-day of shooting. It turns out the FZ-150 can go a full day (in my kind of usage) on just one battery. The non-Panasonic batteries have the "chip" which allows the camera to read their state of charge. I got them on Amazon from Big Mike's Electronics. About $18 versus $47 for the Panasonic branded battery, including shipping charges for both.

A downside is that the camera takes time to digest big photo bursts -- it says it is writing to the card. This takes seveal seconds during which the camera's capablities are reduced. It just seems to me to take too long -- my card is a class 10, so I don't think the card's speed is the limiting factor -- and I blame it on the camera's buffer

Even with this downside, I give the camera 5 stars. The photos are beautiful even under difficult conditions, and the video is sparkling clear, partly a result of very effective image stabilization.

title: BEST CD PLAYER I'VE EVER OWNED!!!
text:
I received this CD Changer yesterday and have put it through enough tests to give a 100% recommendation for acquiring this particular model! I managed to get it working as soon as I had taken it out of the box and hooked it to my receiver. Normally I am a bit of a klutz when it comes to setting up hi-fi equipment, but in this case I have had experience with several previous generations of Sony CD changers and I had looked at the manual online before I even ordered the unit! So in no time at all I played a commercial CD on it, a CD-R and the flash drive as well! So far the player is producing beautiful sounds thru the optical digital connection to my receiver. I highly recommend using the optical digital connection and if your particular receiver does NOT have one, I would strongly recommend getting a new receiver with a digital optical input. I am NOT getting into the argument over digital vs. analog sound, but surely most of you would agree that a digital optical connection sounds better (sounds brighter to my ears!) than the standard patch cords(left and right audio cables) when playing CDS.

Obviously the main attraction of this unit is the ability to play off of a computer flash drive. As I am typing this I am listening to a flash drive which I inserted into the front of the player and it contains over 1,000 tracks! That is easily 50 hours of pure musical pleasure and believe it or not I can set it to repeat indefintely! Obviously for a rainy or snowy afternoon, or maybe even a lazy morning I can just sit in my easy chair and listen to my favorite artists or bands! And yes the CD player does display the song title, artist and album title with a few exceptions. At the very least it seems to always produce the song title and sometimes the artist may not be identified. But all in all, the ability to play off of a flash drive seems to be a revolutionary step forward in enjoying a CD player! I also like the fact that I am NOT tethered to a computer in order to play my music. I love computers but there are times I just want to listen to music and read(newspaper, book, magazine,or even a Kindle!) or have a pleasant conversation with my wife. I like listening to music a great deal of the time and even if it is just background music it keeps me in a pleasant mood! One more thing I should add is that previous Sony CD Changers did NOT have the ability to play MP3 files thru the optical audio connection. This was a bit frustrating for me but now I can listen to CDs, CD-Rs & MP3s thru the optical digital connection! My cup runneth over!

The changer also has the exchange function(unload and reload up to 4 CDs while still playing a CD) which is great and the remote seems to work very well indeed! About the only thing missing is a headphone jack, but one could always attach the headphone to the receiver of course. Honestly this is the very best CD player that I have ever owned, and for the ridiculous low retail price is a no-brainer as far as deciding to purchase one! And finally please note that you have the ability to delete tracks off of your flash drive while it is connected to the player and in my opinion that is wonderful! You can banish any and all offending tunes if you so desire! Sony used to have a similar function on their CD megachangers a few years ago and then did away with that particular function, but now in a sense it is back!! There are other functions obviously like programming tunes,shuffle play,etc. I would strongly recommend this unit to anyone. My only problem is what am I going to do with my old CD changers?!?

P.S. I have only listened to my unit for a few hours but hopefully it will keep going strong and I will enjoy it for many years to come! Kudos to Sony for designing this model and at a reasonable price! Just wish that the Amazon deliveryman could find my doorbell. It would be most appreciated!!!

Richard Pearson

title: Great price...with some tradeoffs
text:
The laptop is light weight, has a good keyboard for typing, has a built-in dedicated memory (2GB), LED back light display, lots of ports for input devices, WIFI, Bluetooth, DVD drive, Quad core processor, Easy to take off maintenance back cover (for cleaning case fans and motherboard and replacing RAM and hard drive) Quality stereo speakers (Dolby Advanced Audio). Overall, it is a very nice laptop. To be honest I was surprised it ran any games at ALL... Most of laptops at this price range sell with less features and lower quality hardware and you're lucky if you find one with a dedicated GPU. A laptop with these specs is a STEAL DEAL.

I don't know where should I start...The laptop has a slow 5400 rpm hard drive, It only comes with 4GB of RAM and comes with windows 8 (windows 7 is better).The laptop comes with Lenovo bloat ware that just takes up hard drive space and uses RAM. Laptop often lags if you have multiple windows open and gets really HOT. The GPU is not fully utilized when running games. Even after disabling all unnecessary background apps and processes and changing all the possible settings I could find to "Performance" and using additional software to speed it up I was getting around 8-15 FPS when playing the game "Alan Wake" on best settings. Another important side note is that the resolution is not "True HD" because its 1366 x 768 instead of being 1920 x 1080. The screen has to be at a certain angle when you are watching movies because the colors will not show the same.

I have already invested into aftermarket RAM (4GB x 2) for better performance and suggest you people do the same. This laptop needs a lot of "tweaking" if you want to get the optimal performance out of it. I would recommend installing Iobit "Advanced System Care" to keep your laptop in shape and disabling any unnecessary apps and startup programs that could hinder the performance of your laptop. In order to keep the Laptop cool buy a laptop cooler stand or put your laptop on a flat surface because the case fans that blow out the hot air out of the laptop are installed on the bottom of the laptop (not on the side like they should be). If the bottom portion of laptop does not get enough airflow the laptop WILL OVERHEAT. In addition, if you have money to spare I would recommend investing in an SSD drive for faster boot ups, better performance, and lower battery consumption.

Cons:
- the clock is HORRIBLE. It will completely stop. It will say 7:50 for 10 minutes. If you press the DISP button you will get an updated clock. I can't emphasize enough how BAD this is.
- the clock is HORRIBLE #2. When your phone audio is paused, there is a large [PAUSE] overlay in the center of the screen. If you have the large clock display, it will obscure some numerals of the time so you don't know quite what time it is.
- To start playing audio from your phone, you have to press the MENU button. Unfortunately there is no pause button. This is ridiculous. On the other hand, you can mute the audio (which makes zero sense with digital playback)
- the bluetooth is somewhat slow to initially connect (for comparison, my cheap plantronics headset is immediate)

Wish list:

- It would be nice to have 'skip back' and 'skip forward' buttons for audiobooks (like on the iphone)

title: It is good for general purposes
text:
The 500 GB AV Link External HDD is compatible with some newer TVs. It is formatted in FAT32 format, as opposed to NTFS in the regular 500 GB HDDs. So, the AV Link version may not be as good as those using NTFS in terms of reliability, and file performance, but FAT32 format gives the AV Link good compatibility with many devices ranging from those produced in the 1980s to the ones nowadays. However, the FAT32 format may require the hard drive to be reformatted to accommodate audio-visual equipment.
Included in the package are the AV Link hard drive, USB 3.0 cord(compatible also with USB 2.0), and a file transmission cord that be attached to SONY cameras and so on for data transmission.
I use the hard drive for general purposes such as keeping computer back-ups, storing videos, music, and documents. It has worked fine so far.
As the above review says, there are some software included in the hard drive. There are specifically: Backup Manager, Data Transfer Accelerator, FAT32 formatter, Password Protection Manager. They may be useful. However, I think that for general purposes I don't have to use them.
So, the portable HDD is to me a good device that meets general needs well, but the advanced software that comes with it may be too technical and confusing for general consumers. For this reason, I will give it four stars.

title: Beautiful, but I couldn't get it to work
text:
This is a new approach to German equatorial mounts that innovatively moves the declination axis and the telescope it holds to the bottom of the polar axis. This improves the weight distribution, keeps the counterweight from hitting the tripod, and allows the mount to be lighter weight than normal for the heavy load it can carry. The mount received a very positive review from Sky & Telescope, and is beautifully made and something to admire.

But I couldn't get it to align with stars so that it would properly goto objects. It has a couple of alignment modes but all of them ended up pointing the telescope 20-30 degrees away from the target. I have a smaller iOptron mount that works perfectly, and I followed the ZEQ25 instructions carefully, including making sure I had the daylight savings time option set properly. I had two email exchanges with the iOptron help desk but nothing they suggested solved the problem so I returned the mount. I want to believe that the mount works and it was operator error, despite my experience, but if so the instructions should have been better, and the help desk comments should have recognized my problem. Or maybe the mount I had just didn't work properly.

One other aspect of the mount was disappointing. The software was less advanced than others, for you have to know the names of alignment stars, and additionally, searching for objects to goto was clumsy. I haven't used the latest Meade and Celestron goto mounts but their software seems more intuitive.

So now I am back to using my old generic EQ3 mount with no goto, but at least I can push it accurately to targets of interest.

title: Great use as a PC gaming desktop in a small form factor.
text:
Plenty of reviews to look at the measurement and comparison of this in GPU speed or per game performance. This is a great entry into the PC console space, yet its also an effective tiny footprint desktop PC that will not disappoint.

The biggest downside of this device is the speed of the Hard Drive they include. The 1TB WD Blue 5400 rpm drive is just dog slow and a huge disappointment in the feel of the "snappyness" of the device. Dell really needs to build these with two 2.5" drive bays. One for a primary SSD and a second for a large capacity storage drive, such as the WD Blue. The first thing I did was yank the 1TB drive and put it into a USB3 enclosure off the back of the unit attached to a USB3 port. I cloned the drive to a Samsung 840 EVO 500GB drive. Night and day in snappy. This works, and honestly, if Dell included it, it would have added to the cost anyway. USB3 to SATA isn't ideal for storage, but the 5400 RPM drive isn't really going to go any slower than it already is.

I replaced the 8GB CAS 11 Samsung Memory kit with a Corsair Vengeance Performance 16GB DDR3L running at CAS 9 and 1.35v. http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00EXPNG5Y . This really wasn't necessary from a performance perspective -- I wanted the extra memory for working with large Excel spreadsheets that exceed a million rows. 8GB just isn't enough anymore.

With the SSD and additional faster memory, the performance index screams on this little box. And its quiet as a mouse. Before I picked this up I was seriously looking at micro ITX asus mainboards to build a small form factor desktop that could handle heavy graphics gaming. This covers all angles.

Another downside is video connectivity. To run my main 24" Dell U2412M Monitor, I needed to pickup a DVI-D to HDMI adapter for $5. I would have appreciated this to include at least HDMI and Displayport. Again... this PC has its roots in being a console... but it would have been nice. To run my secondary U2412 monitor, I'm using a USB3 targus ACP076 dock. Not elegant, but it adds another 3 USB3 ports, additional DVI port and will accept an analog or headphones or mic.

With the minor downsides of this.. it rocks. I send the HDMi through an Onkyo receiver providing switching between my PC monitor and my 60" plasma as well as direct audio. It's amazingly quiet -- I now hear other noises instead of my desktop PC.
The only game I've really pushed it with is FarCry 4... on full quality settings and it's still near 60 fps. I'm sure that something will come out in the next 3 years that makes this run slower than it does now, but for the next 2 years, this will rock, then I'll give it to my kids as one of their next PC's. Currently I'm driving a 1920 x 1200 resolution on the NVidia Geforce 860M that is built into this rig and 1920 x 1200 on the Targus dock for a secondary monitor.

I'm not going to go into the console UI. Others have already done that better than I and I'm on a PC perspective. This like any Windows PC, must have a gazillion patches install after connected to the internet. Typical and not expected, but I'd really love for a manufacturer to send me a PC that is compliant to the current level of Microsoft updates at release. The installed windows 8.1 is not hobbled in any way that I can tell. If you're someone who prefers the Pro feature set for remote desktop and other features, this can be license upgraded through a few keystrokes like any Windows 8.1 OS.

Just a note, you will be tied to Dell's updates on the Nvidia drivers. Running the native NVidia drivers for the 860M will not recognize the adapter in the alpha. It recognizes it with its code name, not the 860M moniker. So we will have to wait for some of the featureset to trickle into the dell based driver as it innovates.

All in all, I'm thrilled and will recommend this as an excellent SFF gaming rig at the price. My bias to SSD and huge memory is just that and isn't really necessary to get the value out of this Alpha.

title: Great lens for Sony NEX
text:
I use this lens with my NEX 5N. I think the Sony NEX camera bodies are very good, but the variety and quality of the lenses that are available for this system (with autofocus) are very limited. This 50mm lens has an equivalent angle as a 75mm on an old fashioned 35mm film camera. In other words, it is a mild telephoto lens (with a narrower field of view than the human eye or a 'normal' lens). This is great for portraits and the fast F 1.8 allows you to adjust the depth of field to isolate your subject from the background. However, this angle makes it hard for some compositions - for example indoor shots of people at a party where you can not move back farther, or many landscape photos. The combination of image stabilization, image quality (especially near the center), aperture, etc make this the best Sony lens so far. Some have complained about the fringing at f1.8 (though at normal display resolutions these are negligible). Personally, I prefer to shoot at around F/2.2 simply because the depth of field effect is a little less extreme (e.g. do you want a photo where the eyes are in focus but the nose is out of focus?). Any fringing you can see when pixel-peeping vanishes at this aperture. Indeed, I prefer the combination of F1.8 and image stabilization more than other lenses that have F1.4: you get a reasonable depth of field and you can take nice hand held shots in reduced light.
When I bought this, the 35mm (normal) lens was not available, and I was worried that I would not like the narrow field of view of this lens. However, after a few weeks I am really glad I got this lens. It is great for taking pictures of your friends acting spontaneously. The wide open aperture provides lovely bokeh (blurred background) and I can make a nice composition without being so close to my friends (people are less spontaneous if you are close to them with a lens in their face, and normal lenses with closeups tend to have perspective distortions that look unpleasant). I use this lens for 75% of my photos (I like taking pictures of people), and only switch to my kit zoom lens for pictures of the landscape and environment. Together these are a great combination, and I am extremely happy with the quality of the pictures. I also recommend the reviews at photo zone.de and photoheadonline - I read them before my purchase and they hint at the strengths of this lens.
