title: Terrible display, though maybe I just got a bad batch.
text:
Let me start out by saying that I'm not going to compare this monitor to far more expensive and fancier monitors, and then give it a bad review for that reason.

Rather I'm comparing this monitor to the numerous Acer G226HQLs that we have in our office. The G226 is a smaller and very similar version of this same monitor. Both monitors are in the same category as far as quality goes, fall into the same price range, and of course are manufactured by the same company.

We recently got a few of these G236HLs, and on all of them there is an absurdly bright bleed-through on the bottom of the screen. With some brightness adjustment, the top of the monitor can be made to appear black while the bottom matches the #6a6d7d which I'm displaying on the good quality IPS panel on my laptop. For those of you that don't know what I'm on about, #6a6d7d is a surprisingly light shade of grey as represented in hexadecimal color notation, such as used in web development.

That's a VERY light shade of grey.

Also, no matter what combination of brightness/contrast I've tried (including all the factory presets), images displayed on the screen are washed out and "overexposed" even at best.

Compare that to the slightly cheaper and comparable G236HL sitting on the other side of my laptop and it's night and day. The smaller, cheaper Acer has a nearly imperceptible backlight gradient when displaying black, and images are quite crisp and show great contrast for a monitor of its class.

The vertical viewing angle on the G236 is also reprehensible. When viewed head-on, with my eye level at the middle/center of the screen about 24 inches away, the top of the screen shows noticeable luma inversion. When viewed head-on with my eye level about 4 inches above the top of the monitor (standard sitting-at-desk posture), the bottom becomes even MORE "overexposed" and washed out, while the top of the screen looks normal.

If I hunch over just right (or tilt the monitor just right), there's a 2 degree [estimated] sweet spot. So if I sit perfectly still all day and never move my head, it could work. Except for the backlight bleed, of course.

Movies look horrible. Bright sitcom-y video looks passable, I guess. Pictures all look overexposed, particularly the farther down on the image you look.

I know it's possible that we just got a few bad units from the same lot, and that there are good versions of this monitor floating around. But as far as I'm concerned, consider the G226HQL instead. It's veritably the same display, just a couple of inches smaller, and it actually does look great for its price.

title: Evaluation of MacAlly NAS
text: I totally concur with the other reviewers of this network storage device. I purchased it a few years ago and used it occasionally for common data storage of our legal records for our five computers. I chose a Raid 0 for the two identical SATA hard drives. These guys croaked eventually and I just installed new ones but have been unsuccessful in getting them to work. The advice given by one reviewer to format the drives before installing them looks promising. I'll struggle along until I get it to work. Positive attributes: cost is low compared with the competition. Negatives: first, what's with the documentation. Developers: people aren't going to use the product unless its well documented and options explained carefully; I've had to do a lot of "between the lines" experimentation and I'm a unix programmer! Second: fix the fan problem -- this noisy fan grates on your nerves to the extent that I've had to sequester it to the basement and keep in always on (you can turn it off remotedly but not on -- so that feature is also worthless). The fans become quieter if you use foul language at them! Third: why are users forced to adopte the root file tree imposed on them. Having a "public" root directory is charming but obsolete. I found I could not rearrange the directory tree to my preferences. Fourth: it's usually hard to turn the thing off (again harsh language helps). I eventually resorted to pulling the plug instead of wrestling with the blue button on front. I could go on (e.g. tight fit, etc.) but the bottom line is: if you're a hacker or hardware guru this might be a good choice; otherwise pay more and get a different one (or use a old computer as a file server to accomplish the same thing for a song). I'm going to recycle the NAS so I say "RIP nas, see you in the underworld".

title: Think twice if you are an average user.
text: I believe that Black Magic has made a quality device, however if you are looking to transfer analog home movies to your PC as a part time project, think twice. I am a backyard home movie person who wants to preserve family events taken by a camera on autofocus...it became clearly apparent that I was in over my head when I sat down one Sunday morning to digitize my home movies thinking that I would be watching them on my plasma after dinner. title: Works Flawlessly.  Read full review if you plan to extend the receiver wire yourself
text:
First and foremost, the product works exactly as described. The instructions were clear and I was able to test that it worked right out of the box by connecting everything and zapping the receiver with the remote. My setup is a Samsung 55" LED TV with Verizon FIOS.

I bought this product with the intention to extend the length of the IR receiver using 40ft of cat6 (aka ethernet cable) since I routed all the low voltage wires in my house and set it up such that all of my audio/video equipment are kept in a closet out of sight. After reading another product review, I found that Cables to Go had information as to how to connect the receiver wires to the screw down terminal on the distribution block:

server.iad.liveperson.net/hc/s-21882319/cmd/kbresource/kb-2668816836916349136/view_question!PAGETYPE?action=view&documentid=381966

Using this information, I used a multimeter to determine which of the three colored wires corresponding to each of part of the 3.5mm jack. I cut the wire on the IR receiver and discarded the end with the 3.5mm jack. I stripped the three wires coming from the IR receiver and soldered them to 3 random wires I stripped from one end of my cat6 "extension". I chose to solder because the receiver wires were very frail, but you could probably get away with twisting the wires together with a wire cap.

On the other end of the cat6 extension cable, I stripped the same 3 wires and terminated them on the screw down block on the distribution block using the following key:

Sleeve = Black Wire -> +12VDC
Ring = Red Wire -> GND
Tip = White Wire -> Signal

After I was done with all of the connections, I made sure there were no exposed wires (i.e. in order to avoid shorts), plugged in the power, and tested again. It was just as functional and responsive as it was out of the box. Of course, you could just connect the 3.5mm jack back on the other end of your extension cable if you wanted, but that was more work than just using the screw down block.

I also posted this information in visual form to the product's "Customer Images":

http://www.amazon.com/gp/customer-media/product-gallery/B001BLTDZA/ref=cm_ciu_pdp_images_dav

title: A real alternative to endless iOS and Android screen swiping
text:
I have been using Android phones and an Apple iPod touch for a few years now and have enjoyed both very much. Lately I have been reading some good press on the Nokia Windows phones and wanted to give it a try. What also got me very interested was that Nokia phones have traditionally had good hardware. I had been using a Samsung Galaxy S Blaze for about a year now and it's been solid but a bit slow. I chose it over faster cell phones because I like a phone that can go a day or two on a full charge. My wife's Samsung Galaxy 2 has a great screen but you better have a charger and a current supply around because extended use will drain it quickly. My Samsung Galaxy also an annoying problem when trying to connect to my built in Bluetooth speaker system in my car. I would have to turn the Samsung Bluetooth on and off to get it connected. This problem never occurred using my older Motorola phone.

Anyway, ordered the Lumia 521 and figured I could sell it on eBay if it was a dog. I got it last Friday, July 26 and have been using it a lot.

This phone is really great: it's very fast and the ability to create a custom display with what you really use makes it super easy and frustration free. No more endless side swiping to get to the app you currently need because the Windows animated tiles show what you want in the way you want. Many of the tiles function as small video screens that display information status related to the app. After using it a while I realized how limited the swiping system is in both iOS and Android.

I cannot emphasis how useful and functional this is it real life when you need to get things done efficiently. Microsoft doesn't communicate this effectively and perhaps people are so conditioned to swipe, swipe, swipe to get what they want that no other way seems possible. But it really offers an extremely effective way to monitor the many information streams that mobile phones can provide. You can design a kind of information cockpit with important streams where you want them and less important info streams in a view able but less conspicuous location. And this increased efficiency translates in a better user experience.

I found the interface design beautiful in terms of legible fonts and colors. A pleasure to use. Touch screen is very sensitive and fast, fast, fast. And linking up to my car's hands off Bluetooth system is quick. By the time I turn on the car engine and back out my driveway, it is always connected. No more Bluetooth tag to get a working connection.

For another viewpoint, Google "Wozniak praises windows phone".

Battery easily lasts a day.

Built in speaker has plenty of volume. The 521 camera is OK, not great and there is no built in flash. For a better camera, look to the Nokia Lumia 925 with Carl Zeiss lens. For now I really don't care to spend the $$ as the pictures are good enough.

This weekend I'll put my Samsung Galaxy S Blaze up for sale. Works great but I am keeping the Windows phone.

title: Tivo is Absolutlely Great Except...
text:
... they don't tell you about the agonizing problems with Switched Digital Video systems. (Google it.)

I had a Tivo Series 3 and I gave up on it a couple of years ago because it just would not work properly on my cable system (Charter) which uses SDV. SDV requires a tuning adapter to sit between the incoming cable and the Tivo in order to be able to watch a lot of high-def channels that are part of a SDV system. If the tuning adapter is not working, you lose a lot of channels.

Well, I figured that by now, the cable companies, the cable card companies, the tuning adapter companies and Tivo must have worked out all the bugs.

They have not.

My Roamio worked for exactly two days before channels went missing and I had to call Charter. Luckily, the tech who came out to my house knew what he was doing with regard to tuning adapters and he got me up and running. The big question, however, is WILL IT LAST?

In the past, it would work for a few days or weeks and then the channels would go missing again.

I will update this review after I have had a couple of weeks with the Roamio. I fully intend to return it before my 30-day trial is out if this problem comes back again.

I would give the Tivo device itself 10 stars if I could. It's that good. But if it won't work with my cable system, what's the point of spending the money?

***SEPTEMBER 3, 2013 UPDATE***
Once again, Tivo has delivered a product that works intermittently. As stated in the comments, this is a known issue and yet Tivo can't seem to build a box that works on all SDV systems. I'm cancelling my service and sending the Roamio back to Amazon. Dropped my star rating to two stars because, in the end, this product is a failure for me, just as my previous Tivo was. This time, however, I won't be stuck with a $400 doorstop.

***SEPTEMBER 30, 2013 UPDATE***
I wanted so badly to use Tivo, I bought another one and tried it with a new cable card and tuning adapter. Same problems. I have now dropped my review to one star. Tivo is selling a product that does not work on all cable systems. Yes, the situation with tuning adapters is documented on the Tivo web site, but they make it seem like it is a solvable problem. It is not. BEFORE BUYING THIS PRODUCT, CALL YOUR CABLE PROVIDER AND ASK IF THEY USE "SWITCHED DIGITAL VIDEO." IF THEY ANSWER "YES", AVOID TIVO DVRS.

title: Very Disappointing
text:
Before I start my review, I want to be clear that I'm basing my review on two things. First, I am a novice when it comes to tablets. Second, I am basing my rating mostly on my disappointment with the device, versus my (apparently) high expectations. For those who understand better the limitations of these devices, and how they operate will probably not find this review helpful. I'm writing this from the perspective of someone brand new to these devices, and had certain levels of expectations, for nearly 400 bucks. I bought this device to easily be able to take with me and be able to do basic internet/email/apps/computing things, plus be able to use it offline for movies/music/e-reading. Obviously I wasn't expecting the same performance as a high-end desktop PC or laptop, but more or less the same operation, minus the attached keyboard. I know...that's my fault for not understanding the limitations of this device, but in the end I was disappointed with what performance and functionality it didn't have.

First of all, in the box is the device, and a usb cord. That's it. Now, I wasn't expecting a giant paper-wasting manual to be included, but there was literally nothing in the box. When I turned it on, it did automatically start giving me tips and tricks on how to access things or whatever, but not a real instuction manual. Yes, I found a tutorial buried in the device later on, but I wasn't impressed with it, and I found it difficult to both read the tutorial, and navigate the screens it was trying to teach me at the same time. Again, if you already know how to use a tablet and navigate around, this is not a big deal, but for me, I found it difficult.

After fiddling with it for a while, I tried using the internet browser to see how it would do. I tried maybe 5 or 6 webpages, and on at least half of them, I kept getting an error message on the Kindle. "Tab not responding. The tab has stopped working and has to be terminated. Do you wish to try and restore?" No = browser crashes, Yes = page tries to reload, only to run into the same error message. Sometimes after reloading a few times, the pages would actually work, but they seemed slow and buggy. The overall load time of certain pages was very slow, even ones that didn't seem to have a lot of graphics or extraneous stuff on them. Moving around and zooming on certain sites was very slow, and there seemed to be a delay between "clicking" on a link and something loading. Also, some pages looked different than the version I see on my laptop. Again, if you are familiar with tablets, and have tempered expectations of internet surfing, and how pages load and can be viewed, you probably would not be as disappointed as I was trying to use the internet.

Next, I tried loading a few apps. Only got to about 3, because the first two didn't work or were not available for this device, and the third one (cable channel stream) did not work because my provider was not on the list of available providers for the streaming service. Yup...not the fault of the device, I know, but again, I tried a few apps, and none of them worked, for whatever reason. My expectations versus what reality was, was disappointing.

Another reason I bought this was to use it offline to watch movies that I could store on the device. Well, apparently it's very difficult to take an older DVD or Blu Ray and simply load them onto this thing. Yes, I Googled how to do this, and tried several third party software programs that were supposed to "rip" movies from the physical disc and convert them to a digital format to load onto the device. None of them worked. I did get one file converted, but it took FOREVER and was 10GB. It would not work on my laptop, but I still tried to load it to the Kindle, in hopes it would work. After 30-40 minutes of transfering, it didn't even register on the device. I had to go through several menus to find the storage folders on the Kindle to find a gray square which I assume was my 10GB waste of space only to find it would not open. I don't know why it took so long to load the file...often times I move several 4-5GB files to and from my computer and it normally takes 5 minuts or so to move this amount of data. Again, I assumed, before I bought this, that I could relatively easily transfer movie files to this, in a short amount of time. But I guess I'd have to find the right combination of third party programs to create movie files, and have hours to sit and wait for them to transfer. Expectations vs reality...very disappointing.

There were also several nit-picky things I didn't like. I really do not like these touchscreens. I can't stand smartphones with a touchscreen, and even this larger screen, I found it very frustrating to use. Several times I thougth I "tapped" a button, only to be waiting for something to happen, when apparently I didn't tap it hard enough. Other times, I would tap a button, only to realize there was a delay between hitting it and something happening on the screen. This problem mainly occured when trying to tap on internet links. Also, it took a very long time to charge this device. I paid extra for the "fast" charger, but it still took probably 3 hours to charge. Part of the time I was using it plugged in, so maybe that accounts for the slow charge time, but if it takes several hours to charge with the "fast" charger, how long would it take otherwise? Another small thing was the length of the USB cord was somewhat short. If I was at a coffee shop or restaurant and wanted to use it plugged in, I would have to be very close to a power outlet...I mean like push the table up against the wall close. I'm glad it doesn't have a bulky power cord like a laptop does, but at least those give you some freedom to move around when plugged in.

I could go on, but this is already a very long review which will probably be buried by fanboys calling this "unhelpful", so I'll leave it at that. It's my own fault for making "crazy" assumptions about where the technology is on these devices, and how practical and functional they are. Maybe if I was experienced with ipads and nooks and the Google tablets, etc...I'd have a better appreciation and understanding of how this one compares. But for someone with limited experience and knowledge, it was a pretty big letdown. I am returning this product.

title: Casio Exilim EX-G1 in one word: Disappointing
text:
I went on a cruise with my wife 3 years ago and bought an underwater camera bag for my Kodak so I could take underwater pictures and video. While these both came out great, trying to snorkel with a giant ziploc-like bag was tough to do and I couldn't easily see the screen to observe the video I'm taking. Diving with the bag was difficult as well. So when the Kodak finally died we decided the next camera we bought would be a waterproof camera. We bought the Olympus Tough series but I didn't like the lag from pressing the button to the time it took a picture. So returned the Olympus and started looking for reviews. There weren't too many options out there and this Casio had just been released. With not too many reviews out, and zero user reviews I still thought I'd take chance on the camera.

First the positives, the camera looks cool and we got a lot of great comments about it. There is very little lag from depressing the shutter button to the time it takes the picture so I was pleased with that. The screen is bright and it's easy to review the pictures quickly. Some cameras I had took forever to start the review and then going from picture to picture. The video was pretty good and was easy to start recording by hitting one button. No knob to turn or menu to go into, just push to start and stop recording.

The negatives, the picture quality wasn't all that good compared to my basic Kodaks that I had. The colors were dull and flat. In lower light it got worse. It was easy to blur pictures if it wasn't very bright. I had several pictures from a trip to Spring Training that would have been fantastic but the camera let me down and there was blurring. Even with some of the settings for the exact situation, the camera didn't do a very good job with certain situations. Underwater pictures were fun and even video came out well. The pictures, however had a bluish tint to them rather than the accurate colors I had with my non-waterproof camera in a bag. So I was a little disappointed with that aspect. Unless there was perfect lighting, the pictures were washed out as well.

My main fault with the camera is the fact that Casio doesn't stand by their product when something does go wrong. They do have a one year warranty and I understand the limits, but on a family trip the camera was knocked accidently off a couch onto the floor. It wouldn't power on after that fall regardless of what I tried. I was not able to take pictures for the entire week. I contacted Casio and sent in the camera. This camera sold me on the claims that it was 1. waterproof and 2. able to withstand multiple drops from 7ft. This camera fell maybe 1.5 to 2 ft maximum and stopped working. This was one drop and not multiple. After back and forth with the company, I realized that they were not going to budge on that 1 and done year warranty and not at least give me some type of credit etc. I decided that I am done with the camera and will ebay it for parts and replace the camera with something more durable and better quality.

I wouldn't recommend this camera or Casio for that matter after this experience. There are now many other waterproof camera options out there and a google search for waterproof camera reviews will give you many other superior options. Move on from this camera.

title: No vignetting, reduces haze dramatically on Nikon 14-24mm lens
text:
Strangely enough, there is no information I could find anywhere about the specifications of this filter or what it would or would not do. I measured the thickness of this filter - it is somewhere between 6.2 and 6.3mm thick (I only have a non-electronic caliper). And this is enough to prevent this Fotodiox 145mm UV filter from causing vignetting on the Nikon lens, a problem that afflicts the regular thickness Fotodiox 145mm CP filter.

This UV filter also had the added benefit of noticeably reducing haze and improving the overall image quality and resolution on this super wide angle Nikon lens, when shooting at direct sunlight photos of the sky. I think it must be because this lens picks up so much UV from all directions in bright sunlight that it gets scattered all over the image and smears the image. I have posted photos to show the difference.

So, apart from having a filter system that works to protect this very expensive Nikon lens finally, this UV filter actually works to improve the image! Test photos that I shot did not seem to add any more lens flare in direct shots at or near the sun, so the multi-coating must be working.

BTW, the new ultra-slim version Fotodiox CP filter is 7mm thick, and this slight difference is enough to still cause a slight vignetting on one side with my 14-24mm lens. Not sure why it is only on one side, I suspect they were trying to make their new ultra-slim CP filter not have any vignetting at all, but since the system fits onto the plastic lens hood of the 14-24mm Nikon lens, slight variations in the shape of the lens hood probably affects the amount of vignetting you get with your lens. More on this later, I am still evaluating both filters, but as so little information is available on these Fotodiox products, I thought I should post this information now.

title: Powerhouse Computer
text:
As an avid gamer and freshman college student looking to buy my first laptop, I wanted only the best for my experience and money. My cousin recommended an Asus for my gaming needs so I began my search for a brand laptop that suited my desires and stayed around $1500. I met my suitor, the ASUS N76VZ-D571, on ProStar.com for about $1200. Unlike any other Web site I had looked at, I could customize my computer to get everything I wanted plus more if I so choose. This computer is superior in its high definition image quality, processing power, and great internet connections. These are some of the basic features I chose for my personal computer:
 -17.3" screen
 -Intel Core i7-3610 QM processor
 -12GB memory
 -Dual 500GB HDD @ 7200rpm
 -nVidia GeForce GT 650M 2GB DDR3 Graphics card
 -Intel Advance-N 6235 Wi-fi + Bluetooth
The design of the computer itself is sleek slate and steel colors with a glowing logo on the front and white-lit keyboard inside. The images on the computer are crisp and clear--the 1920x1080 full high definition quality looks better on my computer than on my TV and it is always the first feature I show off on my laptop. The screen has no glare and includes a white backlight for the best and brightest screen that lights up a whole room at night. The keyboard feels good and is really comfortable; the touchpad, unfortunately, is a bit troublesome. It's simply too sensitive and it definitely gets in the way while using the keyboard. It is much better to invest in a mouse because of this. Additionally, music from my speakers sounded great and the computer even comes with a mini portable subwoofer, but after only two short months, the speakers sounded terrible. Almost like they blew out like car speakers do, the bass sounds clunky, loud and obnoxious. I had read about this problem before I bought the computer so I believe it is the speakers or the computer itself.
Yet, the computer's processing speed makes this a device to turn heads. The power of the Intel i7 3610 QM processor, the speed of the dual hard drives at 7200rpm, along with superior internet access everywhere you go with Intel's outstanding LAN chip, loads pages and applications in a matter of quick seconds, often almost instantly. With said power, large computer games, such as WoW and Sims 3, also run perfectly with no lag. The computer maintains its temperature with the optional Diamond Core cooling I included on my own personal laptop.
Aside from the annoying touchpad and the disappointing speakers, this computer is everything I need plus high quality greatness. I love to brag about it and would definitely recommend it to anybody looking for a good investment in a computer!

title: Great value for the price
text:
I purchased this product as I planned a last-minute visit to the Niagara Falls and, being on a business trip, I had nothing else to immortalize this moment than my smartphone and its lousy camera. After unpacking it, I first tried it indoors and was not impressed at all: mediocre yellowish pictures, noisy and grainy. I tried to disable the (weak) flash and it got worse. I was tempted to return it immediately but decided to give it a try outdoors. When I started to shoot the falls, I became very quickly addicted to this litte gizmo. In most of the cases, the camera is able to deal with the subject, although I would recommend the usage of the advanced scene mode: facing violent contrasts, the camera shoots automatically twice with different exposure parameters, which increases the odds to get a good shot. Smart.

The exposure can be easily fixed manually, using the "manual" mode (in fact, an automatic mode that can be adjusted). In a matter of seconds, over-exposed white water on dark rocks takes texture, to the droplet. It is a bit of trial and error, but delivers quick results. The panorama function works very well, delivery much better pictures than the lousy prints available in the souvenir shop. I also gave it a chance to show how it works with video: better than average sound (if not too much wind), functional and silent zoom and again, surprising image quality. As the light changed due to overcast clouds, I adjusted the settings and the camera obediently followed, again delivering satisfying stills. The zoom works fine. It's not a super-zoom but the resolution is good enough to enable enlargement on the PC.

Happy with the outdoor quality, I decided to give it another try indoors, using the advanced mode P. To my surprise, the various settings, including several white balance modes, enabled to fix the initial issues and I got noise-free, decent-quality pictures under artificial lighting. I fumbled a bit with the flash and while I find it a bit rough, it's within expectations.

Outdoor picture quality is really great for the price - I was really positively surprised by the sharpness and color quality, which is still far from SLR standards but surprising for a compact. The autofocus is decent, shutter speed good, transfer speed correct. The camera behaves predictably. It is more limited indoors but still very decent once one gets used to it. I was not disturbed by the lack of functionality to adjust speed or aperture as I'm using it for point-and-shoot, which it does pretty well in general. It's not a function-rich camera, but what's built in is useful and working well (the online manual may need some polishing though).

I'm giving it five stars because this Sony camera exceeds consistently my value-for-money expectations. It cannot be a substitute for more serious hardware (I own a Sony Alpha and my wife is a NEX user) but it is definitively the camera I will take on business trips or in my breast pocket for a casual walk in the park.

title: Awesome screen and silent. But still several issues to be fixed
text:
Computers nowadays come with more processing capacity than most of us (among non-gamers) need, so I usually don't bother to do some research in that front. I needed a new computer and my priorities were, therefore, the screen (high resolution, touchscreen and no bigger than 13") and low noise levels. You get all that with this machine. But there are some aspects I don't like and this is the reason I gave it only three stars:

- With 128 Gigabytes of physical memory, I would not call this machine an "ultrabook", but an "infrabook" instead. I knew about this limitation so I can't complain about it. What really disappointed me is that to get a bit round this problem I bought a 128GB SD card to have it permanently installed as part of the computer memory. And here I got a sad surprise: the card only makes it halfway into the slot (as opposed to enter completely as it did in my much smaller 11" older notebook). Half of it poked out of the machine, making it an ugly sight, unsafe (you can easily lose it) and not suitable to carry around (without removing it). Money lost in this try.

- On ergonomics: the borders were designed to close tightly and look then "aerodynamic" (so it is kind of annoying to open it - you need strong nails), not for user's comfort. In fact, depending on how you use the computer, the sharp metallic edges will definitely hurt your wrists. Other reviewers liked the solid finish of metal - personally I prefer good old plastic, as it is less conductive of heat and therefore it does not have that "cold" feeling on contact with the skin. But this is a matter of personal taste.

- I can confirm some difficulties with wi-fi connection that another review reported. In a network where my iPhone and other laptops can obtain signal normally this computer often looses connection. Therefore I have to restart the computer to get it back (very nice if you are busy working and with several documents opened...).

- Finally Windows 8. It is difficult to express how much annoying this new system is, and how much time I had to waste trying to make it work relatively similar familiar (i.e to Windows 7) so I would not be lost in their bizarre world of invasive and nonsensical organized (?) screens and shortcuts. I have grown tired of Microsoft during the last years and with this new release I am ready to move to Linux whenever I have some time to do it. Other people are ok with Windows and I respect that, but I wish my choice of not liking it would be respected as well, so I would not to have to swallow (and pay for) it every time I buy a pc. But this has been too much to wish for in a long time already.

My overall assessment: Awesome screen and pleasantly quiet and good looking machine. If you are ok with the limitations above (not my case), it is a good buy.

title: Worst computer I've ever owned
text:
This computer by far has been the worst one I have ever owned- laptop or desktop. Upon receiving it, the first thing I did was remove all the bloatware and leave myself with only the programs I know I will use and anything necessary to run the computer. As the owner of a previous model Toshiba Satellite, I thought I would be safe going with a "nicer" updated version of the same computer. One of the first things I noticed about the computer were background programs running that were taking up nearly 100% of the memory. After doing some digging online, I was able to determine that these were "system updates" so I just let them continue doing their thing. This lasted for about this first month.

The next problem I noticed was the tendency for the computer to start responding extremely slowly and freeze up for 5-10 seconds at a time. Keep in mind at this point I still have very few programs installed on my computer- much less than on my previous Satellite. The standard fix for this is to simply restart my computer and all is good again for a while. I typically have to restart my computer once or twice a week, but occasionally it's so bad that I find myself restarting it a couple times a day. This is a problem I'm familiar with, but it usually starts happening after a couple years, not a couple months. Yes, I do have antivirus software (Kaspersky). The one good thing I will say about this computer is it shuts down and restarts very quickly.. typically in 1 1/2 minutes.

The final problem I'm having is it's tendency to disconnect from the internet. Several times a day it will loose internet connection and then re-establish it. I know it's a problem with the computer and not the internet because other devices connected through wifi are unaffected and never loose connection.

The things I like about it? The touchscreen works perfectly and was calibrated appropriately out of the box. I love the back-lit keyboard that makes it look much like a MAC. The battery life is plenty long enough and has always been enough for whenever I'm off wall power.

Bottom line though, I would never recommend this computer to anyone and am already seriously considering getting another laptop.

Oh and one other minor nuisance that may not be specific to this computer- some of the apps take FOREVER to load. I only have simple apps. Ones like AP news, weather, skype, but they can take several minutes to load sometimes. It's much quicker and easier just to use the webpages. And the photo viewer/browser apps? Forget it. They take waaay to long to load. You're better off just viewing them through windows explorer like you've always done. In my opinion, apps should be contained to phones and tablets for now. They have no place on a computer. I'm a 27 y/o male btw.

title: The Perfect Mouse?
text:
I've had one of these for about 6 months, and just ordered another to use with my Surface when I'm doing mouse intensive stuff. I have owned or used many mice over the years, both wired and wireless. I have to say, this is one of the best, maybe the best.

As a portable mouse, this is prefect. I use a laptop at work, which I take to meetings and home. I can flatten it and can carry it unobtrusively in my shirt pocket or the pocket of my case. I no long have this big bulbous object to lug around. I'm surprised no one came up with this idea before.

As a mouse, it works great. I have used it on many types of surfaces and have never had an issue. I never need a mouse pad. It is precise and slides well. It's comfortable. The buttons and "slider" work perfectly.

I really like the fact that it shuts off when flattened. I have a regular wireless mouse at home (HP) with an on/off switch on the bottom and I never remember to turn it over and shut it off when I'm done, so it's on all the time, which shortens battery life

This is also a good conversation starter. At meetings when I take it out and start to use it. It always sparks interest.

I get about a month or two of battery life, and I use it daily at work. It uses inexpensive AAA batteries, which is nice.

Overall I have to say this is one of the more innovated and functional computer accessories I've had in the last several years.

title: So far so great !!
text:
I have only had this gps for one day. So I am writing a preliminary review on the good and the problem (now resolved) in hopes of helping others. I searched and researched for some time on which gps to get. I have always had Magellan (3 in total) over the past years. They always seem to fizzle out or start acting weird and have had problems with the Magellans having some problems with taking us to wrong locations etc. So, We decided to go with Garmin. I wanted a larger screen because I am a disabled vet with not so great eyesight. My husband drives and I usually work the gps.

So the Garmin 2757 arrived. It took some playing around with it for awhile since I have never had a Garmin and it does have different interplay that the Magellan. But, after I got used to it, I did fine. It is part touch screen but also has a scroll up and down arrow to move screens up and down. At first I tried to use the touch method for moving these things (attractions) up and down and that did not work at all. Then figured out it was my fault not the gps. I purchased separately, but at the same time, a regular plus because I knew it did not come with a plus for in the house, and I knew I wanted to sit in my lounger with it plugged in to put in addresses, play and figure everything out. That worked well and I would recommend anyone to do this same thing. It does have a fairly decent battery life but again I wanted it plugged in rather than have the run the battery up having it plugged into the car or computer.

So we went off on an adventure today for the firs time. And oh heck, we started having a major problem. Every 4 or 5 seconds I lost the bright screen. I kept putting it at about 82% and it kept jumping back to 20%. After a long time I got fed up with it and just turned it off. I was temped to return it but checked the amazon questions and saw someone else and a similar problem. Someone told this person to "reset" to factory and I tried that but it kept jumping back.

So, I called Garmin. The recording said my call would be answer in 1 to 3 minutes but it took and big 4 or 5 minutes to answer LOL. Honestly, I was impressed that I got someone this quickly. The woman who answered was police and professional and I explained my problem. I had already registered the gps so she found my name etc. quickly and she told me to "go to the area that you set the time. Under the squared block of time there is a block that says "automatic". She said make sure I have a check in the box. I did not. I put a check in the box and the brightness returned and it stayed where I put it. So you know it came with the check in the box (and putting it to reset to factory settings should have put a check back in that box but did not in my case). Anyway, I had unchecked the box because each time I set the time it would not stay at the time I put unless i unchecked the box. Confusing? Well at first. The woman explained the problem with that was…. I was trying to set the clock and everything inside my house and probably could not get satellites and that without the satellites it was not understanding what I wanted. So just make sure you are at least close enough to the window (my lounger is not) to get satellites if you are going to fix this up indoors.
Everything should go just fine then.

We took another ride and the gps did great. We downloaded a few new voices (ok we are in our 60's and some of the voice choices are not to our liking). You have to female voice. And can download a decent male voice, the Simpsons Marge and whats his name, and elf, a squirrel (egad) and a yeti. Don't bother with the yeti. He growls or snarls but doesn't actually say anything as far as we could tell. Wish there were a few more choices but we actually are having fun with Dr. Nightmare ! Actually it is quite funny to us so we'll use that until we get tired of it and will go back to one of the more normal voices.

You can download bunches of types and colors of vehicles to use as your car as well. So we are pretty happy with this gps right now. We'll know a bit more over the next days to come and if anything changes we will come up and let you know. Meanwhile, we are very happy with it and also very happy with the help we got on the phone support.

title: Makes other phones seem over-priced
text:
My prior nokia phone died unexpectedly recently, and, out of warranty, I needed a replacement fast. I wanted to stick with Nokia, believing that getting my contacts and other data loaded into a new lumia phone would be easy using the Suite. Being a T-Mobile customer, I thought transferring my account to the new phone could be done easily online. I was wrong. Luckily, I already had an outlook mail account to turn to. After manually loading in my old contacts into that email account (2 hours), my phone was syncing and ready to make calls. Also, a relatively quick call to T-Mobile completed the account setup. I am not that excited about my contact information living 'in the cloud', but hopefully, the next time a phone dies I can recover from it more quickly. Certainly I was disappointed that, in 2013, it can still be a royal pain to manage contacts going from handset to handset. Can't all these digital systems just, get along?

OK. Going from a premium Nokia handset to Nokia's cheapest offering means a loss of some features, specifications, and build quality. What I am learning, however, is that this budget phone is hardly crippled - it runs awesome. Most premium phones offer larger, better screens, better cameras, and better build materials. My last phone was metal, so pulling the 'cheap' plastic cover off the new phone was a little bit strange - so were the 'cheap' buttons. But my experience with premium devices (and I include the Nexus 7 here) has been that, even with top of the line processors, cameras, lots of RAM, etc., most do not really deliver performance and features that make upgrading an OBVIOUS choice. This phone costs 4-5 times less than Nokia's other top offering for T-Mobile, the 925, but hardly feels like a budget phone.

The phone feels great in hand (a little slippery). The glass screen is great, and the buttons click and fall easily to hand. The plastic helps keep the phone light, it is still durable, and does not interfere with antennas like metal can. Having a removable cover and cheap battery easily replaceable is also a godsend considering the inconvenience of permanent batteries. There is no front-facing camera (don't care), 8 gb internal storage, 512 Ram, and a 1 ghz dual-core snapdragon processor. I threw a 16 gb card into the phone, and deleted all the pre-installed cr-apps since I knew I wouldn't use them. Contrary to what I read online, I don't see the storage or RAM limitations as a major issue - 1 gb is the upper-limit for Nokia's phones at this time, and I do not tend to heavily multi-task. Also, there may be 1 zillion apps in the world currently, but I only like a handful of them as it is. I have a tablet for more robust gaming/app needs.

Despite its specs, the 521 runs great. The experience is smooth, the screen is bright and sharp (with some minimal bleed in the dark), the buttons feel good, and texting / browsing is simple and fun. The app store (like all app stores) is set up with a lot of categories, but I still find "browsing" limited - I feel like I need to know what I am looking for. But all my favorite apps were in there. The call quality is great, the speaker phone is louder and clearer than my old "premium" phone, and headphones sound great (better than my nexus 7). GPS worked fast and without hiccups when navigating. The camera is OK in good lighting, and 5 MP is still good nuff for an 8x10 assuming you get a good shot. Given that even 'premium' phone cameras still fail, in my opinion, to really replace a rudimentary point-and-shoot (especially in low-light), this is totally fine with me. There are some interesting camera apps to try out, and I'll look forward to seeing if they deliver better results (by basically doing 'burst modes').

The MS Phone 8 software feels fresh, is very elegant, and really should give Apple and Android the night-sweats. But I have little doubt that it is harder to use out-of-box than iOS. That said I find it very 'premium' feeling. I love the live-tiles, customization, and overall presentation of most of its core features. I did need a couple days to learn the ins and outs a bit (at first the whole setup was confusing). There are some OS features missing that I want to see put in. Most importantly, I like Androids ability to close an open app by swiping it away, and Android and Nokia's pull down menus that let you easily turn off/on things like data, wi-fi, GPS, and Bluetooth (I am trying an app called "quick settings" which is mainly a bunch of short-cuts). Oddly, I can't seem to pick a home page in Internet explorer. Also, stock MS settings are a real battery drain - it is a good idea to read up on web tips for maximizing battery life. For starters, it is so easy to set up email accounts that I did 2 right away - then remembered I need to change the sync settings to balance update/power use. Auto-rotation is not active in all screens/apps, which is annoying when I feel like typing in landscape mode, but then again typing has been fast and accurate in portrait mode so far. There are also features on by default which are totally unneeded. Windows Phone is definitely a modern OS, and a good one at that, but it will benefit from more development. Hopefully the 8.1 update and others will hit this phone as they become available. I really hope they do, as updates are critical to keeping the experience fresh, reliable, and fun. Heck, half the reason I got a nexus was to ensure updates would be forthcoming.

The most compelling reason to go Nokia is probably the free GPS + Navigation. Hands down, they are the best free solution I know of at this time, and they are exclusive to the brand. Most of Nokia's other apps are useful and add value to the overall experience. They are generally reliable phones also, and will survive drops, bumps, and a little water.

The bottom line is that this phone is probably up there with the Nexus 7 in electronic super-values available at this time. Unless you have $300-500 dollars to burn, there are likely no better choices if you want an excellent smart-phone experience for a super-reasonable cost. I would gladly have paid another $100 dollars for a somewhat better screen (gorilla glass and a little higher res?), camera, more RAM, and a larger battery (and Nokia's 'altered reality' GPS app). But as is, I find no real faults here, just huge value. Buy with confidence!

title: Duty Cycle Horrible
text:
I have had many Seagate drives in the past. Everything points to horrible duty cycle. If you run yours 24/7/365 (well, you won't get to 365), like in NAS or permanent on-line storage, it will almost assuredly fail in a year or less. I took out the dead drives and installed Hitachis or Samsung. Those have been working now for years. I had three NASes that stared with Seagate, all three died. Now two with Hitachis have been going for three years and Samsung for two years. I have tried some direct connects, and sure enough, errors and goes bad. I reformatted and now don't run that drive 24/7, I run it occasionally and it has been working for two years. I also had a portable versions (to take up less desk space) and same thing, it was erroring regularly. Reformat and run less than 24/7, becomes reliable again. All totaled, 7 Seagate drives in my life and ALL can't take 24/7 operation for any extended periods of time. So, I have 100% failure with Seagate some were recoverable and kept at 8 hours per day and for 5 days a week, then they work fine. But three are full on dead. Everything off of filtered UPS, always (Filtered CVT --> Filtered UPS - each UPS is front-ended by Filtered CVT - Constant Voltage Transformer) . Nothing else has ever died except the Seagate disks.

Sure, I can run SAS versions in servers, but heat and noise level not suitable for home/small office/personal use. But I would still stay clear of Seagate. Hitachi and Samsung have been the most reliable. I can't verify WD, hasn't been running long enough. 6 months and still running. But I've heard a lot of bad things about WD as well.

So, I could recommend them if you do not intend to run 24/7. If that is your intention, steer clear. If you are running a business on these, I would say don't use these.

Seagate Support - No need to create a case. Duty Cycle needs to be published. If run half a day and then allowed to rest the other half, these should work fine. But 7 failures out of 7 disk in 5 years is a horrible track record and all occurred less than a year. But once taken out of 24/7 duty, they become reliable, well the ones that did not totally die (won't even spin). Too bad Hitachis are hard to come by and Samsung more easily, but both far more expensive than Seagate.

title: Tried to like it, but ended up hating it
text:
I am shocked at how horrible this watch is. I was using an Android Wear watch (the Samsung Gear Live) before picking up the Gear S on this weekend, and just 3 days later I'm more-than-ready to return it to T-Mobile. Here are the several issues I've encountered:

Notifications: first, and most irritating, the watch is completely worthless if you want to use Hangouts and Gmail as your SMS and email apps. You can get notifications for new messages, but you can't respond to them (see below under "Apps" for more info). And, the notifications you do get are very messy: emails run on and on; you can't tell where one message ends and another begins, and you have to swipe around a bunch on the interface to see everything. Swipe here, tap there, swipe there again. Not very user friendly, or quick.

Voice control: S Voice is SO BAD. Coming from using "OK Google" on the Android Wear watch, I'm used to being able to basic things like set reminders and check sports scores. You simply cannot do that with S Voice. If I want to check sports scores I would need to pull up the Opera Mini web browser (not included by default) and Google search it using the mini on-screen keyboard. (If you want to get technical, I could press a button on the keyboard that would allow me to use voice-to-text with S Voice... but seriously?)

Apps: There are some cool standalone apps on this device -- some cooler than some you'll find on Android Wear. Yelp is great, and Opera Mini is pretty nifty. But, on my Android Wear watch I had Trello, Evernote, IFTTT, and others that are NOWHERE to be found on the Gear S. Also, app integrations with the apps on my phone are horrible. Nearly every time I tell my Gear S to open a notification on my Note 4, it will open the appropriate app, but it will rarely load the actual "item" that the notification was referencing. Also, Samsung wants you to use their default Messages and Mail apps, otherwise you can't interact with the notifications. Nope... not doing it. I have already gotten accustomed to using Hangouts with my Google Voice number -- I like the fact that I can text people from within Gamil on my computer, and already had all my friends switch to my Google Voice number in their address books. I am not switching back.

Battery life: my Android Wear watch claimed to get a day's use out of it, and it does. The Gear S claims to get 2 days. It gets 1 day, if I use it at all. If you don't use it, it might last 2 days -- today, for example, I've touched it hardly at all because I hate it. After 9 hours it's at 75% -- so, 2 days might actually happen!

Call forwarding: also, there is the issue with forwarding calls from my Note 4 to the watch. It does work, but every single time my watch disconnects from the Bluetooth connection with my phone and engages the cellular antenna, I get a very large error on the watch's "home screen" saying that Call Forwarding cannot be enabled. I called T-Mobile support, who was unable to figure out why I am getting that error; they referred me to Samsung support who was also unable to figure out why I am getting the error. Very frustrating! And dismissing the error (which pops up every few minutes) requires me to tap on the watch.

Hardware: the one thing I like about it. Actually, since I have a big wrist, I do really, really like the physical design of the watch. It fits perfectly on my wrist and the curve is very nice. The strap is the better than the Gear Live (it has a metal clasp). Also, the charging cradle doubles as a battery so you can actually charge the watch while away from a power source. Super nifty! Too bad the software is completely awful!

The screen: it claims to have an "always on" screen. I call B.S. The screen is always on... if you flick your wrist toward your face. For comparison, Android Wear watches are TRULY always on, meaning, they always show the time. I thought this was REALLY deceiving of Samsung in their marketing because I expected that the watch would always show the time, even when it's not pointed at your face. About 20% of the time when I turn my wrist to look at the watch, it doesn't recognize that motion and therefore won't show me the time. Very annoying. At heart it's a watch; I want it to show the time. Other than this, the screen is very nice and the colors are fantastic.

Navigating the software: you must use your finger. As I alluded to above, voice control is not this watch's specialty. It is very much tied to your finger via swiping and tapping, and the menu system is not the most intuitive. It's not horrible, but it really does feel like you're using a miniature computer on your wrist. "User friendly," "quick," or "easy" are not key words I would use to describe it.

Despite my best efforts at trying to like this watch, I just ordered a new Android Wear watch (I'll be trying the Sony SmartWatch 3 this time, because the Gear Live kept dying on me and the Google Play store kept having to replace it), and I'll be taking the Gear S back to T-Mobile as soon as the SmartWatch arrives.

title: Worth the cash, would buy again
text:
At first I thought this device was defective. After about an hour of unplugging and replugging in different ways was I able to get it to work as advertised. Forget about reading the manual, mine only came with half of one, and it wasn't very helpful at all.

It looks and feels cheap, but it's actually fairly well made. The solder joints on the inside were mucked up, but the components they used were of fair quality and after hitting the joins with a hot iron it looked great.

While the adapter was attached to my Note 2, it felt solid and secure. However, I need to remove my protection case just to use this thing. No matter as I'm probably going to use this without the shell around the adapter eventually anyway.

I'll share how I was able to get full HDMI out, charging, and USB OTG capabilities. Just follow these steps.

1) connect any USB device you want to use, IE keyboard/mouse/etc

2) connect the HDMI cable to the adapter but not to the tv/monitor. Alternatively you can connect to the monitor and not to the adapter. Either way don't connect it to the screen you want to use just yet.

3) connect YOUR charging cable directly from your wall-charger. The cable that was sent with the adapter to provide power must not be high enough quality to power everything and USB does not have enough 'umph' to do it either.

4) plug the adapter into your phone, verify that the phone has recognized your USB device(keyboard/mouse/etc). If not, start over from step 1. If you continue to have issues, your adapter may be defective.

5) now you can connect your HDMI cable to your screen. At first nothing will happen but within 3-5 seconds your phone's screen will turn off and your tv/monitor will turn on.

Over all, it was worth the $12 to get it, just don't forget to get an HDMI cable too if you don't already have one.

title: An Excellent Choice in the Current Field of Bluetooth Speakers
text:
I have been evaluating all the top players in the bluetooth speaker category and I was initially torn between The JBL Charge and the UE Boom but was stopped by the many conflicting reviews. I realized I was going to have to spend more to get the balance I was looking for between battery life and sound quality. I wanted something that would hold up on the road while on motorcycling trips but I was willing to sacrifice a waterproof unit for better sound. The waterproof Braven seemed robust but low powered and not at the sound quality I knew I would be happy with.

I bought this Sony SRSX5 because it is the newest audio technology at the price. I had heard the Bose Soundlink Mini and it was OK but when I got this new Sony I was clear I made the best choice for right now. The sound quality and bass response on this unit is excellent via Bluetooth for both iTunes and Pandora and it is as good or better than the Bose for most music. I can expect excellent performance for plugged in devices but have not tested this yet.

Downsides are: 1. This unit requires a proprietary power charger so it's another thing to carry along. 2. Expensive Sony carrying case not included. 3. Not water resistant. 4. NFC one-tap mode cool but only for Android phone users, iPhones don't yet support NFC. Other Notes: The "Sound" button on the unit switches between regular ClearAudio+ mode and the Surround Sound mode. This mode allows sound to come out of both sides of the unit it seems. I think if it was put near a good sound reflecting surface in this mode you might get some neat effects but it does sound like the music volume is changing up and down as the sounds move from speaker to speaker. Maybe something cool for a party outside, not sure, but I like the standard ClearAudio+ output better so I keep this option off for now. My iPod, iPad and iPhone connect well and connection is strong but Wifi will interfere depending upon proximity. Once the device connects the first time it seems to connect faster on subsequent connections but you must manually make the connection every time you turn it on. The USB out port in back does indeed charge my iPhone 5s. [Update: I was wrong about having to manually reconnect the iPhone/iPod every time you turn the unit on. The speaker does indeed remember the devices and reconnects to the first remembered device within range when you power it on, i.e. I can turn on the speaker and then run Pandora and it just plays.]

Exceptional sound clarity and stability over hours of playing. Battery seems to be performing well. So far I am very happy to have this speaker. I don't like the Sony case though so I will be looking for a leather pouch or holder at the various biker leather vendors I will meet this summer.

title: These are OK but have some problems
text:
The Good:
The connectors are gold plated copper (according to the manufacturer), can hold 10 gauge wire, and the spades are wide enough for the binding post on my power amplifier. They are also affordable in price when compared to other spade connectors

The Bad:
The screws that hold the wire to the connector are tiny. The screw on the bottom of the connector fails to tightly secure the wire. The screw on the top does all the work in attaching the wire securely to the connector. The connectors I received had some type of metal garbage inside of them maybe from the plating process or tapping of the screw holes. I had to use a drill to smooth the inside of the connector to remove the garbage so that I could slide in my 10 gauge speaker wire. No instructions are included.

Conclusion:
Buy them only if you need spades. You may want to consider solder instead of using the screws. If you can use banana plugs, get the Sewell Silver Backs. They have much larger screws and can hold 10 gauge wire. Silver Backs make an excellent connection without using solder. I have used these with no problems. I only purchased the spades to bi-wire my speakers. The spades are used on the binding posts of my power amplifier along with the Silver Back banana plugs.

Update: I think the screws located at the bottom of the connector may be designed to secure non-stripped speaker wire tightly to the plugs. I stripped the wire down to the bottom screw. This may be the reason why the bottom screw does not make a secure connection. I wish these came with instruction so that I could know for sure and re-install the connectors if necessary.

Update 2: I called Sewell and they confirmed what I suspected in my first update. The bottom screws still fail to tightly secure the non-stripped wire to connector. The only way to make an excellent connection using these spades is to toss the tiny screws and use solder.

title: The Ugo of Tablets Kid Version
text:
Let me start out by saying I bought this for my 2 8 year old boys so they would leave my Droid X alone. I did not buy this to operate my small business off site or plan to have the ultimate toy for angry birds.
I have a lot of downloaded aps (thanks the the generous free offers from Amazon). I was able to download all of the appropriate aps to the Colby Tablets. Some did not work but I expected that since a) many aps are not optimized for tablets and b)these tablets do not have the horse power to run some of the more involved applications. I bought this for 8 year old boys in hopes that most of my applications would work and they did. I can get approximately 85% of the applications to work on their tablets. For $100 plus a $12 usb keyboard and cover from Amazon this is a pretty awesome gift for 8 year old boys(or girls). When you think what we had when we were 8, this is pretty sweet. Wifi is the only way to communicate with the world so I installed text plus gold and now they can text each other, and my wife and I. Amazing how fast an 8 year old can type now compared to when we were kids.

There is a good reason this is a $100 tablet:
The touch screen is a resistive type so a while finger tip works a stylus works better. It can be very touchy at times and I have had a ap download come up from the other side of the screen from where I touched. Patience prevails.
This thing can really only run 1 maybe 2 programs at a time. There is just not enough flash memory or processor speed to handle it. It will crash if you try to do too much.
The process of downloading application, scrolling to find them and installing can at times be frustrating and time consuming but hang in there and it can be done. It probably took me at least 5 hours per tablet to move 50+ applications.
Battery life is only about 3-4 hours of game play but recharge time is only a little more than an hour so put is down for a while get outside and play and it will be ready to go again soon.
I had trouble installing an 8gb micro sd card (Sandisk class 4)on one tablet. It kept giving me an error message that the chip was defective. Suggested reformat did not work on the Cobly. I called Colby customer service and did manage to reach someone in about 12-15 minutes only to have them tell me that a "tech" would have to call me back because they were backed up. OK, it's right after Christmas and everyone is trying to do the same thing so I give them some slack at this time of the year. Especially since people buying $100 tablets are not veteran tablet users so there is likely a lot of hand holding. I eventually got into the storage and memory myself, reset everything and also formatted the micro sd on my computer instead of the Colby and the problem was solved. I did not have this problem on the other Colby tablet, it worked fine the first time I added memory card.
The bottom line: This is a slow tablet with some quirky screen play but if you are patient and allow the processor to "catch up" it will work and play the games one at a time. My subject line called this a Ugo, meaning you should not expect Lexus or even Chevy performance from this, but it will get you from A to B for a lot less $. This was 1 of only a handful of tablets at the $100 price point this Christmas. Colby was by far the highest rated by consumers and I would have to agree on a 4 star review (relative to the price point). You can bet next year there will be 10X the number with 2X the operating speed for the same price. I give it 4 stars because it will run most of the aps I already have and it met but did not exceed my expectations for a $100 tablet. I don't think there is a 5 star tablet in this price range right now. Maybe next year.

title: Great receiver with a few minor warts
text:
I recently purchased a Tecsun PL-660 and have found it to be one of the best shortwave portables that has come out in many years. (not counting expensive 'portatops' like the Eton E1XM, Grundig Satellit 800, etc.) I have found it to be very sensitive, with good dynamic range so it isn't very prone to intermod and images when used with a longer antenna. The selectivity with the narrow filter is very good with a good shape factor, unfortunately the wide filter is way too wide. It provides better fidelity at the cost of a lot of adjacent channel interference. Nevertheless, the narrow filter is all that is generally needed for SWLing. If a strong station is found 'in the clear' then the wide filter can be useful.

Listening to SSB is a pleasure with the selectable sidebands (as opposed to just an SSB button and BFO) and fine tuning control. The unit also has a selectable sideband synchronous detector which works well for lessening or even eliminating adjacent channel interference, unfortunately it introduces a small bit of distortion into the audio, which synchronous detectors are supposed to eliminate. Even so, the sync does help a lot and the distortion is minor. It took me a while to notice it. The sync locks well onto weak signals, but if the signal fades too much and the receiver loses lock, switching to a sideband and using the fine tuning control for ECSS is doable.

I have too much RFI in my area to comment on the LW performance, but MW sensitivity is good but not being much of an MWDXer I can't comment on its suitability for DXing that part of the spectrum. Speaking of MW, it seems that the displayed frequency is about 1 kHz low on the MW band, though this isn't the case on the higher SW bands. FM reception isn't bad, it picks up the local stations just fine, though I have other receivers that do better on the more distant stations.

The ergonomics are reasonably good, though the keys are elongated rectangles set in grooves. It's aesthetically pleasing but requires more deliberate effort to enter the frequencies than if the keys were of a more standard shape.

The display is large and bright and contains a lot of useful information. The manual is rather vague about the memories (and other things) but I've found that some (not all) memory pages allow for the storing of mode (USB, LSB and filter setting) along with the frequency. This is a very useful feature.

All in all, the Tecsun PL-660 is a great shortwave receiver, though not without a few minor warts. I believe it is the least expensive receiver with a synchronous detector, and quite a bargain at $120 (strangely the silver version is $15 less). In my opinion, this is one of the best receivers in its price and size class and the only receiver to successfully compete with the Sony ICF-SW7600GR in overall shortwave performance. I can't give it 5 stars due to the over-wide wide filter and the distortion present when the synchronous detector is on, but it deserves a solid 4.5.

title: Great portable Blu-Ray DVD writer - works & powers off a hub
text:
I'm happy to be (apparently) the first to write a review of the Pawtec Blu-Ray writer, and very glad I bought it.

There were three main considerations I had for a portable Blu-Ray / DVD writer, and I think these are shared by others:

1) Will it write to (and read from) any kind of disk I put into it?

2) Will it run off my laptop AND my USB 3.0 hub without a separate AC adaptor?

3) How's the burn speed? (And especially: does it support USB 3.0?)

Here's what I found:

1) The list of compatible disks for this device is impressive. Right after I got it, I tested right away by burning to dual-layer Blu-Ray disks. These are 50 gb capacity and I nearly filled them with files -- flawless burn. It's great to be able to archive valuable stuff this way.

2) It runs great off my hub, the [[ASIN:B0074024XU Manhattan Hub(161718)]]. (Note that all USB hub models are different, and your mileage may vary with a different hub.) Pawtec supplies you with a USB cable, and also a secondary cable in case you need to draw extra power from a second USB port. I attached the USB data cable to a USB 3.0 port on the hub, and the secondary cable to a USB 2.0 port on the hub. (The other end of that secondary cable goes into a special power jack on the back of the Pawtec.) The Pawtec powered up great and work flawlessly. In my second test, I attached the device directly to my MacBook Air's USB 3.0 port using ONLY the data cable -- again, it powered up and worked flawlessly. Excellent!

3) The Pawtec specifications say it does support USB 3.0, and I got good transfer / burn speeds. My test was with thousands of .JPG photo images totaling 40.94 gigabytes. Attached to the hub, the burn completed in 54 minutes, for a data rate of about 12.6 mb per second. Attached directly to the MacBook Air's USB port, the exact same burn took 35 minutes, for a data rate of about 19.5 mb per second. (Mac OS X does a verify after the burn, which takes about as long as the burn, so I am not including that clock time here.)

With all that nice performance, the Pawtec is really small and VERY light. It weighs in on my postage scale at just 11 ounces. You could easily carry this in your laptop case / backpack wherever you go, as long as you slip it into something protective (these are my favorite, and this model is just the right size case for the Pawtec: [[ASIN:B004N6233O OP/TECH USA 4901102 10-Inch Neoprene Protective Pouch Computer Sleeve with Full-Flap Closure (Black)]].

Overall, this is just a great device and a great deal. It's a very clear improvement over my existing portable drive, which I got only a year ago. (For the Pawtec, I did go for the model that has an actual drawer that pops out, rather than the slot-loading model, as I like to have the option to pop the drawer with a paper clip in an emergency.)

I was amused that the box had inside it a slip of paper noting that Pawtec has been developing products "since 2013". But it was also reassuring to see their promise of great customer support and a support e-mail address.

Great new product, and quite deserving of praise.

UPDATE, SEPT. 9, 2013:

The Pawtec is even more awesome than I thought.

I ordered a second one, in black, to use as my permanent desktop disk device.

To test it even further, I:

a) did NOT attach the secondary power cable

b) attached a 2-meter [[ASIN:B00B3P15M8 AmazonBasics USB 3.0 A-Male to A-Female Extension Cable (6.5 feet/2.0 meters)]], so I could place it further away

c) plugged the extension cable into a USB 3.0 port on my hub described above

It powered up perfectly, burned perfectly, and did so in even slightly less time than before on the exact same photo data: 52 minutes, for a transfer rate of over 13 mb per second.

This is far superior to any other disk device I've owned over the years. Great tech, Pawtec.

(Since I now own two -- one with aluminum finish and one in black -- and they both perform identically, I will post the identical review to the product page for each.)
