title: Well constructed case for a good price
text:
I replaced my Apex M108 with this case. It's better built, well thought out and fits a dual-slot graphics card.

The good:
Small size
Plenty of room inside
Easy to work with
Nice appearance
Very sturdy
Good ventilation

The bad:
Manual--helpful photos but poor text.
No slimline SATA connector for DVDrw (the only reason for 4 stars)
No adapter for 3pin front fan.

My only regret was not ordering a slimline SATA adapter for the slim DVDrw at the same time. Some reviews I've read complained about the difficulty of installing a 2.5' Drive. I had no problem. Here's the procedure I used and how it went.

1. Unpackaged (it was packed well), studied the photos--the text isn't much help.

2. Remove the drive trays: The easiest method is to remove the lower tray first: Removed two screws on the side and slide the 3.5" drive tray out (it's held in place with a metal tab on the tray); installed the 3.5" drive in the tray, connector facing the side with the graphics card and set it aside. Remove the top tray by unscrewing the four screws on top; mount the 2.5" drive. If you have a slimline DVD rw, mount it on the top now. I had to slightly bend the tabs and rack it around a little. Leave the DVD mounting screws loosely so you can align it later. Set that aside.

3. Install the motherboard: (mine already had the CPU and cooler in place). The usb3 cable from the front panel is really stiff. I had to bend (crimp) a right angle so it would fit under the power supply later without putting too much stress on the mobo connector. Connect the other front panel connections.

4. If you are installing a DVDrw, remove the metal slug (what a pain) and plastic insert. Pull off the front panel by pulling the plastic tabs out around the perimeter (two on the top and two on each side). pop it forward and swing it out and unscrew the plastic insert where the dvd goes. I removed the fan cover next--it just pops out. Then take a large screwdriver and bend the metal slug up and down. it eventually rolls forward and snaps off. Reassemble the front.

5. Reinstall the drive trays in reverse order. This is the time to Align the DVDrw

6. install the power supply and hook up the SATA connectors to the drives. Do this before installing the graphics card. The space between the graphics card and SATA sockets is tight. (after thought...maybe I had the drive in upside down)

7. remove whichever slot connectors you need to and install the graphic card (mine did not need PCI power connectors)

8. Plug in the front fan. It's only three pin so I used a molex to 3pin fan connector (not supplied)

9. Connect the DVDrw with a slimline SATA connector or slimline to SATA adapter (not included). I used this: [[ASIN:B004ZMYA8C B004ZMYA8C]]

10. Route your cables and install the graphics card.

All in all, not a tough job. The case is amazingly sturdy when finished. After it was completed I decided to replace the front fan with a scythe 120mm I had in another case. It's quieter than the stock fan.

title: Not Good for Streaming Videos from PC
text:
I bought this based on the reviews, after owning an LG BD390 and finding it somewhat limited (e.g., no Pandora). I connected it with via HDMI cable and the set up was relatively painless.

This player has lots of features and seems quite good for Netflix and other online services, of which there are many choices. However, I choose players primarily for their ability to stream video files from my PC over my wireless network. The Sony was extremely limited at this, in fact close to useless. It failed entirely to see any video files of any format in the public videos folder on my PC. It did see the folders and subfolders; it treated them all as empty. I then tried the Tversity server from my PC. Here the Sony could see all AVI and MPEG files, though it played only about half of the former. For the rest it gave an error message saying "unsupported video format." Astoundingly, it could not see any MP4 or WMV files at all, much less play them. I also tried this via my Playon server with exactly the same result.

Playing DVD's was OK, just like any much cheaper DVD player. (I did not try Blu-ray.)

Also disappointing was the ability of the remote to control the few streaming video files it did play. There was no fast forward or indexing or search function that worked. It would only play, pause or stop. Thinking this might be because it needed a special dlna controller, I downloaded Sony's android media controller app. It connected, and then did nothing more than the regular remote.

Bottom line: if you don't care about streaming videos from your PC, you may be OK with this player which offers lots of internet services. Otherwise, don't buy it.

title: Worst camera experience to date
text:
Panasonic had a tough act to follow when my wife's powershot A640 died. We shopped a lot of these entry level cameras for her replacement and found the layout of Panasonic's Lumix ZS10 to be the most tolerable for her large hands. April of 2011 we purchased a kit and my wife was again able to capture lasting memories. Most of her pictures get printed directly from the camera at Walmart or whatever store is convenient for her and it is not until the card is nearly full that I download its contents. I had noticed poor image quality towards the end of the summer when I downloaded her card for the first time and I blamed the grainy/blurry pictures on settings and user error.

Moving forward in September we began tweaking settings and practicing more with the camera to "learn" how to take good pictures from it. Three months later, during christmas break we finally came to the sickening realization that our 380.00 camera was never going to function adequately for us. By December of 2011 the horrible product reviews and quality had dropped retail prices to sub 200.00 which proved to me in an unscientific way that this camera is , in my opinion, a piece of junk. Unfortunately I did not discover the shortcoming of this device within a 90 day return window and Panasonic's customer service can only recommend sending it in for inspection.

I can only assume that those who have written great reviews for this camera either have low expectations for a digital camera or they have never experienced the superior image quality coming from Canon and Nikon entry level cameras. We have now gotten our repaired Canon AS640 back from a repair shop and the positive difference in image quality coming from our old Canon camera is breathtaking. I would not be stretching things much to say in comparison to the images we are getting from the Canon device that the Lumix ZS10 pictures look like they came from an old 110 compact film camera.

"Learn how to use it" someone told me... but it's hard to learn how to take good pictures with a bad camera.

text: This is my 5th voice recorder since 1999. All Sony. They have been great. Reason for so many is that I use them a lot! I still have two others that I'm using but they are "attached" to particular locations. This one I carry with me most of the time, use it to capture the "next big idea" while I'm dring to/from work. And this model records in mp3, perfect to allow others to email to other so they can listen to my ramblings. The sound quality is excellent, easy to use record/playback. If I have a gripe, it's that the user manual is non-existent. I have no problem whatsoever using all the various options, including the "hidden" options in the secondary menu. But that's because I've had previous Sony VRs. Someone who is coming to this device "cold" may not find and utilize all the neat features buried within. For example, you can play back at a different "speed" than the original recording but the pitch of the recording does not change, like with a mechanical tape recording slowed down. No small design / engineering feat, but it's buried within the options menu. Too bad, Sony, you're missing the boat when it comes to touting your features and benefits to buyers/users. title: 8-Cylinder Powerhouse: Major step up from the Average AA/AAA Charger
text:
Good packaging. Excellent product! My research showed that there seems to be one Powerex model that is slightly more powerful/versatile. But this model has not disappointed. Several of my once believed extinct rechargeable batteries are now reconditioned and usable, thanks to this product--a relatively brief time to revive about 80% of my seemingly defunct rechargebles.

Four main selling points on this model:
a) single-bay charging (no mandatory pairing of battery types);
b) auto-float charging (it knows, and tells you when it's "done");
c) the--already mentioned--reconditioning mode...activated by simply pressing a button (after you have the batteries in position);
d) the 110V transformer, that sends 18v to the unit, is very intelligently designed so as to sneak into most powerstrips/surge protectors without hogging 2-3 power slots (the narrow design places the 110V plug leads out to one side of the transformer, and turns them 90 degrees so that the cord--in a standard socket would trail off to the side, instead of up or down.)

If there is ONE gripe...(and I really have to work for this one)...here it is: the reconditioning button, which is made of the same color plastic as the case, can sometimes be bumped and turned on when inserting the batteries. But even this one gripe isn't much of a gripe, because if you DO accidentally hit the button, and don't notice the LED indicators that the unit is in reconditioning mode, the reconditioning process still doesn't take that much longer that merely charging, though it may possibly use up one of the charging cycles...or does it?

By the way, the hands down best rechargeable I've found is the Sanyo/Eneloop Battery. I have not tried the "xtreme" variety of eneloop with this charger, so this review cannot (as yet) tell you about use with that particular grade of battery. I will update this review as I experiment with those batteries, too. But there is no question that the standard (1500 X rechargeable) eneloop charges very rapidly and maintains a charge using this charger.

Best of luck in your gear/toy shopping! I'm very happy to own this "eight-cylinder" powerhouse!

The picture quality will not be a huge quantum leap improvement over nex 5n. The greater pixel count (1.2 zoom factor) is counterbalanced by some increased noise at higher ISO.
The touch screen functionality was greatly reduced, leaving quick access to functions only with a few customizable buttons. The 5n-t had quick access to 5 functions with touch screen, making most manual adjustments very practical and quick.
External flash or flash trigger system could be fitted on 5n, no longer with 5100.

On the plus side for the 5100, the video characteristics appear to be far superior and state of the art.

In sum, if you like the small size factor of these models (a6000 much bulkier), the 5100 seems superior for video and point & shooters. The older models 5n 5r 5t offer more control over still shot functions.

title: A box with a zipper
text:
It's important to consider where you'll be stowing this. For me, it hasn't worked out. I wanted something that would fit in my business satchel and in the airplane seat back pocket for easy access. This doesn't fit well in either, simply because it's a 2" deep box. When you think about all those devices and cords you have, few of them are probably over 3/4" high. Now you'll be putting them in something that is much larger. This isn't something you can cram into a small space.

The inside pockets are ok. The big pocket on one side and two other pockets are big enough for smartphones, Ipod, and most small electronics cords. The small zipper pocket is good for memory sticks & cards and cable adaptors.

The outside pocket has expanded/loosened up quite significantly after putting just a few items in (tickets, receipts, etc. ) during two business trips. It's now too loose for me to risk putting in other items.

I'm not that sensitive to smells, but I know people who are. This item definitely has a unique and strong one (inside only). It doesn't bother me and it's not transferring to anything.

Overall construction is fair. I'm guessing the zipper won't last forever: you have to tug it a little to get it to close. It seems the inside partition was made just a bit too big. But this is called "Amazon Basics" after all, so reasonable expectations should apply.

I'm not saying this is a bad item. I will probably continue using it at times, such as for storing items I put in my luggage. But my original purpose was to bring together my IPhone, IPod, external battery, 2 small cords, and a few cable adaptors. I've switched to storing them in a soft-sided pouch [[ASIN:B004C0VFOO eBags Padded Pouches - 3 pc Set]] However, despite my mediocre opinion of this item, Amazon should get credit for having this item. There are plenty of camera and GPS bags out there, but few reasonably priced general purpose electronics bags. As you're shopping, you might also want to check out [[ASIN:B0058S883K Skooba Cable Stable Mini (750-250)]] or [[ASIN:B003D0ID8U Skooba R750-300 Cable Stable DLX (Black)]].

title: Sounds Great Pound for Pound, but The Pricey Cable Is Not That Able
text:
The Onkyo ES-HF300 is the same pair of headphones as Onkyo's FC300, only with an allegedly higher performance oxygen free cord. If you've already read my review of the FC300, you can skip to the last two paragraphs of this review to see the differences between the two models and my comparative opinions of them. For now, I will discuss the similarities between the two models.

Onkyo's first venture into the modern headphone market is a fairly conservative one. Onkyo developed a mid-priced model with few innovative features, and one that lacks modern amenities such as a single cup wiring, an inline volume / pause / microphone unit in the cord, and multiple cords supplied. However, Onkyo achieved a high value package that sounds better than it's price would indicate, and one that probably will please both audiophiles and mainstream headphone users.

First, build quality. The HF/FC series are built very similarly, made mostly of plastic with comfy pleather on-ear cushions. The Onkyos do have aluminum driver housings, which is a nice upscale touch. I personally felt the comfort factor was high for an on-ear, superior to the Sennheiser HD25s, and about equal to the ATH ESW9A. The Onkyos are somewhat larger than both of the above mentioned headphones, and the grip on the head is somewhere in between the Senns and the ATH as well. This level of grip to me is a good thing, as the phones remain reasonably stable on your head (unlike the ESW9s), and are also less unpleasant for a long listening term than the HD25s). A circumaural set of phones (fully surrounding the ear) will be more comfy for most users, but the supra-aural Onkyos will be good for most listeners for at least 90-120 mins of consecutive listening before any discomfort is noted. My somewhat larger than normal head is comfortably accommodated by the Onkyos at half extension, so large cranium owners can buy in confidence. The pleather used is also reasonably cool, unlike some more expensive models that are ear broilers (e.g. Munitio).

Materials and construction more or less match the price point. More expensive headphones like Munitio and Sony MDR-1Rs look and feel sturdier and more elegant, but the Onkyo is not embarrassing and to my thinking looks much sturdier and durable than the ATH ESW9, a headphone that sells for 30-50% more. The somewhat cheaper ATH M50 feels tougher, but also has a more utilitarian industrial look that looks geekier. The Onkyos are reasonably attractive and will not embarrass listeners at the local café. The Onkyos both fold flat their cups flat but do not further compress with added hinges, so a tight little ball configuration will not be possible.

The cable used is a controversial choice: a Y configuration with proprietary connectors which plug into both ear cups. I guess there might be some great reason why Onkyo chose this cable, but I don't like it. Y cables tend to get tangled up more and tend to break more in my experience with other designs, and they just get in the way more than the single ear connectors seen on so many other models today. At least the cable is replaceable. However, Onkyo cautions you not to regularly unplug and plug the connectors in and out, so the Onkyos are meant to be stored with the cable connected unlike say Yamahas or V-Modas. This suggests to me a bit of concern over long term durability and as the connector is proprietary, this means you have to go back to Onkyo for an expensive replacement if something does go wrong.

Next, what's in the box - Not much! The headphones, an awful cheapie pleather drawstring pouch that provides very minimal protection for the phones, and the detachable 3.5mm cable that is four feet long. The detachable cables are interchangeable, so you can swap or replace cables freely among the models. The cable choices right now appear to be red, black, silver, and the off-white OFC model. The Y cables do NOT use standard 3.5mm connectors both ends, and so must be replaced by only Onkyo cabling (see para above for more details). I think the lack of more cabling options (like a second cable with inline Ipod / phone controls) and the cheap pouch make Onkyo look bad even at this "moderate" price point.

Tech specs: Closed 40mm drivers (pretty much the standard in headphone land), 97 dB sensitivity, 32 Ohm impedance. There is a "dual chamber structure" for "enhanced bass" and "titanium drivers for super clear sound" in both models. The only difference between the FC and HF models is that the HF model comes with the "high purity oxygen free copper cable for quality audio" while the FC models use a lesser non-oxygen free cable that is however tangle proof due to its ultra flat design. (Plus the FC cables come in different colors, and the FC frame can be had in black or purple. Note that the "red" FC model is a BLACK frame with only red cabling.) The tech features in quotes above are quoted from the manufacturer and do not reflect either objective reality or my subjective opinions. The proof of all these marketing terms is really just how the phones sound... so read on!

Both Onkyo models sound quite good, meeting or beating the gold standard in sub-$200 headphones, the ATH M50. The Onkyos sound clearer and crisper than the already quite good M50 does, so this is a win. The M50s have deeper bass, but are also less accurate and the ATHs also have more of a subdued treble. The Onkyos are superior for classical, jazz, and other acoustical music, but are also very good for other genres like metal, electronic, and rock. PRAT is roughly comparable to the ATHs, much better than the more mellow ESW9s. The HD25s sound better for rock and metal, but are much harder to drive with portable devices, do not handles acoustical music as well, and also cost at least 20% more than the Onkyp HF model. The Onkyos are great all-rounders, with a specialty in acoustical music that is relatively uncommon in portable headphones these days when everyone seems to be shooting for smeary gobs of bass that make classical and jazz sound a bit unnatural. Soundstage is decent for a closed headphone at this price point, audibly better than the M50s or ESW9s, yet not immensely superior.

I do not mean to make the Onkyos sound like effete wine-sipping snob headphones. Put on Nine Inch Nails or Muse and the Onkyos will impress and amaze - but then switch over to a Schubert sonata and you will be similarly amazed, a rare thing in modern portable headphones, especially at this price point. The Sony MDR 1Rs or Yamaha 500s will sound noticeably better, especially in terms of clarity, detail, and soundstage, but they also cost twice as much (or more!) than the Onkyos do. Audiophiles looking for portable use phones will be much better off with these than with the overpriced anemic AKG550s.

As far as competitors go, I would much rather own these for classical or jazz listening than either the ESW9s or the M50s. If I listened mainly to electronica, rock, or metal, I would probably go for the M50s for the deeper bass boost, or if I was in a studio environment and / or was rough on headphones, I would also go for the M50s. A notable feature of the Onkyos is that they sound excellent with or without high power amplification, so you can drive these phones with a Touch Ipod or Samsung Galaxy and get full range of sound and excellent volume without an amp. The HD25 really needs higher power than an Iphone or Galaxy 3 can provide, and even the M50 scales up nicely with a little bit more power. Bottom line; if you want a loud set of cans that does not need an amp to work with your underpowered MP3 device, the Onkyos are your best options for under $200.

The Onkyo FC model gets a solid 4 stars from me, due to great sound that punches above its weight in price level. If the frame used a bit more metal, if the carrying pouch was a case, if you had a second cord in the package, and if you had a single cup connector with 3.5mm connectors at both ends, these would earn 5 stars from me. In the meantime, there is nothing wrong with the sound here, and though you can get somewhat better sound for a lot more money in portable device headphones, the Onkyos will be a great combination of quality and value for most shoppers.

Now as for the HF model: a 4 foot cable run playing mostly "lossy" format music (like MP3 and AAC) really does not benefit much from being oxygen free. The regular FC cable models sounded exactly the same to my ears as the 20% more expensive HF did. The O2 free cable included with the HF is also uglier as it looks industrial / medical and is also less practical as it is less tangle free than the flatter more colorful FC cables. Onkyo is trying to be all quasi-mystical here (like Monster) to justify a higher charge for a useless added "feature". You do not need an oxygen free cable for these phones, or at least the odds are good that you need $30 more than you need the oxygen free cable. I deducted a star for the added cost and minimal justification for the extra charge offered in the single added feature that really adds no value. Avoid the HF and buy the FC. (And remember, your only frame color choices are black and purple - "red" is not actually red!)

Came with most of the wiring needed, except for an RCA splitter which was needed to split the Sub-woofer out terminal from my head unit. While the subwoofer did add some low end oomph, it does not hit teh real low frequencies that you can feel - my guess is that it goes as low as 40Hz, and that is it. Turned up enough, it does rattle the rear view mirrors, but distortion kicks in pretty early.

Pros:
------
Compact size - fits under front passenger seat of my 2009 Honda Civic.
Okay performance at medium sound levels - adds some low end punch.
Nice Looking blue illuminated remote control.
Well built - looks & feels solid.

Cons:
-------
Does not hit real low frequencies
Distorts easily if power is cranked up.

Overall, if you are looking for adding a little low end punch to a decent sounding system, and are looking for something that will fit under the passenger seat of a compact sedan, this is a value for money option. However, if you are looking for serious thumping bass, you will be disappointed.

title: Super intelligent, very useful but maybe too smart?  Very impressive.
text:
This was posted on the AT&T branded Gear S on 12/13, (worn since 11/20) hence the update after this first post here.

12/18/14 updated below - please read that too. You will find it interesting. Your view of my rating could be higher or lower depending on how you take my update. Possibly a little creepy especially since this has a mic. Now 4 stars down from 5 due to possible big brother implications. Call me cautious? Call me paranoid?

I was given this as a gift and was, at first blush, embarrassed and surprised at the amount it cost my friend (he got it without plan but specific to my carrier) and thought it a bit showy for me. Boy have I come to change that opinion. This watch almost replaces the phone for me now. I now pretty much use my phone as a hotspot at work for my laptop and then make calls and send texts from the watch. When I have time to kill I can either read the news on the watch or even try and browse using the Opera browser for the Gear S. This watch has so many useful apps like calculator, calendar, compass, voice recorder, fitness tracking, pulse, photo album, CNN news, and tons of other apps. They've even got apps to help you find your car. When bored I end up reading the news. You can even use the watch to play the mp3s on your phone or stream music directly from the watch. The real beauty of this is being able to make a call while driving by just talking to your watch and since its blue-tooth its legal. It connects to the newer Samsung phones by blue-tooth, wi-fi, and S beam. You can use it either as is or you can get its own (additional) sim card and then make the watch a dedicated phone that can also access and operate though your smartphone.

You operate the watch and get to different screens and options by either swiping up, down, left, or right, and with touch, or by voice. You will be surprised at the options this watch has. I've never had an electronic watch before so I've got nothing to compare with, but speaking as someone who would have NEVER considered getting one of these watches now consider it indispensable. The vibrating alarm is another one of the killer features and you can set multiple alarms and it is very easy to set repeating alarms. You know ... to remind you of whatever you need being reminded about, maybe like the end of the workday, time to take medicine, pick up the kid, etc.

The screen is big, crisp, colorful, and at first, I thought that it was too big for me but the screen size is just right and the resolution is awesome. It tethers well to my Note 4 and don't have a sim card for the watch so only use it to answer calls and make calls though the cellphone. What's even greater is this watch is voice activated. Hopefully the next version will be android instead of Tizen so it can work even more apps but in the meantime I find this one heck of a useful watch that I never thought I'd like, but now love. Even though I have a very thin wrist the length of the watch is perfect for it and the watch strap is very easily adjusted to accommodate very thin wrists. You can even easily change the watchbands, if you need, by popping the watch out of the band.

If you decide to use the skin for this watch (the skin is beautiful, easy to apply, and invisible after application) it will decrease the sensitivity of the touch screen. I've tried it with the film but am annoyed at the loss of sensitivity so, currently, I'm using the watch without the protector. I got accidental damage insurance on this so I guess I'll chance going without the protector due to the lack of responsiveness with the (invisible) skin on.

12/18/14 I just became aware, today due to my negligence, that this SMART watch has figured out, on its own, where I live (via GPS), when I leave for work, the route I take and gives the road warnings and comparison timing by text to work, it knows the time I start work, where I work, when I leave work, my days off, and the route I take home. It even tells me when I get home later than normal. The watch also tells you if your ride to/from work was longer or shorter than the day before. It is tracking you everywhere. It must be using the GPS in the phone, time of day, regularity, steps taken, and possibly other movement types to the watch along with data from the phone. I now find it a little scary that this can track and figure out what you're doing and where. I hadn't been paying attention to those messages that were coming off the watch until I cleared them all. I guess we've got to wonder just how much tracking is going on without our knowledge and just how much this thing can really do. Scary and now has me thinking and wondering if the security implications are worth it, but it is still a dang awesome smart watch! Much more impressive now that I know this watch figures out what you do the more you use it. If you are paranoid of the man then this watch is certainly not on your agenda. Its basically a 24/7 tracker, something that some nosy folks may find quite interesting since this can follow where you are to the exact location every second you wear this watch. Perhaps a tad too smart? Very Orwellian.

Don't forget to clear your notices on the watch or it will take forever to clear all the different types of notices when you finally realize you've been letting them pile up. Delete after you view. Don't remember a month later. It took me forever to clear everything that built up for 28 days, not to mention the space the files took up.

title: Exactly As Advertised
text:
And therein lies the problem.

It's a perfectly serviceable and inexpensive disk drive; I've had none of the noise issues other reviewers have mentioned. All in all, works pretty well.

Except for what it lacks, which is everything except the drive itself.

It doesn't come with any of the mounting or connecting hardware, no SATA cables, and no software. This means that you have to download the drivers yourself, and it does not come with any of the registered software that allows you to play Blu Ray movies. In other words, it's a Blu Ray drive that won't play Blu Rays unless you buy an outside software.

This is a major failing in my opinion, but I can't fault the page. It says very clearly what's included, caveat emptor. Be warned that you will have to spend the money on SATA connectors and extra software to get full functionality out of this drive.

Other than that, it's a fast and serviceable disk drive. 2.5/5 for quality of build and missing necessary components.

title: It really is superb!
text:
Those who have read my reviews know that I very rarely rate anything at 5 stars. This camcorder rates at least that many. I've had a Canon Vixia HD camcorder for a couple of years, and it's a fine camcorder, but the TM900 surpasses it both in image quality and in ease of use. I've been using the TM900 for almost a month now, bought it Used, advertised as "Very Good" condition on Amazon, and I'm delighted with the purchase.

To start with, I should point out that I'm a person who greatly prefers to use manual controls when shooting either still images or video. The TM900 does a competent job in good light in "intelligent automatic" mode, but to get the best out of it (again, as with all cameras) it should be used in Manual mode. "Automatic" settings often are underexposed unless there's ample light, but with Manual mode, the TM900 is a very good low light camcorder. Manual mode is so easy to use, it's a shame to use this camera any other way.

Many people have commented on fan noise. My TM900 has is NO audible fan noise when shooting. During playback, there's a faint whisper which could be fan noise or a faint whisper of wind (most of my video is done outside) but it's not intrusive at all. Using an external microphone would eliminate even that whisper, but I haven't bothered with an external mic yet.

As with all cameras which are new to a person, there's a learning curve. Your first video clips may not be your best ones, but you'll quickly learn to use manual settings to best advantage. It's so easy! And it's so smooth, using the ring which surrounds the lens at the front of the camera, that you can adjust exposure or WB "on the fly" as you shoot. (I don't recommend adjusting WB "on the fly", but it can be done easily, and adjusting *exposure* while shooting can be a great help in getting an excellent final video.)

Images are superbly sharp, probably better than with the Canon, which does produce superbly sharp images. But for me, the ease of adjusting exposure and focus are the very best things about the camera. They make correct exposure much easier and more accurate than I could achieve with the Canon.

White balance is more difficult to get right. I found that automatic white balance (AWB) is very good, though not absolutely perfect, most of the time. Custom WB is possible, and it's easy to make a custom WB with the TM900, but custom WB is not often an improvement over AWB. The preset WB for Sun is pretty accurate; the preset for Cloudy conditions is very good, though maybe it's a touch too saturated for my taste. There is no separate WB preset for Shade.

I usually stay with automatic focus, which is the default even when the camera is in Manual mode. That's good, because manual focus is only easy to do when there's good light and when the subject is relatively still. However, if the subject isn't moving around too much (my dogs are always running) manual focus can be a big help in separating the subject, like a person's face, from a high-contrast element like a fence in the background.

There have been several comments about where various switches are located and so forth. Really, the ergonomics of this camera are just fine. They are a little different from the Canon, and there are a couple of things I like better about the Canon's off-on button for example - but even that is easy to adapt to.

In summary - someone wrote that the TM900 is "almost superb". I disagree. It really IS superb.

title: I like the blue color LED the most for daytime although ...
text:
UNIDEN BEARCAT 980 SSB

After my Cobra 29 Classic LTD bit the dust after only 3 years, I didn't buy another Cobra 29 but got this radio instead because of the SSB and updated display which you can adjust the brightness of for day and night use.

I like the blue color LED the most for daytime although the red reminds me of the lights that the military uses for low light signatures and is very Holloweenie at night...ooh, scary.

Unit is light weight and transfers well from truck to car.

SWR calibrate function is way more sensitive compared with the Cobra 29 and my Firestik II antenna was way off as a result but now both the car antenna and the truck antenna are nearly the same which is cool. Now, whether in the car or the truck, I just get in, install the coax plug in the power and go. I do still check the swr every now and then but it's right on at 1.00 and perfectly level at channels 40 and 1.

The radio has a antenna check and a voltage check and a microphone check function in the Diagnose part of the menu which is cool. It will show how much voltage radio is getting when the engine is on or when it is off which kinda helps to see if your alternator is at 14v and battery at 12v so it doubles as a troubleshooting tool for those as well.
If this function helps me from getting stuck with a couple of dead batteries or an 'about to die' alternator even just once, this function alone will have paid for itself 10 times over.
The antenna check -checks- the connection of the coax cable from the radio to the antenna and works well.

OK, now for the business end of the radio...

I find that the receive and transmit are ok...just ok. Radio check from other drivers on the road are that the radio sounds good from about a mile or maybe 2 miles away on a cloudy day but no further. I can tell it's ability to receive is weak by just listening to the radio on 19 and waiting to hear drivers at truck stops and it's usually not more than a mile or so.
I guess you can turn a couple of pots inside the radio to turn up the modulation on both the AM and SSB.

SSB is a new function for me. So far, USB and LSB don't seem to have much on it to listen to but I guess not too many drivers have it or I have a low powered stock radio that isn't receiving too well.
The microphone jack on the unit is a 6 pin! but the included adapter will accommodate any 4 pin mic you have from your old setup.
The included microphone is well, one that looks like it's design was from the movie The Transformers. I guess some drivers will actually use this microphone if this is their first radio, but I would advise an Astatic or a Road King microphone instead of this weak, cheaply made p.o.s. stock microphone...Uniden, why did you even bother? I mean C'MON guys.You could have given us a beep on/ off function but you gave us this stupid microphone instead, thanks.

Let's see here...well, it's a quiet unit and I don't hear the power window motors or the heater fan motor through the speaker like I did with the Cobra which is a huge plus.
Like almost every one else, that friggin beep noise is an issue and the fact that Uniden didn't see fit to give us a menu option to turn it off is just a stupid oversight.
The knob to turn the radio on and the volume knob are one in the same like on most radios and is wobbly and not solid feeling like a radio of this price range should feel in my opinion. I like the Cobra radio a lot better for the solid feeling knobs they have and it's a big deal to me, so fix it UNIDEN!

I'm not sure how well this radio is designed and how well it will stand up to wet weather here in the Northern part of the USA but time will tell if UNIDEN coats it's board inside with a resin so that water isn't an issue since CBs are left out in cars and trucks. In fact, why doesn't Uniden just make all their CBs to marine standards and call it a day?

For some reason, Uniden didn't include Bluetooth so that I could pair it with my truck stereo and listen to it over the speakers in my truck bypassing the small internal speaker in the CB.

My headset mounted Bluetooth is something I really want to use instead of a microphone so that I can keep my hands on the wheel and why Uniden isn't even thinking about how Bluetooth is a modern day utility is besides me?!

Any how, that's pretty much it and I know there are ways around some of the things I complained about, I just think that this radio has a lot of growing up to do before it's worthy of heavy big truck use by professional drivers.

title: Great (starter) scope!
text:
Found the Nexstar 4SE a great starter scope, and good value. The tripod is solid, and the 4-inch scope is relatively easy to transport. I had a small refractor in school, and this was my foray back into astronomy- I was blown away by the clarity, and what I could see. I got a 8-24 mm lens to use in place of the stock, and have seen awesome views of the moon, Saturn, Jupiter. With the Neximage camera, I took some beautiful shots of the planets, catching even the Great Red Spot of Jupiter (it wasn't visible via the eyepiece though I could see at least 4 of Jupiter's moons using the eyepiece alone).
Like what the others say, the AC adapter is a must- batteries did not last very long.
The Goto function is easy to use, though I wish I didn't have to input the time/date everytime. Tracking was very accurate for me, even leaving it for an hour- I used the 3-star align method. Has a built in wedge for polar alignment though perhaps I haven't mastered doing this yet- taking timelapse pictures still had significant star trails.
That all being said, in retrospect I should have gone bigger. The 4SE is great for solar system viewing, but I found it less suited for deep space objects. And so, I think I've outgrown this and am looking for a larger scope :) (no fault of the 4SE)

title: Best RV GPS, great GPS in general
text:
I have used Magellan GPSs in cars and Motorhomes for many years, when they came out with RV specific GPSs the default one for me was the Magellan, but after doing a little research I chose to buy the Rand McNally 7710 7 inch model. I have used the 7710 for about two years now, on 5-6 trips comprising something like 4 or 5 months on the road, in all areas of the country and Canada, we take long trips. In short, I am a power user of both Magellan and Rand McNally GPSs, but know nothing about Garmin.

I love the 7710 mostly for the size and features, the dash board screen provides a wealth of information such as current location, nearest cross street, and much more. The speed dash board shows your elevation, speed, sunrise and sunset time at your current location, there is a feature to tell you when to add fuel, and your average speed, both uphill and downhill. It also had three odometers for trip millage, total hours, total hours moving, and average speed. The map display also shows current speed and will alarm if you exceed the posted speed, you can turn off this alarm and adjust how much over the posted speed you need to be to trigger the alarm. Other alarms notify you of a change in the speed limit, turn coming up, and construction or road narrowing. Also avalable on the map is a display of the road you are currently on and by clicking on the road name you can change it to display the next cross street, now that is a nice feature, really helps when looking for a street and you need some warning to move over. Easily accessible points of interest right on the map display. The colors are also easily adjustable.

The display is easily readable in all but direct sunlight, direct sunlight on the screen, not just in the car, and Rand McNally makes a sun shield that I bought and that fixed the problem. I find the display very readable with the sun shield in all light conditions.

Maps and routing, this unit uses Navteq maps which I have found are not as good as the Magellan maps. One of my cars has a built in GPS which also uses the Navteq maps. They are OK, and we have always been able to find our way but the Magellan maps are just more detailed and complete. I have just updated the maps in the 7710 for our next trip so have high hopes that they have fix the issues. Before I got the Rand McNally I used the latest Magellan, for a car, in the Motorhome and had issues with the routing a few times, bridges that would not take my weight, underpasses that were too low, and roads that did not allow RV because of mountains or other issues. Since getting the 7710 I have had no problems with this kind of thing, none whatsoever. The RV weight, length, and height are adjustable and you can change the routing for either the RV or a car.

This is a great unit and I would not be without it on a Motorhome trip.

title: Inexpensive way to fix coverage holes in your home network
text:
(I am sorry but I have to downgrade my original review)

I live in a brick and concrete condo with metal studs in the inside walls, which turns the inside of the condo into a Faraday cage of sorts. I have always struggled getting good signal propagation throughout the unit, about 1000 square feet total area. Even mobile phone service has been a problem, until very recently when I switched to T-mobile I couldn't have a cell conversation unless I stood at one of our windows.

I had solved the propagation issue for a while by adding an extension cable to my router's antenna. I moved it into a different wall and with a reflector, this more or less allowed decent connectivity throughout the unit until neighbors started to use stronger routers a couple of weeks ago. I noticed that suddenly we were getting disconnects from any device that we tried, but only on one side of the house. A wifi analysis app showed me that either somebody upgraded a router and it was extremely powerful, or he fielded an extender and between his two signals it was drowning mine.

Installing this device was pretty painless. I had to do the manual setup, but that's because Verizon never enabled the one-button feature in my particular router. All I did was connect to the extender with a Kindle Fire HDX, logged into it, gave it the password for my access point and 30 seconds later I was done. It only took me two tries to find a spot in the house that would fix the weak signals issue.

The device itself is a neat little plastic doodad, no bigger than a plug-in air freshener. If your router has a one-button setup feature, you should be able to get it up and running within a minute of opening the box. The packaging itself is very nice, the kind of packaging you would expect from an Apple device (the manual is in a folder that is identical to how iPhone manuals are bundled).

Documentation is fine, but that's from just making it into the first two steps. The device also included an ethernet patch cord, which was a nice touch ,and a small-format CD, I don't know what would happen if the user needs the CD and his drive isn't compatible with that kind of CD.

I will revise this review once I have a chance to hit it hard from the weaker sides of the house. My initial testing showed videos that used to stutter are now playing smoothly.

UPDATE (7/16/2014): The device decided to stop working within a day of my original review, couldn't reach it even through the ethernet port, hard reset didn't work at all.

I assumed it was a defective unit, so I exchanged it. The replacement unit lasted a couple of days longer before it started giving us grief again and I have asked for a refund.

My main motivation for attempting to use this device? I am forced to use the router specified by Verizon FIOS since the cable boxes rely on it through the MoCa port, which to me is idiotic (or a con to keep us using their routers). My condo has metal studs and it wrecks hell on any kind of signal propagation, I actually had to relocate the original antenna with an extension cable just so I could get minimum coverage within the house. Verizon was too happy to advertise that I could upgrade to a newer router for $100, which is ridiculous.

I was really hoping that this doodad would do the trick, but after two defective units I decided to move on.

Yesterday I plugged a TP-LINK TL-WDR4300 into my FIOS router and turned off the radio in the FIOS router. Now I have excellent coverage in my house and it still cost me $33 less than going with the Verizon device. Ironically, the web UI on the WDR4300 is basically identical to the one on the WA850RE so I felt right at home configuring the new device.

title: Good quality umbrella, two-in-one
text:
I bought this one to use with some LED light panels. The BIG plus about this umbrella is that you get both a shoot through umbrella for when you either want that look or perhaps you want to squeeze every last lumen out of your lights. PLUS you get the "bounce" umbrella if you put the cover back on.

A bounced light off a white background is going to be softer than shoot through (albeit the difference to this amateur is minute). I do generally prefer the way light wraps around a subject when I bounce rather than shoot through.

As for the reviews talking about how hard it is to put the cover back on, it's actually quite simple. The trick is to hold the umbrella slightly open and hook one side then the other, then work your way around. Don't be afraid to very gently "flex" the metal supports either. I found it pretty intuitive. Is it something you'd want to do with 30 seconds to spare and a crucial shot coming up? No. But it goes back on fast enough.

Quality is good upon first inspection, most fotodiox stuff I have is. The "bounce" is very similar to my PBL white/black umbrellas though it uses a different approach. The black has a silver backing on it that is covered up by the diffuser umbrella (kind of a sheer white satin).

I use these as essentially portable "Soft boxes" for my LED video lights and they work great. I use this one with a 600 LED light and it's the right size for that I think.

So in summary:

- You get a bounce AND diffuser umbrella
- Quality is good, price is cheap enough that even if it breaks, you can replace
- Putting cover back on IS NOT that difficult/scary
- It's an umbrella ?

title: Good Idea, BAD product

title: If you hook your computer to a big flat screen, this thing is a godsend, worth twice the price
text:
I'm using this keyboard right now, as I recline in my beloved Ekornes chair and watch the words appear on our big LED screen across the room. It's so relaxing compared to using a laptop or box. I've got other wireless kbs but the addition of the trackpad here is what makes this a screaming deal; my deluxe Logitech mouse/kb combo cost 85 and I was always losing the mouse, plus it's a hassle to have to keep them together. This kb is all-in-one, smaller and lighter and thinner, and just better in every way.

Being able to sit across the room and surf or write or watch music videos and all the free movies on yt etc is almost ridiculously convenient. Plus this thing is so small, very easy to put aside anywhere. The trackpad also offers two finger scrolling, a very useful feature on long pages. The keys spring nicely too, a nice medium touch. Size is perfect, as the mini kbs are just too small for my medium large hands.

I've got my laptop plugged into the flat screen, and this into my laptop, so I can write emails etc while listening to music files on my VLC player (best media player out there, and it's free!) and my back is happy for hours, as opposed to sitting at the desk.

For 25 bucks, this is an insane value if you like to sit far away from the screen. As a very unexpected bonus, my eyes are slowly getting better at detail as I look across the room at the screen. I always feel like being right in front of a monitor hurts my eyes, and now I know it for a fact. Hit ctrl and + and you can make any page as huge as you need, of course, but I find that forcing my ocular muscles to work a bit with smaller fonts makes them stronger.

All told, this is one of the most useful things I've bought in a long time, and would be happy if I'd paid 50.

title: The Downsized Upgrade
text:
Aside from a brief and craptacular experience with the Motorola Xoom a couple years ago, I've been an iOS user.. multiple generations of iPhones, iPad 2, and iPad 3. Generally happy with the ecosystem, apps, and user experience, but I've been itching for a smaller form factor for a while and didn't like the idea of chipping in on the iPad Mini - it read like a reactive, rushed, sub-par product. Around the time I started reading up on the first-gen Nexus 7, there were rumblings of the 2nd gen, so the clock started ticking on dipping a toe back into the Android pond.

My preordered Nexus 7 FHD 32GB arrived a couple days ago, and I can't find a thing I don't like about it.

Speed. There's an agility in its performance that's reminiscent of the iPad 3 - but more impressive. It's a fast machine. Apps snap into action. Nothing I've thrown at it so far makes it lag.

Resolution. Other reviews extoll the pixel mathematics; from my perspective, it's stunning. Better than anything I've seen in a tablet. Netflix streaming movies are crisp, photos are brilliantly rendered, and the overall onscreen environment is exceptionally pleasing to the eyes. If screen resolutions on tablets never evolved any further, this would be a great stopping point. Just beautiful.

Form factor. For me, the 7" tablet is the sweet spot. Sure, I like watching movies or reading on a 10" tablet, but there's no fidelity or experience loss in this size. It's nice to hold, and doesn't feel cheap or flimsy in the slightest.

OS. My glimpse into the Android ecosystem during the early-adopter days of the Motorola Xoom wasn't favorable. Herky-jerky performance, weird onscreen typing lag, lack of tablet apps - it wasn't a meaningful experience. The difference between then and now is nothing short of astonishing. There's a level of polish and detail that speaks to an average iOS user like me, yet contains all the paths into the 'under the hood' aspects of Android that illuminate the nerd appeal. I love the fact that there's so much to learn and do with this OS, unlike iOS where you're largely just along for the ride.

Price: Doesn't really need further championing. You get an amazing product with all the bells and whistles for an exceptionally reasonable price. It seems like every Apple device I buy immediately goes into a cushioned case, gets a screen protector, and I transport the thing like it's an donated organ. After such a significant buy-in for an iPad, who wants to deal with a shattered or scratched-up screen or dented chassis? The lower price point on the Nexus 7 doesn't mean I'll baby the Nexus 7 any less, but I don't feel the same compulsion to make it live like Bubble Boy, and I can just use the device in an everyday sense. Replacing a damaged N7 won't be as financially painful as an iPad.

One tip: the first couple times I plugged in (Apple) headphones, I was getting crackly sound, or no sound at all. The headphone jack didn't feel look it was inserting all the way (but felt like it was going as far as it could), and I wondered if I had a bum unit. Turns out, you have to push it in a bit harder than you'd initially like to, which will result in a satisfying snap and boom - full audio. Felt a little silly afterwards, but hopefully that helps others with the same question/issue.

Gen 1 Nexus 7 users and Android fans in general don't need to be convinced - they ought to be largely happy with the upgrades present in this iteration. But for iOS users like me looking for the same kind of 'change', this is it. Check it out at a retailer, hold it, swipe it, play with it. You'll 'get it', and then you'll get it.

title: Let's be honest: a GREAT deal for a "budget" LCD-LED tv!
text:
SUMMARY: I have to give this TV "only" 4 stars :). The blacks on it are washed out & shadow detail is not great. BUT this TV is under $800 for 47"! Great deal!!

I purchased this TV on June 24, 2012 and chose No-Rush Delivery delivery because I didn't need it right away, and why not get $1 free mp3s? At $749, it was cheaper than any other store online or in-store!!

So at this price point, I cannot bring up the complaints that CNET had (2.5 stars, OK rating). Surely, if I want beautiful deep blacks and consistent bright colors, I would be required much more than this. But I surely cannot afford that. My budget was $700-750, and this Panasonic was a better deal than competing Samsung models--but those were 42" models.

Thus, I am very happy with my purchase. The colors on this VIERA are beautiful at almost any angle; 47" is more than big enough for my apartment.

NOTE: I am not sure if any generic USB Wifi dongle will work & will test this later. I surely don't want to pay so much extra for the Panasonic TY-WL20U Wifi adapter (currently $52.49 direct from Amazon).

POSITIVES:
*120hz
*LED
*IPS display = great viewing angles, like your iPad.
*Colors are great IMHO
*SmartTV "Smart Viera" via built-in Ethernet or Wifi dongle (sold separately).
*Lots of Connectivity: 4 HDMI inputs, 2 USB connectors, hybrid component/composite adapter, Ethernet.
*Slim design!
*Price = great deal! 47" for the price of a 42"

NEGATIVES:
*Wifi-ready, but Wifi dongle not included & must buy separately.
*Color: Blacks are soggy & muted :(
*Media Player built-in can only play MP3s & not M4As from iTunes.

EDIT: It does play M4A files, but it doesn't read the audio track's info properly, and artist/song name shows up as asterisks.

COMPARABLE TVs:
$819.99 Samsung UN46EH6000 46-Inch 1080p 240 CMR LED HDTV = more expensive, and colors bad in their own way; CNET 3 stars.
$719.99 Toshiba 46L5200U 46-Inches 1080P/120HZ LED TV = cheaper, but no Smart apps or connectivity; CNET 3 stars.

It easily lets you import PDFs to write on, and you can export as PDF to print to share. By using another application called DropSync, it will sync all your notes to Dropbox (which you get an extra 50GB from buynig this tablet), viewable on your computer.

title: Very Solid and Well Designed at a Great Price!
text:
Despite the relatively low price, this is a very good quality TV wall mount. I'm using it on a 42" LG LCD, which weighs about 40 lbs, and mounted to wood studs. I considered purchasing a mount from a different manufacturer that's identical to one that I'm using on a larger TV, but it is about 4 times the price. After reading the positive reviews of the Cheetah mount, I decided to try it out.

This mount comes with all the required hardware, plus 2 levels and a braided HDMI cable. I had this installed in about 3 hours; much of that was my own time spent taking measurements to make sure the placement was right and properly leveled. Otherwise, installation was very easy. The kit comes with a small leveling tool and also a miniature level which clips to the mount. I used my own level to make sure it was right, but the tool that comes with the kit seemed reasonably accurate.

The wall mounted bracket needs to be assembled prior to placing it on the wall. Two horizontal pieces each for the upper and lower frame are attached together via a small bracket and 6 screws/nuts each. The frame can also be configured to use just one-half of the upper and lower pieces for smaller TVs. After drilling the four holes in the wall studs, the provided lag bolts were used to very securely attached the frame to the wall.

The brackets for the TV also fit perfectly, with enough holes to be able to center it on the back. Since I don't plan on using the tilt feature, I installed the two provided locking pins to keep the TV flat relative to the wall. It was easy to lift the TV and place the top hooks on to the wall mount, but I had to lift slightly on the TV to get both of the bottom locking mechanisms to latch on. After that, the TV was properly secured to the wall.

Overall, this a very well designed mount. It is very sturdy and I have no doubts about it keeping my TV firmly attached to the wall. If you're looking for a solid TV mount for a great price, I'd highly recommend this one.

title: Just like the original but better
text:

I thought the sound was fantastic, but around a month ago, they started to sound slightly faded/muffled in one ear. I've used them heavily, such as while working out and sleeping, but as they were still under warrantee, Klipsch replaced them without question. When the box came, it turns out they sent me the S4 II instead of the S4 (I, original, whatever) I had before, so here's what I've noticed after having them for about a month:

The sound is basically the same as the original S4. That is to say, amazing.
The bass is strong but definitely not overpowering.
The fit is also pretty much the exact same as the originals, which means they're very comfortable. The most comfortable earbuds I've used actually.
They are noise isolating, which means they block out outside noise, and they do a decent job of that, but they're not active noise canceling and certainly not the "best noise canceling headphones ever" as stated in another review.
The biggest and most noticeable change is the cord. The new flat cord is supposed to prevent tangling, and while it will still occasionally tangle, it's a huge improvement over the original S4 and most other earphones I've used.
Is it worth upgrading from the original? Certainly not, but for anyone looking to get a new pair of headphones, these are fantastic and I would recommend them without hesitation.

title: Beautifully built, but not an essential purchase for Q owners
text:
The first thing you notice when you handle the Q Zoom is the quality--this is one of the smoothest zoom lenses I've ever used, regardless of price. Although the manual focus ring is a little less of a quality feel, being light plastic and prone to scratching, much of the res of the lens is metal or heavily built, and the zoom action is very well damped giving a very luxurious feel. In today's world, this is the only wide angle and portrait length lens for the Q that has a full bevy of useful features like autofocus... But other than the novelty of being able to shoot those focal lengths on the Q, this lens makes less sense than you might think. Why wouldn't you want a fantastically wel built zoom lens for your Q? Two things--size and image quality.

The size of the zoom is tiny compared with other interchangeable lens camera zooms, but huge compared to any collapsing built in zoom on a small-sensor a. And therein lies the problem--the Q approaches the size of the Somy Nex 5 when the zoom is attached, which really negates the main size advantage the Q has over that and other mirror less cameras.

I could forgive the size if the image quality was superb because, after all, it does handle extremely well and is very fluid to shoot with... But the image quality is somewhat disappointing. It's ok, certainly not bad, and I have made some beautiful photos with it. But it's clear the Zoom doesn't have the resolution the Q's tiny high-res sensor demands, and the contrast is also lower than the 01 Prime and 03 Fisheye. The resulting images look more like they came from any other compact camera and not the little wonder that is the Q.

It's not horrible, by any stretch, and if you need the focal length range and/or want the Q to be your only camera, it's a sensible choice. If you use your Q more as a niche, fun, carryall shooter, though... I'd pass and wait for wide and tele primes that match the quality of the 01 Prime.

title: Installing the Posrus Pen Tablet Cover Sheet
text:
The Posrus Cover Sheet for the Wacom Pen Tablets should be a worthy addition to reduce pen nib wear. However, there is a problem with it in that it ships without any instructions on how to apply the cover sheet squarely to the tablet surface, and it is not the same size as the tablet's active area.

As you receive the cover, it is a thin, flat translucent plastic sheet with ⅛" wide adhesive applied to the edges on one side. Over the edge adhesive strips is, of course, a glossy paper covering and then over that whole side is a static cling sheet of light weight flexible plastic to prevent finger prints before application.

The size of the Posrus Tablet Cover Sheet at first seems odd. It is ⅛" wider than the tablet's active area, but ¼" longer from top to bottom, so applying it evenly requires some care. I managed that by laying the Cover Sheet on the active area before removing the backings and marking the position temporarily with yellow sticky notes just beyond the edges. Then I pealed the static sheet back about a third of the way from the top edge and used an X-acto knife point to lift a corner of each of the four pieces of the adhesive backing paper, folding a tab of the backing out from the edge at an angle. That made it easy to put the cover in place between the yellow notes, peal the paper from the top edge adhesive and burnish that edge in place with a finger nail; followed by removing the rest of the backings and burnishing the rest of the adhesive strips.

The only question I have now that my cover is in place is whether the sharply cut edges on the cover will damage the pen nib, possibly more than the Wacom tablets surface, if in my exuberance I pass the edges of the cover and try to swing back onto it again without lifting the pen. I guess avoiding that will be part of the learning process.

Alright, first off, I made the mistake of ordering the OTHER Sony flat doors for diving, that apparently did not fit my AS30. So, take note, this case is only for the AS30 and the newer white model. I tried to return my wrong flat doors to the Sony store for a simple exchange, no dice, so I'm stuck with some proprietary parts. Docking a star here.

I primarily purchased my ActionCam for use underwater, so this housing is essential. The lack of buttons on the side, that the standard case has, is not really a big deal to me, as I would rather have less areas where water can potentially leak.

What I do have serious problems with is the overall user experience with this case. I read the instructions and it is unbelievable how much work one has to put into this housing to "supposedly" have this unit last longer than a year. Sony suggests inspecting the O-ring every time and buying "their" grease to lubricate the O-ring, etc. What?!
How come GoPro users don't have to do these extraneous steps? Can't the housing be designed to maintain the life of the O-ring, longer than a year?
You already should buy anti-fog sheets / flotation attachment, now Sony wants you to buy extra O-rings and grease... Gimme a break. With a GoPro, you don't need to buy s*** to go straight to underwater diving, let alone a new housing to begin with.

Anyways, I have used this housing once already to go snorkeling and it worked quite well. No problems and videos look pretty decent, comparatively. I read their instructions to rinse this case with fresh water (after use in salt water), but missed the fine print to keep the buckle closed, whoops. Hopefully, the front lens will dry out okay for another use. Again, bad user experience.

I just can't believe this unit has so many things that can potentially go wrong that I'm scared to even use the bloody thing.

O-ring misaligned? Damaged camera. Didn't rinse the unit with fresh water after? Damaged housing and camera. A grain of sand got on the O-ring? Damaged camera. Hairline crack on the o-ring? Damaged camera.

You get the point. I just feel the user experience and design should be set to "normal" use standards, or maybe the instructions are too paranoid. Time will tell.

title: This lens is great for macro work - it's a microscope for your camera
text:
This lens is so much fun to use! You already know it's manual focus, but the MP-E designation might confuse people. It just stands for 'macro photography', but this lens will work with EF or EF-S lens mounts equally well. It should probably be designated as an L lens for the quality of images it produces. Everyone raves about this unique lens, and I do too. But I'm going to try something different. Instead of talking about how good this lens is, I'll give some notes on use to help give potential buyers an idea of what to expect from this lens, and the best accessory products I've found for getting images with a high production quality.

You need a macro rail to nail focus because handholding this is very difficult without the image stabilization that's on the 100mm f/2.8L IS Macro lens. You are also fighting against effective apertures at the different high magnifications this lens can achieve. As you fight these higher effective apertures, you also have to contend with diffraction that will make the images less sharp. The upshot of all this is that by the time you're at 5X magnification, you should be photographing at f/2.8, which means you are probably going to be focus stacking. I have discovered after a lot of use with this lens that 4X magnification at f/2.8 is the peak sharpness and that 5X magnification at f/2.8 (effective aperture of f/16) has slightly more detail but is less sharp. These low effective apertures mean that you'll either be taking the photographs at a calculated exposure time in Bulb mode, or you'll be pushing 30 seconds of exposure time. You will need a flash if you want to have reasonable exposure times as well.

A very well priced macro rail is the "Velbon Super Magnesium Slider, Macro Rail" which is much more reliable than the stuff offered from Cowboy Studio or Neewer. The reason I don't recommend the stuff from Cowboy Studio or Neewer is because they will flex with the weight of your camera as you move the lens in and out along the rail which will cause misalignment of your images when you're stacking them, and that defeats the whole purpose of attaching a macro rail to your tripod in the first place. The cheap focus rails will also wobble a lot more.

Next you should get some photography stacking software. You don't need stacking software if you want to take abstract looking photos, but if you want your subject in focus, you need to stack your images. Photoshop can do basic stacking, but it isn't very good with this advanced lens and will give you weird halos in the final output and you will also have patches of blurry areas among the sharp regions. Zerene Stacker is what I recommend as the best software I have found for stacking images with this lens.

Finally, you should think about what kind of flash you want to use with this lens. You can either light with a TTL cord and a standard speedlight, or you can use one of the macro flashes that attach to the front of the lens. I think the flashes that attach to the front of the lens produce images that look the best, but I personally think the Canon macro flashes are too overpriced. I recommend getting the "Meike MK-14EXT Macro TTL ring flash for Canon". It's almost identical to the Canon ring flash in terms of functions, but it produces images that actually do look identical. It's also at a much more reasonable price.

Also, there is the option to go beyond 5X with this lens using the Extender teleconverters and Extension Tubes. Both work. With a 2X Extender, you can achieve 10X magnification which is insane, but you're going to be focus stacking like crazy for that photo. Diffraction of light also causes a hit to 10X image quality in the same way that 5X takes a hit relative to 4X magnification. And Extension Tubes will help you go a little beyond 5X with less impact to image quality than the Extender would create.

Okay, after reading this review, I think you'll know everything you need to get started and you'll know about all the accessories you should have to take great photos. There is a great online community for people getting started in macro photography at Photo Macrography Net. Visiting that website should help people figure out what they're doing.

title: Could have been so great.
text:
I've now had the X-pro 1 + 35 f1.4 for about a week. I have been through alot of cameras in my life but I have never been so torn about a camera before. I really want to love this camera.

The build quality, the retro design, the size, the weight. All perfect! Short of my 5D Mark III this cameras IQ is superior to any camera I have ever used. It's high ISO capabilities are legendary. The photos are clear and crisp and look great in most cases. The autofocus, while somewhat sluggish, I find it to be decent enough and more accurate than the X100. Q menu is an awesome addition.

All these positives I mentioned would seem like enough right? Then why Fuji would you create such a mess with the rest of the camera? So close to perfection, yet so far away.

Chattering aperture blades that can drive a person mad. I shot a company party and was getting looks from coworkers asking me what was wrong with my camera. Aside from that, autofocus is extremely loud, the EVF is sluggish and slow to update. The shutter speed dial is very stiff and hard to rotate while looking though the VF. The customization is so limited. you are only allowed to customize the FN button, while the control dial which is the best dial on the camera remains dormant, unused and non programmable. The arrows buttons, also cannot be customized. Missing a live exposure preview for aperture and shutter speed like all other fuji cameras. Focus by wire renders the manual focus of the lenses virtually useless for anything other than fine tuning. Various memory card problems. Minimum shutter speed cannot be set rendering auto ISO useless.

I just dont understand how a company that creates cameras and lenses with such fine optics screws up the most basic features that so many lesser cameras get right. And they do it with one camera, and then repeat many of the same exact mistakes the following year. It's heartbreaking to have to return this camera but I cannot justify the price with so many bugs and design flaws. What a shame. Kudos to you folks that can overlook the negatives as I am truly jealous and will shake my head in disappointment every time I see someone carrying this black beauty in their hands with thoughts of what might have been.

If Fuji can address the majority of the issues I mentioned I would be glad to change my review to 5 stars and instantly buy one again. One can hope.
