title: Fantastic Turntable
text:
I received the Audio Technica AT LP120 USB Direct Drive turntable for Christmas (yesterday), and it is absolutely outstanding!

I replaced a 1967 Dual 1019 that has not worked well for several years, and I had not realized how much better a new turntable could be. The AT LP120 is so much better I can't begin to describe the improvements!

The instructions were well-written, so setup was simple. I had it playing within 30 minutes of starting to open the box. The cartridge and counter weight were packed separately to protect them during shipping. They were simple to attach to the tone arm. Balancing was also simple. Then, a single cable connected the 120 to my 1967 Sansui Receiver using the Phono input. Lastly, I plugged it into a standard 120 Volt outlet.

Then, I started playing my old records. How nice to hear classic vinyl again, smooth and silky in a way CDs never are! The quality of the sound is so good, I can't tell it's vinyl except for the silky nature of it. I don't hear many pops or clicks and no wow or flutter. The highs are crisp and the lows are deep and solid. Definitely nostalgic! Like being back in 1967 again!

I haven't tried connecting the USB port to my PC, yet, but it seems very simple. There is software to load via a CD and then you connect the USB cable. I will do that after I get a good fix of old vinyl, but that could take a week or more.

title: Suffers the same problems as all the Canon uw cases
text:
I really like the Canon camera S-series, from the S60 to the S90 I have owned them all. However the underwater enclosures all suffer the same problem, no matter how carefully they are cleaned/soaked/washed eventually the o-rings become sticky and the buttons no longer work at any depth. The buttons lock in position if pressed - the spring is not powerful enough to pull it back. On the enclosures for the S60 and S70 this happened around 20-30 dives. The S90 case lasted about 50 dives. Canon does not make an o-ring service kit, nor would they repair under warranty (or even repair at my expense), this is apparently normal wear and tear! Many a dive has been tarnished by the fact that the camera locked up at a crucial moment.

You can carefully dismantle the buttons and clean the o-rings. It will then last another 20-30 dives. I have not found an o-ring of the correct size to replace the factory parts and quite honestly would not want to, just in case they leaked. The only item Canon sell is the large plastic ring that seals the rear door.

It seems this problem also occurs on other Canon cases. My dive buddy bought a Canon SD model camera on my recommendation and also bought the matching UW case - against my advice. After 40 dives his case failed with a button stuck. Of course the button released at the surface. He did the o-ring cleaning dance and the UW case worked for another 40 dives. Now we both do preventive maintenance at around 30 dives.

I have no experience of the other 3rd party cases that are available, however after 5 cases I should learn or Canon should learn. You need to really look after these cases more than would be expected. Saltwater and the ocean is a very harsh environment and the design of the case needs to be consistent with those conditions.

title: The Best Player for Audio
text:
This player is simply the best option for someone looking for audio quality. I'd been using my HTC Inspire for all my music, and between the DHD and the 10-band EQ on PowerAMP, it gave pretty decent quality, though there were significant problems. The J3 completely blows anything I've ever tried out of the water.

The sound quality is absolutely top notch, COWON isn't just blowing hot air when they say that JetAudio 3.0 is the best. The lows are full and rich, the highs clean and crisp, and it doesn't give up anything. The sound is completely consistent whether you're listening to a lot of treble or if the bass is pounding. This is one of the biggest issues I've had with players, that when you try to get lower bass, it reduces the overall sound when the bass kicks in. That doesn't happen with the J3, at all. Not only does it come with about 30 different presets, it also has up to 4 programmable presets that allow you to have control over every single aspect of the sound, letting you dial it in absolutely perfectly. In addition, the sound settings carry over both to the video player and even the radio, allowing terrific sound quality even on radio stations, which is something very few players have to offer.

So enough about the sound, let's talk about the player itself. The device is quite small actually, and very light. The screen isn't the largest, but it's a beautiful AMOLED screen, and it displays everything crisp and bright, very nice. It has dedicated buttons for power, volume, AND play/pause and skip tracks. I haven't seen a whole lot of devices with dedicated buttons for play/pause and track skipping. The touch input is very responsive, although in the music menu I have had some issues scrolling sometimes. The menu of the J3 can be a little bit confusing at first, but is really quite simple and easy to use once you've figured it out. It took me all of 3 minutes to get a feel for it. Portrait view shows the album artwork and the controls, while landscape shows a very cool album browser that lets you browse your music in a new way, not unlike the Cover Flow on iPods. The accelerometer is VERY sensitive, and that can be a little annoying sometimes, but overall it's not too big of a problem. The other issue that I've noticed is that a lot of the tags do not translate perfectly to the J3. You may have to use a program like mp3Tag to adjust the tags for your music if you want them not to display in alphabetical view.

The J3 has a video player, and the AMOLED screen makes movies look wonderful, despite the small screen size. It also has a built-in flash player, which I haven't tested yet, but looks quite promising. It comes with some other extras, like pictures, and a few simple apps, and even a little game, though nothing terribly entertaining.

The J3 comes in a very stylish package, though it was a little unstable. The package was protected quite nicely though, so the shipping was very nice. In the package there's a set of COWON stock headphones, which aren't bad for what they are, but are quite uncomfortable. I wouldn't recommend them. You'll want at least a pair of intermediate quality headphones to take advantage of the sound quality the J3 has to offer. The package also includes a very uninformative starting guide, drivers (for Windows 98, go figure), and the dedicated cord. The cord is the last problem I have, as it doesn't go into the device all the way, making it kind of iffy whether or not it's plugged in. It's a USB cord, so I imagine it would work with most USB plug-in chargers, but I bought the official COWON wall charger to be safe.

In addition to the very nice 32GB size, the J3 has a slot for a microSD card, and I believe now you can add up to 32GB of extra space that way (16 at the least), and when you think about the cheapness of microSD cards, this is a very nice feature.

Overall, this product has been amazing so far. I've never heard my music the way I've heard it on this device. Does it do the most things of any mp3 player? No. If you want a mini-computer, get an iPod Touch or an Android Tablet. But it does quite a few things, and it does audio better than any device in its class. If you're looking for a small, stylish device to fill all your audio needs, look no further.

title: Save your money
text:
I did a lot of research and thought these would work for me - they didn't. I didn't need high fidelity headphones (hp) because I was mostly going to use them to listen to TV. Turns out, I should have saved my money.

Pros: Sennheiser has a great reputation.

Cons: Here we go....

- They are too small for my head. Granted, I have a big head, but the earpieces don't extend down far enough to cover both ears. I always have one side pinching down on an ear.

- They are too tight. I can only wear them for about 30-45 minutes before they become uncomfortable.

- The power button and other controls on the headset are almost worthless. It's almost impossible to differentiate the volume button from the on/off button from the pwr button, etc. I have to take them off my head to use the buttons. It could have been a simple zero-cost fix to design them better, but they chose not to do it.

- The "squelch" (for lack of a better word) is annoying. There is a certain amount of background hiss during dialogue on the TV. I can live with that. What's really irritating is when there is a break in the dialogue. The noise reduction kicks in and the headset goes totally silent. title: Great case and well worth the price
text:
I'm very pleased with this case. I bought a similar rooCase for my Galaxy Tab and went back to rooCase for my new iPad case after spending a couple of hours reviewing other cases. I actually bought an Apple Smart Cover with the iPad, but I quickly gave up on that. The grooves simply aren't deep enough to withstand much pressure and the iPad frequently slipped out of the groove when I was typing, which never happens with the rooCASE.

The sleep/wake function has worked flawlessly, and I like how you can pull the inner case out of the folio to remove some of the bulk if you don't need to prop up the case. Just remember that if you intend to do this for a meeting, do it before the meeting since it will make a loud, ripping noise, which you'd expect from velcro.

I've also found it handy to be able to switch the inner case from landscape to portrait despite the fact that I wasn't sure that was a feature I'd use much when I looking at the case.

Another thing I find to be a big plus is that all the ports are easily accessible with the folio closed, which they're not with my Galaxy Tab case. With that one, I have to leave the folio open to connect it to the charger.

The only reason I removed one star is that I'd like to see higher-quality leather. I think the quality of this leather is fine for the price, but I'd be willing to pay more for better leather. I'm not talking about pricing people who don't want to pay a lot for a case out of the picture, but I'd love to see rooCASE start making cases at different price points depending on the grade of the leather, and I'm sure there are others out there who would be willing to pay more for a better grade. These cases last a very long time as long as you take care of them, and you can use them for your next device as long as the device design remains the same. If not, the case is a selling point when you sell your old device to get your upgrade.

title: It works - sort of, but the documentation stinks
text: I bought this very cheap charger to charge a Sony NP-F550  lithium battery that I only use in my Neewer 160 LED camcorder light. I do not have the Sony camera and charger to charge and check the state of the battery, only this $4 charger. The charger came with absolutely no instructions - zero - nada - nichts! It has a LED that can be green, red and sometimes yellow - but what do these colors mean? You have to guess! When is the battery fully charged and ready to be removed from the charger? You have to guess! Does it even know when the battery is fully charged, and to stop charging the battery to avoid cooking it? You have to guess the answer to this one too! On the outside of box are printed some very limited characteristics of the charger. It is supposed to charge a 4.7 volt battery in 2.5 hours. This is totally misleading. My 4.7 volt battery takes more than 4 hours to reach a state of charge anywhere near "full". The LED stays solid red whenever the battery is in the charger - at the start and 5 hours later. It seems to just keep charging the battery to death.  The charger also runs very hot, especially the underside where it will get no ventilation if you mount it flush against a wall power outlet as you are supposed to. No wonder several reviewers complain that it "pops" and starts smoking after a while. I power mine through a short extension cord so the underside can be exposed to the air for better cooling. And I stay in the room all the time it is connected to power, in case it catches on fire. You cannot leave this device unattended. That all said, it is cheap and $4 won't break the bank if you have to toss it in the garbage after a while, to join appropriate company. It works for me (sort of), but I do not feel it deserves more than 2 stars.

title: *insane Gollumesque giggling*
text:
Canon would like you to know that they can make a 40 megapixel image sensor. They just see no reason to, as they have better things to do with chip real estate.

Canon's finally delivered a DSLR that combines the best of still shooting and video without compromising either, although it seems to have knocked their product matrix sideways by rendering the 7D irrelevant. For sports photographers, the blisteringly fast frame rate for still shots is competitive with some very expensive gear indeed. For videographers, video quality is excellent and isn't limited to the 4GB/12 minute shot limit that previous Canon cameras were stuck with; the half-hour recording time is more than enough to make sure you can get a long sequence all at once without having to worry as much about losing some of it between shots. And the autofocus function is one of the most sophisticated I've seen -- the touch screen enables insanely easy spot focus, and though I've not tried it myself, my understanding is that it does quite well with moving objects. Canon has also chosen to opt out of the megapixel wars once again; 20.2Mpx is only a modest upgrade from the 18 that was standard on their previous generation of APS image sensors, but you'll need to invest in some extremely expensive lenses in order to have a reason to care about the difference. (Incidentally, the new 18-55mm STM kit lens is sweet -- fast, silent, and straightforward. It is focus-by-wire, though, so if you're not a fan, get the body without a lens.)

It does have a few downsides, but I don't feel like they really affect the star rating. One is that the wifi function is absolutely byzantine -- you will definitely want to read the (separate) wifi manual, and at least in the initial firmware it lacks the web interface that the Wireless File Transfer modules for Canon's higher-end cameras have. (It also supports EyeFi cards, presumably because Canon already had the drivers in the OS build and didn't see a need to take them out.) Another is that I have yet to find an on-screen live audio monitor; Magic Lantern has traditionally provided this as a third-party addon, but they have yet to hack the 70D, so you may have to do some black magic with cables and headphones to get usable audio monitoring. (It also does not yet seem to be supported by gphoto, meaning that using it on a Linux system is likely to be exciting in all the wrong ways.)

So, on the whole, this isn't yet a hacker's camera, but for pretty much all regular purposes, it's damn close to perfect. It's pricier than the Rebel series, but if you've got the budget it's worth it.

title: As good as the positive reviews here, not as bad as the negatives..
text:
I am a huge subscriber to reviews before purchasing items. $5 items to $5000 items, doesn't matter. I do not like to buy twice, if I can avoid it. Let me say the positive reviews here were helpful, and mostly accurate (maybe a little hype in finish quality, will address again in a moment), all in all the positive reviews here, thankfully swayed my purchasing dollars this way, versus popping double or more for another brand/model. The negative reviews have a common thread to them, that I would like to offer my views on the matters. As well as share my experience thus far.

Common negatives in other reviews (that to me are easily remedied or are a bit over emphasized);
Upon opening the box;
1) Smelly rubber tire smell. Yes there is the familiar rubber smell of Asian (read PRC) manufactured goods. I believe it is the foam wraps on the two legs. It dissipates quickly. For comparison, I have some foam handled dumbbells that are 6 months old and still smell. So yes I was worried about this smell with the tripod, thankfully this smell dissipated within about 24 hours.
2) Loose screws. OK for many consumers this can be startling and if you are not use to checking your products for loose screws you may not even be aware of how many items you own with this problem. I found two loose screws in the leg tensioners. I found one OVER tightened screw in the base the pistol head mounts to on the center column. This base plate has three set screws coming from the bottom up, they are allen screws, one was driven clear trough the plate up and proud of the baseplate surface, thus not allowing the pistol grip spin fully into seat. Backed the set screw out a few turns to flush, mated the two plates and was in business. Later I returned to these three set screws and used them the proper way. Do not tighten the pistol grip base all the way to the center column base, rather, leave about a 1/32nd (1/2mm) gap between the two plates, then dial the set screws up to lock everything stable. This prevents your plates from becoming seized together. Back to the loose screw issue, look I buy racing motorcycles valued at many times more than ALL of my photo gear combined, it is a rule of thumb to inspect our bikes before putting them in use (for obvious safety reasons). Its just a fact of life, some things will get by quality control in the factory, even routinely so, the best quality control and safety measure you have is your own two eyes. Even car dealers have to inspect vehicles as they arrive from the factories. I inspect most everything I buy and if its a simple few loose screws I tighten them and go on about my day. No big deal. Especially when I know I did not buy the equivalent of a Mazzeratti here.
3) Wont fit in bag with the head mounted. This is the one that annoyed me! I WAS considering returning the tripod due to this 'problem'.. Well, glad I didn't jump the gun. I have the solution, and it is not pivoting the head (that actually didn't really work well). What I stumbled into was the feet, the rubber pivoting leveler feet can be dial up! duh! By dialing up the rubber feet you reveal the optional spikes. So I check out the spikes and get to thinking, geeze maybe? hmm? and YES the stand WITH head mounted now fits in the bag, snuggly but not bad at all. I have the spikes just barely revealed, no more than a 1/4 inch (6mm), from the rubber feet. Though don't forget to dial out your feet if you are on a wood or tile floor, otherwise the amount of spike I have revealed is harmless to carpet and beneficial outdoors. I bet that's the last time I adjust those feet. Try it, you'll be glad you did.
4) no cheapo mini tripod in box / no instructions in box; cheapo tripod? so what.. Instructions, found online, typical these days. Say that reminds me, thousands of dollars for Adobe Design software, instructions found where? Oh yes, online.. this is a non issue in this day and age. The real issue will arise when the entire inter web / cloud is taken out, certainly someday it will all fail or be hacked. But I digress, manuals online are the norm for many manufacturers.

My partial experience in use;
1) Standing on an icy road in 40 mph winds, 6D with 24mm L and 70-200 L, long exposure shots of 30 seconds or greater, I have zero movement, shots would reveal it if it were there. The stand is rock solid, if yours is not go back to checking tensioners all through out. They ARE adjustable. I did have to tighten the pistol grip movement, did not move while standing and shooting, but moved when I grabbed the stand, camera rig and all, hastily threw it over my shoulder and bounded to my next composition, then yes it pivoted, A LOT, like totally out of whack. I have since made less than 2 turns on the ball tensioner set screw and now I am solid.
2) thumb release clips at top of legs? figured they locked the legs outwards to prevent accidental closing, nope. They release the legs to pivot further out to the next incremented stop position. So theres ways to lower or change your angle of view, or accommodate weird terrain setups. The legs are not locked in the out position, they in fact do just fold right in. I can not see how you would accidentally fold in a leg while standing there doing your thing, you have to actually pick the leg up off the ground to fold it in. I personally like that I do not have to fuss with another lock just to stand up and fold in a leg, especially when I'm doing frequent moves.
3) the center column can be flipped upside down to get you a nice low position, perhaps useful for some macro work? Unscrew the bottom cap on the center column, pull the column up and out, flip and re-insert through the bottom. BAM now your plate is down low.

Hope some of what I share clears the air on some issues. I would say for the price, it is a fair valued tool. I did not expect more. I am more than happy with the functionality, and the build is plenty sturdy. The way I work, this stand will be put through the wringer, I am certain it will hold up a good long time.

title: Makes Using the iPad Better
text:
Right when I snapped this case on, I thought, "Wow, that actually fits pretty nice!" The back of the case is an ultra-hard plastic that locks on tightly, but does not overlap the front panel of the iPad---it's well made. The exterior is leather, and the inside is a soft microfiber that cushions the front glass when closed. The magnets in the case also turn the iPad on and off correctly, for those of you interested in that.

The case is pleasantly slim, and it's about all you need for protecting the iPad from scuffing while you're shoving it around on the counter-top or into a backpack. The sides have nicely sculpted cutouts to expose the external jacks and buttons (with no sharp edges, which is nice).

The front flap flips open to lie flat against the back, or you can tuck it into a tab on the back, which enables you to position it at one of two angles: the lower angle is nice for using the iPad in your lap, and the higher angle is good for sitting on a table.

I have to say, this case only provides moderate protection against drops. I dropped mine from chest height onto a hard floor with this case on it; it hit the floor on its corner, and it did suffer some slight damage, so this case is probably best thought of as just scuff-protection. I'm still okay with that, because anything bulkier would start to get in the way, and the damage that did occur was minor enough that I don't notice it.

It would be VERY cool if they could also add a strong magnet to the back tab to line up with the central magnet in the front flap: in that way, those magnets could snap together to hold the flap in the tab more securely. As it is now designed, the flap is only a press-fit, so I often find myself accidentally pulling the flap out of the tab when scooting it around in my lap, something the extra magnet might address. I've sort of learned to try to hold the case together when moving it around in that configuration, but the extra magnet would be a cool feature.

Overall, I'm very happy with this case---it's just right, and I think you'll like it as well.

title: Excellent Sailing Ship Simulator After 2 Years of Use
text:
These sounded great out of the box - warm, bass oriented sound, though basically accurate mids and treble. Excellent for electronic and metal, but held its own with any genres. Oddly, these phones always sounded much louder than their impedance and sensitivity numbers would suggest!

The cups were meant to be circumaural (fitting around ears) but my somewhat larger than average ears never fit inside the small ovals. Worked OK as supraaurals fitting on top of ear - comfy enough even for long term wearing, and isolated reasonably well. Could even be used on the subway.

However... build quality was not exactly exceptional. Lots of plastic and the pleather head wrap began to fray after one year of ownership leaving one end of the band exposed. The thin fixed in place dual connector wire never inspired much confidence, and now has become stringy, brittle, and braided, and cannot be replaced. These were babied and always transported in the excellent hard carrying case supplied; if I had not done this, the 400s would probably have broken and / or ended up in tatters.

Worst problem: the dual axis hinge design was cheaply made and has aged very poorly. After two years of ownership - the headset now sounds like the "Master & Commander" soundtrack is playing continuously when I wear them. I.E. massive groans and creaks from the band and cup forks every time I move my head. This makes the phones basically unusable unless you listen to music with constant loudness. Any peaky stuff with slow less loud moments allows the creaks to become very audible and distracting.

Though the price for a new set has fallen by about a third since I bought these, I would still hesitate to recommend these if you want headphones to last very long, or if you treat equipment roughly. The sound, though decent, was not exceptional, and something like the ATH M50 will sound as good or better than these, and the M50s are built like a tank and last forever. (I have a pair of M50s that are as old as the MS400s that are still problem free and which sound not at all like an Age of Sail documentary...) Unless you just like the color red, I would suggest choosing another audio option.

title: Not as good as I had hoped
text:
Out of about 12 DVD's that would not play, this unit fixed 5 of them.

The parts used to "strip a thin layer" actually left huge circular gouges in the disk. It made it much worse than they were.

It took 16 more passes with the buffering disks to get the scratches to a point where they were just slightly visible. The disks were ruined completely, never to be played again. The 'cleaning' parts are a joke as well.

Note that most disks (that ended up working) required me to take several passes (at 2 minute intervals each) to get to a playable state. Which is very annoying. Since you have to either sit there and watch it for 2 minutes, or remember to go back and hit the button again to start a new cycle every 2 minutes. At 5 minutes at least you could multitask and go do something else. But 2 minutes isn't long enough to do anything else, so you just have to sit and watch the thing spin.

Note also that after a few passes, the buffering disks will smooth out and if it's wet it will grab the disk as it spins and you can hear gears crunch when it does. So you must buy new buffering disks frequently because it doesn't take long for these to 'wear out' and for this to happen (even after sitting 24 hours to dry out). So be prepared to spend money (probably their plan).

My recommendation, go buy new DVDs at Amazon.com to replace the ones that won't play, DVD's are cheap now with BluRay being more popular. You will save headache, stress, time and hassle.

Now if you're a pro, like a pawn shop, with more than 20 DVD's to repair, then I highly recommend you invest in a quality DVD repair system. Don't buy this.

I ordered this product thinking it was back ordered until late February 2012. To my pleasant surprise, I received my shipping notification and tracking info well in advance, I got my order today, 1/23/12.

The case is sturdy and high quality leather (not much of a smell to it either which I consider a plus). It came packaged in a nice black box with protective wrapping. The case allows for easy insertion and removal of the TP tablet, and holds the dock in place without issue. It has a nice feature that allows you to unbutton the dock from the rest of the case, allowing you to just use the case as a cover/stand for the tablet. There are magnets which help keep the case closed and the screen protected. The inside of the case is a soft material that adds even more of a protective feeling. There are cutouts of all the ports on the dock and tablet, except I have some small issues with the spacing of these (more on that in a bit). Overall, the case is well designed and extremely professional looking.

While the product itself has more pros than cons, it did not get 5 stars from me for a few reasons, mainly regarding the cutouts for the camera. While the cover is spaced fine with the camera when just the tablet itself is inserted, the cutouts seem to be thrown off when the tablet is inserted to the dock (for both the front facing and back facing cameras) There also is no cutout for the speaker, but that seems to have little effect on the sound quality and volume. This all being said, the dock cutouts seem spot on ... even the straps in the top corners do not impede with the charging port, which is great.

One last "gripe" I have (and it may just be because I'm getting used to it) is the ease of actually docking the tablet when in the case. There seems to be a lot of resistance when trying to get it to dock, but that may be because the leather is still being broken in. On the flip side, undocking is pretty seamless and easy.

The final closed set up is a bit bulky, but that is to be expected for any set up like this. I measure it right around 1.5 inches thick when all closed up.

Overall, this case will probably be one of the best values to protect your TP. This, along with my carrying bag from Targus, should protect and help organize the tablet/dock for years. Seems to be great service from the company, I definitely recommend to buy.

title: Small and powerful, but lacking in software reliability
text:
This is my first NAS unit and I equipped it with two 3TB WD Red drives, the NAS is connected by CAT6 Ethernet directly to my Modem.

The Bad:

The NAS reboots every once in a while resulting in a long wait while streaming a movie to my Xbox360, also the main reason why i chose this over a comparable Synology is because this is capable of transcoding, I only wish I could completely turn transcoding off now but it seems to be impossible to completely disable.

When streaming to an AppleTV, you need to use an app (QAirplay) that you open in a browser of a computer or phone connected to the same network, then you browse for the media content you want to stream to your AppleTV and send it, so if you plan on using an AppleTV you should be prepared to not be able to browse directly from your TV like you can with other DLNA devices.

The phone apps are cool but it takes a long time to connect through myqnapcloud and if you get a call or use another window or app on iPhone and then return to the Qnap app you have to wait to re-connect, it should keep the connection active for at least 5 minutes

The QMusic App for iOS does not allow you to configure it so you can connect while you are away from home, you actually have to be on the same wifi subnet.

The NAS does not always show up in windows explorer, or the mapped network drive. While transferring large files, i had to run a 50 ft cat6 cable from my computer to the NAS because the connection would time out. I tried ssh and ftp to transfer the large files as instructed but only a direct connection and using file station would work.

The Good:

This does not skip a beat when sending 720p video wirelessly to my Xbox360, with 1080p it does skip once in a while but not frequently enough to discourage me from using it to watch 1080p video. Also if it does skip with 1080p, it only pauses for 3-5 seconds then resumes playback.

This comes with a full Twonky server license, this is in my experience the best way to get video to my Xbox360

Surprizingly, and probably to the disappointment of many who later buy sound bars/systems, many Samsungs/LGs around this size/price range do not have a digital out. That's idiotic even for low end systems.

Packaging was excellent. (Though if you have delivery concerns re: security/theft note it ships in a Vizio box - people are going to know it's a brand new flat screen. I arrived home to it just sitting in my common entranceway.)

Set-up is straightforward and super-fast. Remote is well-built but nothing special. Sound is suffcient for casual viewing, but for gaming or an immersive movie watching experiance you'll need to upgrade. (That's true of almost all internal TV speakers.) Sound maintains well at high volumes.

Black levels are quite good for such an inexpensive TV. Level of detail is great and I haven't noticed any artifacts, trails, etc. BUT, as other reviewers noted, there is a brightness issue with this unit - noticed it right away. Menu options are basic and, because there is no real backlight control, it doesn't seem changing settings would remedy the problem. I spent a couple of days going back and forth, trying to decide whether I should return this TV - it's just nowhere near as bright as the 46" Samsung LCD in my living room. But because we are using it in the bedroom, typically with the lights low or off, I've decided to keep it. title: Simply Amazing for the Price
text:
This lens is so great for me personally in almost all facets. I love macros, nature landscapes, and night time lapse photography. This lens is almost perfect for all of them.

Focus: The focus ring is buttery smooth which is great due to the manual nature of the lens. As someone who has only really used Auto lenses (other than the ridiculously wide rokinon 8mm) this lens is a little tough to get used to when trying to get quick shots in the move. It's ok though most of the time due to the focal length.

Focus Distance: This camera says it's minimum focus distance is around .5 feet but it's feels MUCH closer. I can literally touch objects with the lens good and still get sharp, focused photos. I use this now as a macro lens over my 70-200!!

Sharpness: This lens is frighteningly sharp at F/4 - F/8. Even wide open at F/2 there is tons of detail. As I previously said I use this as a macro type lens occasionally an it is TACK sharp. Even today at the Monterey Aquarium I could see the pores on a fishes scales at f/2 ISO 800 1/40. I have never seen a sharper wide angle.

Build: Very sturdy and comparable to my friend's Canon 17-35 L lens. Beautiful and heavy as well. I feel like this could survive a drop or two.

Price: For the price this lens cannot e beat. Only $340 for this sharpness is a steal!
Other Stuff: CA is a little bit of an issue but easily corrected in Lightroom or Photoshop. Very little distortion except when very close to things like bricks. Of course great lowlight performance due to the F/2.

For who: Mainly landscape photographers who can take their time with composition. This really can take some lovely macros that have a lot of background in them too. Overall this lens is a little more for intermediates rather than beginners.

Overall: Unbeatable for the price if you can get past the full Manuel nature which really doesn't take much practice.

title: Best I've Used So Far
text:
With over six months of 7x24 continuous use, this device is precisely what I had been looking for in a home/residential based networking environment. I've worked as a network engineer for over 20 years and have procured/provisioned/config'd and tested most of the major enterprise router brands (Cisco, Wellfleet, HP etc etc). Having owned/used Netgear/Linksys/Cisco home-based routers over a period of many years, I wasn't prepared for the huge amount of functionality available in this device. The capabilites of this router are clearly over the top. They are too numerous to mention in this review but rest assured, if you need to provision this router for some unique capability in your home net, this router will almost certainly be able to comply.

Setup can be as simple (or complex/detailed) as you need it to be. The menu system is quite intuitive and has a logical look and feel. I really like the category tabs and the manner in which they appear. THey provide quick access links to virtually any area of the routers feature set you wish to navigate. Each major area of the setup choices includes a brief narrative (technical but also user-friendly) detailing what it is you'll be setting up.

A couple of the features which prompted me to choose this router over the others are QOS, Guest Network, Real-time mapping and monitoring, robust port forwarding (to allow user-defined and well-known ports access to my Synology NAS's from the internet), robust firewalling, VPN and the built-in networking tool set. Several other routers I considered had some of these features available but none had all the features. Haven't had the need to use it yet but this box contains DLNA/UPNP server functionality which is a major plus for some (can also function as an i-tunes server). There are many other features available and the routers OS so far has been extremely responsive and rock solid!!!

Of course all the features and configurable parameters in the world aren't worth anything if the base performance of the router is not top notch and consistent. I can say that this router performs better and more consistently than any of the others I have used in a home networking setting. I have conducted HD video/audio thruput tests using multiple wifi and ethernet attached clients simultaneously. The results have been extraordinary. Four hd video streams and several audio streams all running concurrently have not resulted in any stuttering/bufferring or any degradation in playback quality or performance. I use a 100mb/sec internet uplink and have been able to supply multiple concurrent users hi-speed access to streaming audio and video without any speed related issues.

I have not had any WIFI range or performance related issues with this router. I have had wifi issues with other routers in the past, particularly loss of wifi range over time. I especially like the external antennas on this box. I have found range on both bands to be consistently better than any other router I have used. Read the instructions, tells you how to properly align the antenna masts for the best thruput and range. Don't expect range on the 'N' band to be on par with the 'G' band - they are not equivalent on any residential router that I know of. Thruput on the 802.11N band is phenomenal, just plan on locating your 'N' devices as close to the router as is possible for the best signal quality.

I have read a few reviews which claim data performance/thruput degradation (primarily on the wifi) over a period of time. This can be caused by a number of factors and does not necessarily point to the router as the at-fault device. I am always a bit suspicious of such claims made without the addition of hard evidence, particularly when the reviewer fails to mention any statistical data such as the state of their network backbone. One can readily acquire such data thru the use of a software based backbone analyzer. Several are available as try-before-you-buy products and are fully functional and some even continue to work even after the trial period. I mention these because I encountered just such a situation which caused a huge performance drop in my own network after performing a firmware update on one of my printers. On conducting a network monitoring test using one of these tools, I discovered the printer was sending out snmp broadcasts as fast as the ethernet card in the device could send them. Disable the SNMP engine in the printer - Problem Solved. There are many other factors that can cause network performance issues that are not necessarily related to the router. My own personal experience with this router has shown it to be a thruput king. It continues to provide excellent thruput without the need for periodic resets (many of the residential routers on the market these days seem to have performance issues requiring a periodic reset). This could be related to insufficient on-board ram, route and other caches that load up with data and need to be reset etc etc. I have experienced no such problem with this router.

Bottom line: highly recommended, particularly if you need the "over the top" feature set incorporated in this device. Would I buy again? Without Hesitation....

title: Does what it's supposed to and does it very well!
text:
Short version: We love it! Buy it!

Long version: The sound is amazing, the subwoofer is deep, the dynamic range is outstanding. And it's a beautiful piece of equipment! What's not to love?

I'll tell you.

We bought a Samsung UN55D8000 3D HDTV at the same time, and fully expected the two to talk to each other. They do. They argue.

The most egregious example of this was when I pointed our Logitech Harmony One universal remote at the system and press "Watch TV". It's configured to turn everything on (which it does) and the satellite picture and sound came up beautifully... for 10 seconds. Then the input changed! All by itself! It would take 4 steps of going through various menus just to get our satellite back on the TV!

After a Samsung technician came out and spent an hour and a half troubleshooting it, we finally found the culprit: a feature called Anynet+ was enabled and for some reason, the Home Theater was changing inputs. Anynet+ is a bell/whistle that really doesn't need to be there... especially if you have a universal remote. What it does is control the home theater's volume and power from the TV remote. Since we use a universal remote, it's entirely unnecessary and causes more problems than it fixes. I'm telling you: if you buy a Samsung Smart TV, a Samsung Smart Home Theater, and a universal remote, the first thing you'll want to do is disable Anynet+ in the settings. Trust me.

Like any Blu-Ray player, it's going to take a minute or so for the disc to load and start playing. Well worth the wait: the image is crystal clear and the touch controls on the front panel are responsive. If you CHOOSE to connect this player to your home wifi network, make sure your network is 802.11n speed. I choose not to connect the player to my home network unless I'm checking for - and downloading - software updates. Which yours will likely need out of the box (though I don't see much difference).

At any rate, I'll summarize this novel by saying that the HT-D6500W is phenomenal hardware and it looks good doing what it does. Just disable Anynet+ and you should be fine.

EDIT: One of the great features of this receiver I forgot to mention is calibration mode. It comes with a small microphone that you plug into the ASC jack on the flip-down front panel, and position in the middle of the room. Each discrete speaker then emits a test tone (at significant volume!) and balances out the speakers for the acoustics of YOUR room. Awesome! Just make sure you do this when the house is completely silent and all speakers are placed where they're going to stay. I've now had this equipment for a couple of months and we absolutely love it!

title: Major Video Issues - Otherwise Good Camera
text:
4-stars for camera design and still image quality, 1 star for video.

I have tested and compared images, video, features, and usability for all the top ultra-zoom compacts including Fuji F770EXR/F750EXR, Canon SX260HS, Sony HX9V, Panasonic ZS-15 and ZS-19/20. This was the last camera I compared and I was expecting to really like it as Image Quality is my first priority criteria, followed by video, then features/usability. Here's my main takeaways:

- Well lit, ISO 100-200 shots: Fuji gets 3rd place. Canon SX260HS has best detail with least noise. Panasonic ZS-15/19/20 are next best with slightly better detail than Fuji with a tiny more noise. Sony ties for 3rd with Fuji with slightly less detail and noise (Sony has the most agressive noise reduction of the 4 so there is a little bit more detail smearing.)

- Fuji is almost unusable for video. When you pan the camera the video stutters. Even worse, when you zoom, camera has MAJOR problems focusing to the point the camera will not focus properly at all most of the time beyond 7X zoom. The lens motor is also the most audible out of all the 4 cameras. Panasonics you can barely hear the lens. Sony wins with Panasonics coming in a close second.

- Low-light / High ISO: Fuji comes in second. Sony wins. Panasonics come in third - images are unusable beyond ISO 800, too much yellow color splotching all over. At ISO 400, it is practically a tie between Panasonic, Fuji, and Sony. At crazy ISO 1600 and up, Fuji wins with usable images (barely) followed by Sony but you really can't expect much from these small cameras with small sensors at those kind of ISOs.

- Flash: Fuji comes in third. Very strange flash that only pops up manually (which has its benefits). You must press tiny button on side of camera really hard. Flash is not motorized and it looks like a part of the camera that could easily break in the future. Flash is underpowered compared to the other cameras.

- Design/Usability/Software - Fuji is heaviest of the 4 cameras but has a nice rubberized feeling body finish. Panasonic is amazingly small. Sony in-between. All of them have different styles of software. Panasonic has best set of software features. Sony very limited in scene modes. Fuji has nice software but many of the options are locked out when in any mode other than manual. Panasonic's wins as far as the Intelligent Auto function. Very reliable. Canon had troubles focusing sometimes.

Overall, Panasonic wins. Fuji would be a close second, tied with Sony if the video wasn't so terrible. Search YouTube for videos including this example:

<...> (and this is probably one of the better ones where the person went very easy on the camera panning very slowly and zooming slowly without panning)

title: Worth the price
text:
I've had a number of different Sony Handycams over the past two decades. My first one was a then-top-of-the-line analog camera and cost about $1300 back when that was real money. When the digital models first came out, they were in a similar price range and I figured that something with better resolution than the former NTSC standard should be the final word. But TVs got bigger and standards got better so it was time for something new.

This time around I didn't start off with the top of the line but went through a series of cheaper HD cameras until the price dropped. With this model, the price was well in line with what I was hoping to get for the money, and even if I add the prices of all those interim cameras, I still ended up spending less than I would have had I gotten an HD camcorder when Sony came out with them.

So how does this one measure up? In general, very favorably. The picture quality is remarkably good. 1080p doesn't mean that you get the same quality as every other 1080p camera. This one is better than most. And 1080i gives you only half the lines every other frame. So a lot of competing cameras that seem "almost as good" aren't giving a lot of people what they think they are getting. Even at the highest resolution setting with this camera, you can still get three hours of recording easily using the internal memory and a modest 32GB card. And hard disks are cheap so I can't think of a reason to use lower quality.

The features work. High end cameras have long had modes for landscapes, sports, backlit subjects, and hosts of other situations. This one has many more. But for practical purposes, the camera does a good enough job using face tracking and other features to get the exposure and focus right even without needing special settings or adjusting things such as when there's a bright window behind the subject. In almost all cases, I'm able to leave the settings alone and just shoot.

Menus are easy to navigate, the instruction manual is relatively clear (but make sure that the sections you are reading are for this model, and skip over parts with footnotes saying features are for other models only)and the camera is easy to use. Most more advanced functions, such as smile detection, work fine. But other advanced functions such as GPS could have used a few more options. If I drive into a tunnel, my car's GPS still has a good idea where I am. I know a camera can't be equally precise, but this GPS either works or it doesn't. A "use last known location" option would have meant I'd likely be able to tell whether an indoor photo was from Peru or New Jersey. And after many decades you are more likely to forget these sorts of things than you might think.

Compared to high end cameras of the past, some features are noticeably missing. Those include a large array of special effects and on camera editing that appeared with early digital video cameras. With this one, you don't get much more advanced than being able to fade in or out. On the other hand, few of those features are needed if you have any video editing software on your PC or Mac. Another feature that's noticeably absent from all but the highest end cameras these days is a viewfinder. Using this and many other cameras outdoors can be quite difficult and can amount to guesswork when it comes to knowing what you are recording. But setting the brightness of the display to the highest level makes things usable even with the sun directly to your back. Still, the lack of any shield makes it less optimal than using a viewfinder, and rotating the display so the subject can see it means not being able to take the video from behind. Also, reliance on the touch screen for all settings is a good compromise since it allows the button free camera to be much smaller. But it also means that pressing a single button to turn the fader on or adjust the brightness is almost out of the question. While you can set one custom soft key for one commonly used function, you'd need to go through a series of menus to make many other changes that formerly took a press of a button and are now virtually impossible to do while recording.

Another feature missing compared to cameras in the past is zero lux shooting. This one goes down to 3 lux and does a credible job, but with an expected lowering of resolution.

For photos, light is also important. 8.9 MP is not bad resolution, and beats out still cameras I've used in the past. Couple that with 30x optical zoom and it should seem as if I could leave a lower resolution still camera at home. But that would be a mistake. Without at least a rudimentary flash, using this for indoor photos can be like using an Instamatic without a flash cube.

Physical buttons are limited to a sparse but necessary half dozen, but with auto power on, and on-screen buttons for record and zoom, only three are absolutely essential. For practical purposes you will probably want to use the physical record and zoom buttons, but this layout makes the camera easy to use for both right and left handed users. Connectors are limited to a built in USB cable, and HDMI, microphone, power, AV and USB jacks. The USB cable might be all you need if you do video editing (and perhaps disc creation) on your PC and can even charge your camera, but an HDMI cable will make it easy to view things on a TV instantly. And with a Sony TV you won't even need to set the input source or turn on the TV. The AV jack will work for TVs that lack HDMI.

Overall, the quality of the images is excellent. The 30x optical zoom allows you to retain image quality over a large range, and focusing on something close, such as a piece of paper, will not only let you see crisp individual letters but can let you see the fibers of the paper itself. As long as there is sufficient light, the picture quality is top notch. With lower light it might not have the full sharpness, but its ability to adapt to low light situations is excellent. Videos won't look dark or improperly exposed even in moderate light.

Although there are a handful of things I'd like to see (and major ones such as a viewfinder) my biggest concern is with video quality. Those features that are lacking could not be expected in a camera at this price range so I can't fault the camera just because Sony failed to make a more expensive mid-line model. And the video quality is what I would have expected only in a top end model just a few years ago. So although the camera is not ideal, it gives far more for the price than I would have hoped for a few years ago and enough for the price that I don't need to look at higher end models. For the third time in my life I can say that this is the last video camera I will ever need.

title: An honest review from a month-long owner of these headphones
text:
I'm normally much more detailed with my reviews, but I'm going to keep this short and honest. I ordered these almost exactly a month ago. The sound hasn't been bad at all considering the price, and I am not a person who abuses his headphones, so these have not been tossed around or neglected. Today the left ear went out on me, which tells me all I need to know about the quality of this product. I saw some questionable reviews before I had purchased, but I figured I would try these out for myself. I've learned my lesson, and now I want to help you save your money by politely recommending that you invest in some better headphones than these. I hope sharing my experience helps!

Also, just as a side note, before purchasing these headphones I found a lot of reviews of this product questionable, saying that it is the best headphone they've ever purchased. I still decided to go through with trying these out, and in all honesty, these are average/mediocre headphones. I can say with confidence that if these are the best earbuds anyone has ever bought, then this must be the first pair of earbuds they've ever owned. It's just a bit sketchy is all so beware.

UPDATE:
I wrote my original review a couple of weeks ago and just wanted to provide a quick update. I had failed to mention that because of the deal I found on these headphones at the time of purchase, I decided to get two pairs in case I really liked them, or in the event that one didn't last. Since the first pair lasted just under a month, I've moved on to the second pair, and a couple of weeks in I can tell the same issue is starting to happen, with one of the sides crackling (music not played at maximum volume), and sometimes cutting out completely. I just wanted to reiterate my original review and advise against purchasing this product. It's worth putting the few extra bucks toward a better quality pair.

Also, I noticed that nearly immediately after my review was posted, that the first person to see my review marked it as unhelpful. I found it extremely odd considering I gave an honest and unbiased review of my experience with the product. It's almost as if the seller might be monitoring the reviews or something to that affect. In any case I'm not going to make a big deal of it, but this just added to the "sketchy" nature of the past reviewers saying these were the greatest ear buds ever. Again, I hope my experience having owned two pairs of these helps, but if you still decide to gamble on these I hope they last longer for you than they did for me. Going to reach out to the company regarding their limited warranty to see if I can't get a refund.

SECOND UPDATE:
I reached out to customer support and told them about my experience with the first pair of headphones. They sent me a new pair without hesitation. I can appreciate that they replaced the item for me, and the headphones have been working fine to this point. With that said I've added a third star to my rating. Perhaps my experience was a fluke, but I will write another update if I run into any issues with my new pair.

title: [D80] Not for all situations, but capable of producing really great pictures.
text:
I have a Nikon D80 and am not a professional. The lens and autofocus works fine with the D80, perhaps a little noisy. At first I wasn't crazy about this lens, but after spending some time with it, I like it. Many of the other reviewers are correct about light - this lens NEEDS it. So if you're expecting to shoot inside or in bad light and get good images, this probably isn't the lens for you- this will be a great outdoor lens with telephoto that is effectively 450mm in my camera because it doesn't have a full-frame sensor. If used correctly will produce great images.

At 300mm the image is not razor pro sharp but still usable, even at f/5.6 - perhaps not as crisp as the more expensive lenses, but still usable for probably anything short of getting it printed in large format.

A couple things I've noticed that have helped to get great images from this lens:
- Using it outside in bright daylight and between the focal lengths of about 100mm to 200mm and an f/8 - f/11, this lens will produce beautifully crisp images. Outside of these settings the image is still pretty good - just sometimes leaves you with that "it could be a little more sharp" thought if you zoom in while viewing photos you've taken.
- If handheld, use as high a shutter speed as you can to reduce camera shake. Remember the rule of no shutter speeds less than the inverse of your focal length (300mm = 1/300th is the slowest you should go). Since my D80 has the cropped sensor, I usually bump up the shutter even a little more, for 300mm I'll use 1/400 or 1/500 if my goal for that shot is to get super sharpness.

Don't expect to shoot any dimly lit wedding receptions without flash, but for outdoor adventures, photographing your kid playing soccer, etc. - it's got a good zoom for when you really want it, pretty decent image quality, and best of all, it's a lens you won't be afraid to take outside and risk losing thousands of dollars if it gets damaged.

title: Nice picture, quiet when on Eco.
text:
This is a nice little projector for the money. When you are running it on Eco mode, it is nice and quiet. The picture is absolutely GORGEOUS, and it works well even when your windows aren't blacked out in your bedroom-converted-to-a-movie-room and you just HAVE to watch Star Trek: Into Darkness because you finally got your projector up. Plenty of options for fine-tuning your picture and lining up your projector. Excellent keystone tuning.
Couple of negatives, though. The auto-iris is noisy (the clicking noise drove me so nuts we shut it off) and the fan can be as noisy as any other off the Eco setting. The lamp went out after five days, and we had to get another. It took a bit to get since the first customer service person just left it go when they saw replacement lamps on backorder and didn't even let us know. However, the second person we spoke to (when we called to find out why we hadn't received the lamp in 3-5 days as promised) went the extra mile and pulled a lamp from production stock - staying late to make sure he got it and to give us a call back confirming its shipment.

Overall, this is a fabulous unit in its own right, not just despite its price. I recommend if you want a great picture without forking over four figures for a projector, but don't want to spend hundreds on a piece of junk. We're pretty picky about picture quality and this unit definitely delivers.

title: Forget spontaneous photos if you use this with the holster.
text: We returned our OtterBox Defenders immediately.  While they certainly would protect the Samsung Galaxy S4 from earthquakes, gunfire from terrorist insurgencies, and phone throwing toddlers, they were unsuitable for our purposes. First, it is a struggle to put the case and holster on the phone.  Then, when you want to remove the case and/or holster, it is an even greater struggle - very difficult. It is not like other products, where the encased phone simply slips in and out of the holster.  You must unclip the whole thing and then futz with it to take the holster off.  The biggest problem is that the holster blocks the main camera.  Therefore, if you want to take a photo with the main camera, you must remove it from the holster.  But the removal is not a simple, spontaneous move.  You cannot take spontaneous photos if you are using the hoster.  Finally, the scant directions that come with the case are insufficient. If there is some trick to taking the case off without inadvertently damaging it, there should be better instructions.  If there is no trick, but this is the way the case is designed, it is a bad design. I will go back to the drawing board to find a case that protects my phone but gives me the flexibility to use my phone.

title: Can be Carried and Stowed on Regional Jets
text:
I already have the Think Tank Airport Security, and it's an excellent product, other than when full of camera gear, mine practically takes three men and a strong boy to heft it. In preparing for a trip to South Africa to photograph wildlife, I determined to downsize my equipment list to what could be taken on-board regional jets, on which we were to fly for parts of our trip, both here and in Africa. So, I really appreciated Amazon's format allowing me to ask this question of users of this product and was pleased to receive a positive affirmative answer.

And that's the way it is. This bag - loaded with two Nikon D-3s bodies, an 80-400mm zoom, a 17-35mm zoom, a 24-120mm zoom, a 1.4 teleconverter and an SB 800 strobe still weighed in at 23 lbs. and easily fit in the overhead of every plane we traveled on. Plus, it's sufficiently well made and padded that if it did have to be gate checked, it would be okay. But it doesn't. In addition to its compact size, I appreciate this bag's inclusion of a locking cable by which the bag can be secured to a bench or other large item. I never would go away and leave my carryon luggage unattended, but even sitting next to it, it's nice to know that there really is no way somebody could snatch and run when you are not paying especially close attention.

Yes, wheels would be nice, but that would also require some sort of retractable handle, and suddenly you'd be shut out of carrying the Airport Essentials on small airplanes.

title: Best gaming monitor yet
text:
Pros:
+ This is the first monitor to combine 2560 x 1440 resolution with 144hz, G-SYNC, and Ultra Low Motion Blur (ULMB). I have tried all these features (GTX 680 as the graphics card) and they work as advertised and with no hassle except as noted in 'Other thoughts' below.
+ Very smooth motion. The effect of higher refresh rate is significant even on the desktop. Even mouse pointer movement is smoother and more responsive compared to 60hz.
+ The monitor is thin, reasonably light, and the stand is very adjustable.
+ The on-screen display is easy to use via the little joystick on the back.

Cons:
- My brother and I both got panels with minor defects. There are no dead or stuck pixels, but my panel has two spots that look like small bits of dust that can't be wiped away. My brother's panel has a small dark spot near one corner, as though there is dust on the backlight. These don't really get noticed in normal use, but for $800 it should have been flawless.
- It uses a TN panel, with all the viewing angle issues that come with it. For example, the bottom of the panel appears slightly brighter than the top.
- Much like the older Asus VG248QE, the screen comes from the factory using overly bright settings which make it look a little washed out. If you like, you can correct this with a color profile or by lowering the gamma in your AMD/Nvidia control panel. The on-screen controls do little to affect it.

Other Thoughts:
* G-SYNC only works with full-screen games. G-SYNC will not function with windowed games or games in windowed-full-screen mode.
* G-SYNC and ULMB can't both be used at the same time.
* ULMB can't be enabled at 144hz refresh rate, only 120hz and below.
* I find the image quality to be much more tolerable with the brightness reduced from 80 to 54 in the on-screen display, and the gamma set to 0.6-0.7 for all color channels in the Nvidia Control Panel.

title: AM2+
text:
This motherboard is a little bit mislabeled. It does support AM3 processors. However this board uses DDR2 memory and although AM3 processors can step down to that, they natively run on DDR3, which this doesn't support. However, since it does use DDR2 it is also compatible with the older AM2 (up to DDR2 800mhz)and AM2+ (up to DDR2 1066mhz) processors. This was what I was looking for since I had a motherboard failure, but the Phenom 1 (AM2+) processor that was on my old board was still good.

I use this for a multimedia PC. It has 7.1 audio and an option to plug in digital audio (SPDIF). Although I use a separate card, the on board video does support digital cable and Blu-Ray playback and has HDMI out.

I haven't owned it long enough to speak to reliability. My past experience with MSI has been the products work well, while they work, but seem have a shorter overall life span than most of the other brands I use. For example, although the one this replaced was not MSI, the one it replaced was a few years older than a different MSI board (in another machine) I replaced several months ago. That board, (supposedly military grade) seemed to have a substancially shorter lifespan than my other boards. I decided to give them one more try with this, hoping for better results.

title: Great assistive technology, wallet part could be thinner
text:
If you need to get out of the house in a hurry and find your keys or wallet, you'll be happy you have one of these. As an absent-minded professor, I find this product very helpful. E.g., when I take my wallet out of my purse to order something online and leave it on my extremely messy desk and forget it's there, I just press the "2" on the key fob, and I can find my wallet. I use the wallet to find my keys more often, so the fact that it can work either way is really useful. I have a colleague who works with clients who have mild TBI (traumatic brain injury) or ADD (attention deficit disorder, or as I like to call it, "atypical attentional style"), and she says her clients find this product very helpful also.

Minor limitations that don't bother me much: It isn't strong enough to work between floors of the house, so if I'm downstairs and my wallet (or key ring) is upstairs, the signal isn't strong enough to cause the beep. If I'm on the stairs or on the same floor, though, it works fine. So, just keep moving around the house, pressing the button, and you can find what you're looking for. I haven't had a chance to try it outside yet. It has helped when I lose wallet or keys in my car.

Design suggestion for the manufacturer: Because the wallet unit is much thicker than a credit card, it can fall out of a wallet fairly easily. Maybe a velcro strip on the back of the wallet unit where the other part of the velcro strip could be glued into the wallet would help it stay put. Or, if it's possible to make the wallet part thinner so that it really would fit in a credit card slot in a wallet, that would make it a better product.

I have bought two of these, because the wallet unit fell out of my wallet somewhere and I never found the unit. Obviously, I think this is a good enough product that I was happy to just buy another one. My new wallet unit is currently super-glued into its wallet compartment, and so far, has stayed put, two months later.

In spite of these limitations, I do recommend this. It's really been a time-saver.

title: Nice system - some assembly required
text:
After having thefts occur at numerous area farms, we were looking for a basic security recording system to help monitor our family's farm property. The Swann SWDVK-425554-US D1 Security Recording Kit certainly fits the bill. It has many positive features that we were looking for in a security system. Foremost, we don't want to have to "mess around" with it often. Thus, the "set & forget" continuous 4-channel recording for up to 15 days+ is a positive. Since we are monitoring outdoors, however, the motion detector feature is not really practical. Wind, horses, birds, etc. will all set it off, and there's (to me) always the fear of missing something.

We are still working through the set-up on this, actually. We have to locate power to where we want to mount the base unit while still having plenty of distance to mount the cameras. Since each camera comes with a long cable, that should not be an issue based on our planning. However, we also want to make sure the base unit is also secure. What good is a security system if it can be stolen, as well? As such, we are considering building a lockable box. It won't be like putting it in an anchored/fireproof safe, but if we build a large box we can put a monitor in, as well, then close it up to protect from dust and moisture. Keeping that in mind, you WILL need a display for this, in some capacity. It does support VGA, so an older monitor should suffice.

If you desire to use the Internet-based "live viewing", keep in mind you'll also need an internet connection. I've not gotten to the point of trying to configure this yet, as we do not have a network drop in our shop. As such, I'm hopeful I can use a wireless adapter. I just need time to work through it. It's a nice feature, but is likely to require some thought and configuration before I can use it. But it would be a VERY helpful feature to me for checking on the property and horses when travelling.

So all this said, there are several things you should consider regarding this system. It is NOT just "plug and play":
- You will need to plan the location of your cameras to record as many areas (or zones) as possible
- You will need to carefully plan the location of the base unit to ensure your cameras all reach, as they are NOT wireless
- You will need to install the cameras and run the wiring to the base unit. If you have an attic (vs. open rafters) this will be more difficult
- You will need to ensure there is sufficient power at the location of your base unit
- You will need to acquire a display for your unit, such as a computer monitor
- You should plan to use a UPS device to protect the base from power surges while also recording during power outages.
- You may wish to acquire an external hard drive for saving/transferring video for backup (to keep data for a longer period)

Overall, this is a very nice unit and appears to be of good quality workmanship. As noted, it has many great features which will be helpful in keeping our farm secure. It is NOT an alarm system, but would actually be more helpful in catching a criminal who has made an attempt to steal something and has gotten away (it's hard to put an alarm on a gate). Just be aware of what you are getting, what you will need to provide, and what you will need to consider to set it up and you will find this to be a nice system.
